subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: Mr. Ramesh, aged 42 years, a daily drinker for 15 years, is admitted on the second day after stopping alcohol with tremors, sweating, sleeplessness and anxiety. He is diagnosed with alcohol dependence syndrome. (a) Define the terms substance use, harmful use, dependence, tolerance and withdrawal. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features of alcohol withdrawal and the complications of chronic alcohol use. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management, including detoxification and relapse prevention, and the nursing care of Mr. Ramesh. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Time course of alcohol withdrawal
labels: tachycardia – 12–48 hours: withdrawal seizures and alcoholic hallucinosis – 48–72 hours (up to 5 days): delirium tremens with confusion

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (3 marks)

  • Substance use – taking a psychoactive substance (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, opioids and others) for its effect on mood, perception or consciousness.
  • Harmful use (abuse) – a pattern of use that is already causing damage to physical or mental health (for example, liver disease, depressive episodes) or social harm, without dependence.
  • Dependence – a cluster of physiological, behavioural and cognitive phenomena in which the use of the substance takes a much higher priority than other behaviours that once had greater value. ICD-10 features (three or more in a year): strong desire (craving), difficulty in controlling use, withdrawal state, tolerance, neglect of other interests, and continued use despite clear evidence of harm.
  • Tolerance – the need for increasing amounts of the substance to achieve the same effect, or a reduced effect with the same amount.
  • Withdrawal – a group of physical and psychological symptoms that occur when the substance is stopped or reduced after prolonged heavy use, usually opposite to the effects of the drug, and relieved by taking the substance again.

(b) Alcohol withdrawal and complications of chronic alcohol use (5 marks)

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (begins 6–24 hours after the last drink, as in Mr. Ramesh)

  1. Simple (uncomplicated) withdrawal – 6–24 hours – coarse tremors of hands, sweating, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, raised BP, craving.
  2. Withdrawal seizures – 12–48 hours – generalised tonic–clonic fits.
  3. Alcoholic hallucinosis – 12–48 hours – mainly auditory hallucinations with a clear sensorium.
  4. Delirium tremens (DTs) – 48–72 hours (up to 5 days) – a medical emergency: clouding of consciousness, disorientation, vivid visual hallucinations (insects, animals), severe tremors, fever, sweating, tachycardia, BP fluctuations, dehydration; can be fatal.

Complications of chronic alcohol use

  • Gastrointestinal – gastritis, peptic ulcer, fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, oesophageal varices, acute and chronic pancreatitis.
  • Nervous system – Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia due to thiamine deficiency), Korsakoff's psychosis (amnesia with confabulation), peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar degeneration, dementia.
  • Cardiovascular – hypertension, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias.
  • Nutritional – malnutrition, vitamin B deficiencies, anaemia.
  • Psychiatric – depression, anxiety, suicide, alcoholic jealousy (delusional), other substance use.
  • Social and legal – family disharmony, domestic violence, financial loss, absenteeism, road accidents, crime.
  • In pregnancy – fetal alcohol spectrum disorder.

(c) Management and nursing care of Mr. Ramesh (7 marks)

1. Detoxification (management of withdrawal)

  • Assess withdrawal severity with the CIWA-Ar scale (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) every few hours.
  • Benzodiazepines – chlordiazepoxide (or diazepam) in adequate doses, tapered over 7–10 days; lorazepam in the elderly and in liver disease.
  • Thiamine (vitamin B1) – given before any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy; high-dose parenteral thiamine in those at risk; other B-complex vitamins and nutrition.
  • IV fluids and correction of electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); anticonvulsants if seizures occur; treatment of medical complications.

2. Relapse prevention (after detoxification)

  • Drugs – disulfiram (aversive; causes an unpleasant reaction with alcohol), naltrexone (reduces craving and the "high"), acamprosate (reduces craving), baclofen or topiramate, as prescribed.
  • Psychosocial interventions – motivational enhancement therapy, cognitive behaviour therapy (identifying high-risk situations, coping and refusal skills), relapse prevention counselling, family therapy, couples therapy.
  • Self-help groups – Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) for the patient, Al-Anon for family members.
  • Treatment of co-existing depression or anxiety; occupational rehabilitation; regular follow-up at a de-addiction centre.

Nursing care of Mr. Ramesh

During withdrawal (detoxification phase)

  1. Monitoring – vital signs (pulse, BP, temperature) and CIWA-Ar score 2–4 hourly; level of consciousness and orientation; signs of impending delirium tremens (confusion, hallucinations, fever) or seizures.
  2. Safety – a quiet, well-lit room (dim light increases misinterpretation and hallucinations), bed with side rails, seizure precautions, supervision; remove harmful objects; avoid restraint unless absolutely necessary and as per MHCA 2017.
  3. Medication – give benzodiazepines as prescribed, observe for over-sedation and respiratory depression; give thiamine before glucose.
  4. Fluids and nutrition – encourage oral fluids, record intake and output; high-calorie, high-protein, vitamin-rich diet in small frequent meals.
  5. Reassurance and orientation – explain that the symptoms are part of withdrawal and will settle; orient to time, place and person; consistent staff.
  6. Sleep – a calm environment, reduced stimuli, relaxation.

After detoxification (rehabilitation phase)

  1. Therapeutic relationship – non-judgemental, empathetic, firm and consistent; accept the person, not the drinking.
  2. Deal with denial and rationalisation – help him see the link between drinking and his problems; support motivation using motivational interviewing.
  3. Health education – effects of alcohol on the body and family; medication (for example, never drink alcohol while on disulfiram, avoid hidden alcohol); healthy coping with stress; planning for high-risk situations.
  4. Involve the family – educate about the illness, encourage support without nagging or enabling, refer to Al-Anon; address domestic violence if present.
  5. Occupational and recreational therapy, building a daily routine, return to work.
  6. Follow-up – regular visits, early recognition of relapse warning signs (craving, contact with drinking friends, missed appointments); relapse is treated as a learning step, not a failure.

Investigations – blood alcohol level and breath analyser (if recent drinking), complete blood count (raised MCV), liver function tests (raised GGT, AST more than ALT), blood sugar, serum electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate, renal function, ECG; ultrasound abdomen; screening tools such as AUDIT and CAGE.

Common nursing diagnoses for Mr. Ramesh | Nursing diagnosis | Expected outcome | |---|---| | Risk for injury related to withdrawal seizures and delirium | Passes through withdrawal without injury or complications | | Disturbed sleep pattern and anxiety related to withdrawal | Sleeps 6–7 hours; reports reduced anxiety | | Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements | Eats a balanced diet; weight stable; vitamins replaced | | Ineffective denial related to minimising the drinking problem | Acknowledges the effect of alcohol on his life and accepts treatment | | Interrupted family processes | Family takes part in sessions and learns supportive behaviour |

Services available – de-addiction centres in medical colleges and district hospitals, Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts run with the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, and community awareness under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan.

Prevention of alcohol-related problems

  • Primary prevention – public awareness about the harms of alcohol, life-skills education in schools and colleges, restricting availability and sale to minors, higher taxes, strict enforcement of drink-driving laws, and healthy recreation in the community.
  • Secondary prevention – screening of patients in general wards, OPDs and primary care with AUDIT or CAGE and brief intervention for risky drinkers, before dependence develops.
  • Tertiary prevention – treatment, rehabilitation and self-help groups for people with dependence, to prevent relapse and complications.

Nursing importance Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which are life-threatening. Skilled monitoring with CIWA-Ar, safe use of benzodiazepines and thiamine, a therapeutic relationship and family involvement help the patient pass through detoxification safely and stay abstinent afterwards.

Conclusion Alcohol dependence is characterised by craving, loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal and continued use despite harm. Withdrawal begins within a day of stopping and may lead to seizures, hallucinosis and delirium tremens, while chronic use damages the liver, brain, heart and family. Management consists of detoxification with benzodiazepines and thiamine, followed by relapse prevention with drugs, psychosocial therapy and self-help groups, supported throughout by careful and compassionate nursing care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: (a) Explain the features of opioid intoxication and opioid withdrawal. (5 marks) (b) Describe the management of opioid dependence, including detoxification, opioid substitution therapy and harm reduction. (6 marks) (c) Explain the nursing management of a patient with opioid dependence. (4 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Opioid intoxication and withdrawal (5 marks)

Introduction – Opioids include natural opium alkaloids (opium, morphine, codeine), semi-synthetic drugs (heroin – "brown sugar", "smack", buprenorphine) and synthetic drugs (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl). In India they are used by smoking ("chasing"), sniffing, swallowing (opium, codeine-containing cough syrups, tramadol) and injecting. Opioids are the substances for which people most often seek treatment at de-addiction centres.

Opioid intoxication

  • Initial euphoria ("rush"), followed by drowsiness ("nodding"), apathy, slurred speech, impaired attention and judgement.
  • Pinpoint (constricted) pupils, slow breathing, bradycardia, hypotension, constipation, itching.
  • Opioid overdose – the triad of coma, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression; may be fatal; pulmonary oedema; risk greatest after a period of abstinence (loss of tolerance) or with sedatives and alcohol.

Opioid withdrawal (begins 6–12 hours after the last dose of heroin, peaks at 36–72 hours and subsides in 5–10 days; longer with methadone)

  • Craving, restlessness, anxiety, irritability, insomnia.
  • Lacrimation, rhinorrhoea (running nose), yawning, sneezing, sweating.
  • Dilated pupils, piloerection ("goose flesh"), hot and cold flushes.
  • Muscle and bone aches, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.
  • Tachycardia, mild rise in BP and temperature.
  • Withdrawal is very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening (except through dehydration or in people with medical illness).

(b) Management of opioid dependence (6 marks)

1. Management of overdose (emergency) – airway, breathing (bag–mask ventilation, oxygen) and naloxone (an opioid antagonist) IV, IM or intranasally, repeated every 2–3 minutes until breathing improves; observe for several hours because naloxone acts for a shorter time than many opioids and the patient may sink back into overdose.

2. Detoxification

  • Buprenorphine (sublingual), given in reducing doses over 1–2 weeks, or clonidine (reduces autonomic symptoms – monitor BP).
  • Symptomatic treatment – NSAIDs for aches, antispasmodics for cramps, loperamide for diarrhoea, antiemetics, a short course of benzodiazepines for insomnia and anxiety.
  • Correction of dehydration and nutritional deficiencies; screening for HIV, hepatitis B and C, TB and abscesses.

3. Long-term treatment

  • Opioid substitution therapy (OST) / agonist maintenance – daily, supervised buprenorphine (often combined with naloxone) or methadone, which reduces craving, illicit use, injecting, crime and HIV transmission; available at government de-addiction centres, drug treatment clinics and OST centres under the National AIDS Control Programme.
  • Antagonist maintenance – naltrexone (after 7–10 opioid-free days) blocks the effect of opioids; suitable for highly motivated patients.
  • Psychosocial interventions – motivational enhancement, cognitive behaviour therapy, relapse prevention, family therapy, Narcotics Anonymous, vocational rehabilitation, therapeutic communities.

4. Harm reduction (to reduce the harm of drug use for those who cannot stop immediately)

  • Needle and syringe exchange programmes, OST, condom distribution, HIV and hepatitis testing and treatment, abscess care, overdose education and naloxone – provided through targeted interventions for people who inject drugs.
  • Avoiding sharing of needles and syringes; safer injecting practices.

(c) Nursing management (4 marks)

  1. During withdrawal – monitor vital signs, pupils, hydration and withdrawal severity (for example, with a clinical opiate withdrawal scale); give medicines as prescribed; encourage fluids and a nutritious diet; warm baths and relaxation for aches and restlessness; ensure sleep.
  2. Safety and observation – prevent drugs being brought into the ward (searches as per policy, supervised visits); observe for overdose if the patient uses drugs secretly; keep naloxone and resuscitation equipment ready.
  3. Physical care – care of injection sites and abscesses, wound care, nutrition, treatment of infections; standard precautions (risk of HIV and hepatitis).
  4. Supervised dosing in OST – observe sublingual buprenorphine dissolving under the tongue, record doses, watch for sedation.
  5. Therapeutic relationship and motivation – non-judgemental attitude, firm limits on manipulative behaviour, motivational interviewing, identifying goals.
  6. Health education – risks of overdose after abstinence, not mixing opioids with alcohol or sedatives, safe injecting if still injecting, HIV prevention, adherence to OST.
  7. Family involvement – counselling, support groups, reducing stigma; help with job and social rehabilitation; regular follow-up.

Complications of opioid dependence

  • Infections from injecting – HIV, hepatitis B and C, skin abscesses, cellulitis, thrombophlebitis, infective endocarditis, septicaemia.
  • Overdose and death, especially with mixing of drugs or after loss of tolerance (release from prison or hospital).
  • Chronic constipation, malnutrition, dental decay, menstrual irregularities, sexual dysfunction.
  • Psychiatric problems – depression, anxiety, suicide, other substance use.
  • Social and legal problems – unemployment, debts, theft and crime to buy drugs, family breakdown, arrest under the NDPS Act.
  • In pregnancy – low birth weight, preterm birth and neonatal abstinence syndrome in the newborn.

Nursing care plan for a patient undergoing opioid detoxification | Nursing diagnosis | Nursing interventions | |---|---| | Acute discomfort (pain, cramps, restlessness) related to withdrawal | Assess withdrawal score; give buprenorphine or clonidine and symptomatic drugs as ordered; warm baths, relaxation, reassurance | | Risk for deficient fluid volume related to vomiting and diarrhoea | Encourage oral fluids, record intake and output, IV fluids if needed | | Risk for injury (overdose) related to drug use in the ward or after discharge | Supervision, naloxone ready, education on loss of tolerance | | Risk of infection related to injecting practices | Wound and abscess care, standard precautions, HIV and hepatitis testing and counselling | | Ineffective coping and denial | Motivational interviewing, group therapy, coping and refusal skills | | Interrupted family processes | Family education, support groups, involvement in discharge planning |

Discharge planning and follow-up

  • Link the patient to a buprenorphine or methadone maintenance centre or naltrexone programme close to home before discharge.
  • Teach the patient and family the early warning signs of relapse – missing appointments, meeting drug-using friends, craving, mood change.
  • Encourage Narcotics Anonymous, vocational training and return to work; involve community workers.
  • Patients who come forward voluntarily for treatment are given protection from prosecution under Section 64A of the NDPS Act, which the nurse can explain to reduce fear of seeking help.

Special situations

  • Pregnancy – opioid-dependent pregnant women are maintained on buprenorphine or methadone rather than detoxified, because withdrawal can harm the foetus; the newborn is observed for neonatal abstinence syndrome (irritability, high-pitched cry, tremors, poor feeding, diarrhoea) and treated in the nursery.
  • Adolescents – need family-based treatment, school support and life-skills training; injecting must be prevented.
  • People living with HIV or hepatitis C – opioid substitution therapy improves adherence to ART and hepatitis treatment; services should be integrated.
  • Patients with pain (surgery, cancer) who are on OST – the maintenance dose is continued and pain is treated adequately; their pain must not be dismissed as drug-seeking.

Nursing importance – Patients with opioid dependence often feel stigmatised and expect rejection. A nurse who combines safe withdrawal care and overdose prevention with respect, motivation and practical links to long-term treatment greatly improves the chance of recovery.

Conclusion Opioid intoxication causes drowsiness, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression, while withdrawal causes craving, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, yawning, dilated pupils, aches and diarrhoea. Overdose is reversed with naloxone; dependence is treated by detoxification with buprenorphine or clonidine, long-term opioid substitution with buprenorphine or methadone or antagonist therapy with naltrexone, psychosocial treatment and harm reduction. The nurse ensures safe withdrawal, supervised medication, physical care, motivation and family support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: Explain the nursing management of a patient with substance abuse.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing management of a patient with substance abuse follows the nursing process and continues from detoxification to long-term rehabilitation. The nurse's attitude – accepting, non-judgemental but firm – is the foundation of care.

1. Assessment

  • Substance history – type of substance, age at first use, quantity, frequency, route (injecting?), last use, previous withdrawal, complications, attempts to stop, treatment history.
  • Physical assessment – vital signs, nutritional status, liver, injection marks, abscesses, signs of intoxication or withdrawal; screening for HIV, hepatitis and TB.
  • Mental status examination – mood, suicidal ideas, psychosis, cognitive impairment; co-existing psychiatric illness (dual diagnosis).
  • Social assessment – family relationships, work, finances, legal problems, support systems.
  • Drug screening of urine or blood as advised; standardised tools such as AUDIT or CAGE for alcohol.

2. Common nursing diagnoses

  • Risk for injury related to withdrawal (seizures, delirium).
  • Ineffective denial related to minimising the problem.
  • Ineffective individual coping.
  • Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements.
  • Disturbed sleep pattern; risk of infection (injecting).
  • Interrupted family processes; deficient knowledge.

3. Nursing interventions

  • Safe detoxification – monitoring withdrawal scales and vital signs, medicines, fluids, nutrition, a calm and safe environment, seizure precautions.
  • Therapeutic relationship – trust, empathy, consistency; set clear limits on manipulative or demanding behaviour; consistent ward rules.
  • Motivational interviewing – explore ambivalence, help the patient see discrepancy between goals and drug use, support self-efficacy.
  • Confronting denial gently with facts; encourage acceptance of responsibility.
  • Coping and relapse prevention skills – identify triggers and high-risk situations, refusal skills, stress management, relaxation, healthy activities.
  • Health education – effects of the substance, complications, medications (disulfiram, naltrexone, buprenorphine), risks of overdose, HIV and hepatitis prevention.
  • Family intervention – psychoeducation, avoiding enabling and codependency, improving communication, involving families in follow-up; referral to Al-Anon or family groups.
  • Group therapy and self-help groups – AA, NA; occupational and recreational therapy; vocational rehabilitation.

4. Special considerations for vulnerable populations

  • Pregnant women – risk of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder and neonatal withdrawal; refer early; opioid-dependent pregnant women are maintained on buprenorphine or methadone rather than detoxified.
  • Adolescents – family-based therapy, school involvement, life-skills training.
  • Elderly – slower drug metabolism, greater sensitivity to benzodiazepines, falls and confusion.
  • People with HIV, homeless people and women facing violence – integrated and sensitive services.

5. Evaluation and follow-up – abstinence or reduced use, improved health, functioning and family relations; regular follow-up visits; early help after a lapse.

Conclusion Nursing management of substance abuse involves thorough assessment, safe detoxification, a firm but accepting therapeutic relationship, motivational and relapse-prevention work, health education, family involvement and attention to vulnerable groups, followed by long-term rehabilitation and follow-up.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: Explain disulfiram (Antabuse) therapy and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Disulfiram (Antabuse) is a drug used in the relapse prevention of alcohol dependence. It works as an aversive (deterrent) agent – the patient knows that drinking alcohol while taking it will cause a very unpleasant reaction, so he avoids alcohol.

Mechanism of action

  • Alcohol is normally broken down to acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid by the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase.
  • Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde accumulates in the blood if alcohol is taken, producing the disulfiram–ethanol reaction.

Disulfiram–ethanol reaction (within 5–15 minutes of drinking, lasting 30 minutes to a few hours)

  • Flushing of the face, throbbing headache, palpitations, tachycardia, breathlessness, sweating, nausea and vomiting, chest pain, giddiness, blurred vision.
  • Severe reactions – marked hypotension, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, convulsions, collapse and even death.

Dosage – usually 250 mg once daily (range 125–500 mg) after an initial period, as prescribed; its effect persists for up to 1–2 weeks after stopping the drug.

Indications – motivated patients with alcohol dependence who want to stay abstinent, preferably with a supportive family member who can supervise the dose.

Contraindications – patients who are not willing or are intoxicated, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, severe liver disease, psychosis, pregnancy, and patients who cannot understand the risks.

Side effects – drowsiness, metallic taste, headache, skin rash, impotence, hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy, rarely psychosis.

Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Informed consent – the patient must fully understand and agree; disulfiram must never be given secretly (for example, mixed in food by family members) – this is unethical and dangerous.
  2. Ensure abstinence – the first dose is given only after the patient has been free of alcohol for at least 12–24 hours; check for alcohol on the breath.
  3. Baseline assessment – liver function tests, ECG and BP as advised; monitor liver function during therapy.
  4. Supervised administration – preferably in the morning, observed by the nurse or a family member, to improve adherence.
  5. Patient education
    • Avoid all forms of alcohol, including hidden sources – cough syrups and tonics, mouthwashes, aftershaves, perfumes, sauces, vinegar and some sweets.
    • The reaction can occur up to two weeks after the last dose.
    • Carry a card stating that he is on disulfiram; report jaundice, dark urine or numbness.
  6. Emergency care of a reaction – lay the patient flat, oxygen, IV fluids, monitor BP and ECG, antihistamines and supportive treatment.
  7. Combine with counselling, relapse-prevention therapy and family support – disulfiram alone does not cure dependence.

Conclusion Disulfiram deters drinking by blocking aldehyde dehydrogenase and causing an unpleasant, sometimes dangerous reaction with alcohol. It is useful only for informed, motivated patients, and the nurse's key responsibilities are ensuring consent and abstinence before starting, supervising doses, monitoring the liver and teaching the patient to avoid all hidden sources of alcohol.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: Explain the classification of psychoactive substances with their intoxication and withdrawal effects.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychoactive substances are chemicals that act on the brain to alter mood, perception, thinking and behaviour. The National Survey on Extent and Pattern of Substance Use in India (2019) found that alcohol is the most commonly used substance (about 14.6% of people aged 10–75 years), followed by cannabis (about 2.8%) and opioids (about 2.1%).

Classification by effect on the central nervous system

  1. CNS depressants – alcohol, sedative-hypnotics (benzodiazepines, barbiturates), inhalants (solvents).
  2. Opioids (narcotic analgesics) – opium, morphine, heroin, codeine, tramadol, pethidine.
  3. CNS stimulants – cocaine, amphetamines and methamphetamine, MDMA ("ecstasy"), caffeine, nicotine.
  4. Cannabinoids – bhang, ganja (marijuana), charas (hashish).
  5. Hallucinogens – LSD, psilocybin (magic mushrooms), mescaline, phencyclidine. - ICD-10 and ICD-11 list substance classes: alcohol, opioids, cannabinoids, sedatives/hypnotics, cocaine, other stimulants, hallucinogens, tobacco, volatile solvents and others.

Routes – oral (alcohol, opium, tablets, cough syrups), smoking (tobacco, cannabis, heroin "chasing"), sniffing/snorting (cocaine, inhalants), chewing (gutkha, khaini), and injection (opioids, buprenorphine).

Intoxication and withdrawal effects

Substance Intoxication Withdrawal
Alcohol Disinhibition, slurred speech, ataxia, aggression, drowsiness, coma Tremors, sweating, insomnia, seizures, hallucinosis, delirium tremens
Sedatives (benzodiazepines) Drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, respiratory depression (with alcohol) Anxiety, insomnia, tremors, seizures, delirium
Opioids Euphoria, drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression Lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, yawning, dilated pupils, goose flesh, cramps, diarrhoea
Cannabis Euphoria, red eyes, increased appetite, altered time perception, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis Irritability, insomnia, anorexia, restlessness (mild)
Cocaine / amphetamines Euphoria, hyperactivity, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, paranoia, seizures, stroke "Crash" – fatigue, hypersomnia, depression, suicidal ideas, craving
Nicotine Alertness, increased heart rate Irritability, craving, poor concentration, increased appetite
Inhalants Euphoria, dizziness, slurred speech, ataxia; sudden death from arrhythmia Mild – irritability, sleep problems
Hallucinogens (LSD) Visual distortions, hallucinations, synaesthesia, panic ("bad trip"), flashbacks No significant withdrawal

Nursing relevance

  • Recognising the pattern helps the nurse identify the substance, anticipate dangerous complications (seizures in alcohol and sedative withdrawal, respiratory depression in opioid and sedative intoxication, suicidal depression after stimulant use) and plan safe care.
  • Mixed use (for example, alcohol with sedatives or opioids) greatly increases the risk of overdose.

Conclusion Psychoactive substances are classified as depressants, opioids, stimulants, cannabinoids and hallucinogens, each with characteristic intoxication and withdrawal effects. Knowledge of these effects enables the nurse to recognise substance use, manage emergencies and plan safe detoxification.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: Explain motivational interviewing and brief intervention in the management of substance use disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Many people with substance use problems are ambivalent – they want to change and at the same time want to continue using. Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, person-centred counselling style that helps people resolve this ambivalence and strengthen their own motivation to change. Motivational enhancement therapy (MET) is a brief structured treatment based on MI.

Stages of change (Prochaska and DiClemente)

  1. Precontemplation – not thinking about change; denies a problem.
  2. Contemplation – aware of the problem, considering change, but undecided.
  3. Preparation – intends to change soon; making plans.
  4. Action – actively changing behaviour (stopping or reducing use).
  5. Maintenance – sustaining the change for months; preventing relapse.
  6. Relapse – a return to use; the person may re-enter the cycle at any stage. - The nurse's intervention is matched to the patient's stage (for example, giving information and raising doubts in precontemplation; planning and skills in preparation and action).

Principles of motivational interviewing

  • Express empathy – accept the person's feelings without judgement.
  • Develop discrepancy – help the person see the gap between present behaviour and personal goals or values.
  • Roll with resistance – avoid arguing or labelling; resistance is a signal to change approach.
  • Support self-efficacy – build confidence that change is possible.
  • The spirit of MI is partnership, acceptance, compassion and evoking the patient's own reasons for change.

Core skills (OARS)

  • Open questions – "What concerns you about your drinking?"
  • Affirmations – recognising strengths and efforts.
  • Reflective listening – reflecting back what the person says and feels.
  • Summaries – pulling together the person's own statements in favour of change.

Brief intervention

  • A short (5–30 minute) session given in primary care, emergency departments or general wards to people with risky or harmful use, often after screening (AUDIT, CAGE, ASSIST).
  • FRAMES model:
    • Feedback on personal risk.
    • Responsibility for change lies with the person.
    • Advice to cut down or stop.
    • Menu of options for change.
    • Empathic style.
    • Self-efficacy – encouraging optimism.

Role of the nurse

  • Screen patients in wards, OPDs and communities for risky substance use.
  • Use MI skills during every contact; give brief interventions and written information.
  • Refer patients with dependence to de-addiction services; follow up and reinforce motivation.

Conclusion Motivational interviewing uses empathy, developing discrepancy, rolling with resistance and supporting self-efficacy, through OARS skills, to help patients resolve ambivalence according to their stage of change. Brief interventions using the FRAMES model allow nurses in any setting to reduce risky substance use and to motivate patients to seek treatment.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: What is the CAGE questionnaire?
answer_html:
The CAGE questionnaire is a simple four-question screening tool for alcohol problems:

  • C – Cut down – Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?
  • A – Annoyed – Have people annoyed you by criticising your drinking?
  • G – Guilty – Have you ever felt bad or guilty about your drinking?
  • E – Eye-opener – Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover (eye-opener)?
  • Two or more "yes" answers suggest clinically significant alcohol problems and need detailed assessment.
  • It is quick and useful in wards and OPDs; the AUDIT (10 questions) is a more detailed WHO screening tool.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: What is Alcoholics Anonymous?
answer_html:
Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) is a worldwide, voluntary self-help fellowship of people recovering from alcohol dependence, founded in 1935 in the USA by Bill W. and Dr Bob S.

  • Members meet regularly to share experiences, strength and hope, and help one another stay sober; the only requirement is a desire to stop drinking.
  • It follows the twelve-step programme (admitting powerlessness over alcohol, making amends, helping others) and uses sponsors (experienced members) and anonymity.
  • It is free, non-professional and available in many Indian cities.
  • Related groups – Al-Anon (for family members), Alateen (for teenage children) and Narcotics Anonymous (for drug users).
  • Nurses encourage patients and families to attend as part of relapse prevention.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: How is opioid overdose recognised and managed?
answer_html:
Recognition – the triad of unconsciousness (coma), pinpoint pupils and slow or absent breathing, often with cyanosis, bradycardia and hypotension, in a person known or suspected to use opioids; a syringe or packet may be found nearby. Management

  • Call for help; open the airway, give rescue breaths or bag–mask ventilation with oxygen.
  • Naloxone (opioid antagonist) 0.4–2 mg IV, IM or intranasally, repeated every 2–3 minutes until breathing is adequate.
  • Place in the recovery position once breathing; monitor SpO2 and respiration.
  • Observe for several hours – naloxone acts for a shorter time than many opioids, so overdose can return; naloxone may also precipitate acute withdrawal and agitation.
  • After recovery – counselling, referral to treatment and overdose education.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Substance Use Disorders
question: What is harm reduction in substance use?
answer_html:
Harm reduction refers to policies and practices that aim to reduce the health, social and economic harms of substance use, without necessarily requiring the person to stop using at once. It meets people "where they are" and treats them with respect. Examples

  • Needle and syringe exchange programmes – clean injecting equipment to prevent HIV and hepatitis C.
  • Opioid substitution therapy with buprenorphine or methadone.
  • Naloxone distribution and overdose education.
  • Condom distribution, HIV, hepatitis and TB testing and treatment, abscess care.
  • Information on safer use, not driving under the influence.
  • In India, harm reduction services for people who inject drugs are provided through targeted interventions and OST centres under the National AIDS Control Programme.

unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: (a) Define personality disorder and classify personality disorders with examples. (4 marks) (b) Explain the aetiology and clinical features of borderline personality disorder. (5 marks) (c) Describe the treatment and nursing management of a patient with borderline personality disorder. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (4 marks)

Definition A personality disorder (PD) is an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the person's culture, is pervasive and inflexible across many situations, begins in adolescence or early adulthood, is stable over time, and leads to distress or impairment in personal, social or occupational functioning. Personality disorders affect about 6–10% of the general population and are common among psychiatric patients.

Classification (DSM-5 clusters)

  1. Cluster A – odd or eccentric
    • Paranoid PD – pervasive distrust and suspiciousness; reads hidden threats into innocent remarks; bears grudges.
    • Schizoid PD – detachment from relationships, prefers solitary activities, emotional coldness.
    • Schizotypal PD – odd beliefs (magical thinking), eccentric behaviour and speech, social anxiety, unusual perceptions.
  2. Cluster B – dramatic, emotional or erratic
    • Antisocial PD – disregard for and violation of the rights of others, deceit, impulsivity, lack of remorse.
    • Borderline PD – instability of relationships, self-image and emotions, marked impulsivity.
    • Histrionic PD – excessive emotionality and attention seeking, seductive behaviour, shallow emotions.
    • Narcissistic PD – grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy.
  3. Cluster C – anxious or fearful
    • Avoidant PD – social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to criticism.
    • Dependent PD – excessive need to be taken care of, clinging, difficulty making decisions.
    • Obsessive-compulsive (anankastic) PD – preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control (different from OCD).
    • ICD-11 now diagnoses a single "personality disorder" graded as mild, moderate or severe, with prominent trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and an optional borderline pattern specifier.

(b) Aetiology and clinical features of borderline personality disorder (5 marks)

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) (emotionally unstable personality disorder, borderline type, in ICD-10) is a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image and emotions, with marked impulsivity. It affects about 1–2% of the population and is diagnosed more often in women in clinical settings.

Aetiology

  • Biological – genetic vulnerability; heightened reactivity of the amygdala and reduced control by the prefrontal cortex; serotonin dysfunction linked with impulsivity and aggression.
  • Psychosocial – childhood trauma (physical, sexual or emotional abuse, neglect), early separation or loss, insecure attachment, family chaos.
  • Biosocial theory (Linehan) – an emotionally sensitive child growing up in an invalidating environment (where feelings are dismissed or punished) fails to learn how to regulate emotions.
  • Psychodynamic – failure of separation–individuation in early childhood; reliance on primitive defences such as splitting and projective identification.

Clinical features (DSM-5 – five or more)

  1. Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment.
  2. Unstable, intense relationships alternating between idealisation and devaluation ("splitting").
  3. Identity disturbance – unstable self-image or sense of self.
  4. Impulsivity in at least two self-damaging areas – spending, unsafe sex, substance use, reckless driving, binge eating.
  5. Recurrent suicidal behaviour, threats or self-harming behaviour.
  6. Affective instability – intense mood swings (dysphoria, irritability, anxiety) lasting hours.
  7. Chronic feelings of emptiness.
  8. Inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger.
  9. Transient stress-related paranoid ideas or dissociative symptoms. - Common comorbidities – depression, substance use, eating disorders, PTSD; the risk of suicide is high.

(c) Treatment and nursing management (6 marks)

Treatment

  • Psychotherapy is the main treatment
    • Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) (Marsha Linehan) – teaches four skill sets: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, through individual therapy, skills groups and coaching.
    • Mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, transference-focused therapy, CBT.
  • Medication – no drug cures BPD; used for target symptoms – mood stabilisers (lamotrigine, valproate) for mood instability and anger, low-dose antipsychotics for transient psychotic symptoms, SSRIs for co-existing depression; benzodiazepines are avoided (disinhibition, dependence).
  • Crisis management – short hospital admission during suicidal crises; treat comorbid substance use and depression.

Nursing management

  1. Therapeutic relationship with consistency – a warm but professional relationship; be reliable, punctual and honest; prepare the patient in advance for staff changes and the end of the relationship to reduce fear of abandonment.
  2. Clear limits and boundaries – explain ward rules and consequences in advance; apply them consistently and without anger or punishment; avoid special favours and secrets.
  3. Team approach to prevent splitting – one agreed care plan, regular team meetings, the same responses from all staff; do not take sides when the patient praises some staff and criticises others.
  4. Safety – assess suicide and self-harm risk regularly; remove harmful objects; appropriate level of observation; develop a written safety plan (warning signs, coping steps, people to contact) with the patient.
  5. Emotion regulation and coping – help the patient identify feelings and triggers, express anger in words, and practise DBT-type skills (deep breathing, grounding, distraction, self-soothing, problem solving) instead of acting on impulses.
  6. Encourage responsibility – involve the patient in decisions and goal setting; praise appropriate behaviour; avoid both rescuing and rejecting.
  7. Impulse control and healthy lifestyle – structured daily routine, sleep, physical activity, avoidance of alcohol and drugs.
  8. Family psychoeducation – explain the illness, validating communication, crisis plans.
  9. Nurse's self-awareness – patients with BPD can arouse strong feelings (frustration, anger, rescue fantasies); clinical supervision helps staff stay therapeutic.
  10. Discharge planning – follow-up appointments, DBT group, crisis helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416).

Nursing approach to some other personality disorders | Personality disorder | Key nursing approach | |---|---| | Paranoid | Respect personal space, be honest and consistent, explain every procedure, avoid whispering or laughing near the patient | | Schizoid | Accept the need for distance, do not force social activities, introduce group activities gradually | | Histrionic | Give attention for appropriate behaviour rather than dramatic displays, encourage expression of real feelings | | Narcissistic | Remain neutral, avoid power struggles, set limits on demands, help the patient cope with criticism | | Avoidant | Supportive acceptance, social skills and assertiveness training, gradual exposure to social situations | | Dependent | Encourage decision making and self-care, praise independent actions, avoid fostering dependence | | Obsessive-compulsive (anankastic) | Allow time to complete tasks, encourage flexibility, discuss fears of making mistakes |

Geriatric considerations – personality traits usually persist into old age; some dramatic behaviours lessen, while rigidity, suspiciousness and dependence may increase with illness, loss and cognitive decline. A new change in personality in an older person suggests an organic cause (dementia, stroke, frontal lobe disease) and needs medical evaluation.

Nursing importance Patients with borderline personality disorder are often labelled "difficult". A consistent team, clear boundaries, careful safety planning and teaching of emotion-regulation skills allow many of them to improve markedly over time.

Conclusion Personality disorders are enduring, inflexible patterns of behaviour grouped into clusters A (odd), B (dramatic) and C (anxious). Borderline PD, rooted in biological vulnerability and childhood adversity, causes unstable relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity, self-harm and intense emotions. Treatment centres on psychotherapy such as DBT, with symptomatic medication, while nursing care emphasises a consistent relationship, clear limits, a united team, safety and coping skills.

question: Explain sexual disorders – their definition, types and the nursing management of patients with sexual disorders.

dyspareunia) may occur at any stage

answer_html:
Definition Sexual disorders are disturbances of sexual functioning or sexual interest that cause marked distress or interpersonal difficulty, or that involve harm or risk of harm to others. They are broadly grouped as sexual dysfunctions, paraphilic disorders and, in DSM-5, gender dysphoria. Sexual problems are common but often hidden because of embarrassment, myths and stigma.

Types

1. Sexual dysfunctions – disturbances in the sexual response cycle (desire, arousal, orgasm, resolution) or sexual pain, present for about 6 months and causing distress.

  • Male
    • Erectile disorder – persistent difficulty in obtaining or maintaining an erection.
    • Premature (early) ejaculation – ejaculation within about a minute of penetration, before the person wishes.
    • Delayed ejaculation; male hypoactive sexual desire disorder.
  • Female
    • Female sexual interest/arousal disorder – reduced interest, arousal or pleasure.
    • Female orgasmic disorder.
    • Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder – vaginismus (involuntary spasm of the pelvic floor muscles preventing penetration) and dyspareunia (painful intercourse).
  • Substance/medication-induced sexual dysfunction – due to SSRIs, antipsychotics, antihypertensives (beta-blockers, thiazides), alcohol and opioids.
  • Causes – physical (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, hormonal problems, spinal cord injury, pelvic surgery, smoking, alcohol, drugs) and psychological (performance anxiety, depression, stress, relationship conflict, guilt, cultural taboos, past sexual trauma, lack of knowledge and myths).
  • Dhat syndrome – a culture-bound syndrome of South Asia in which young men attribute weakness and sexual problems to "loss of semen".

2. Paraphilic disorders – recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, urges or behaviours (for at least 6 months) involving non-human objects, suffering or humiliation, or non-consenting persons (including children), which cause distress or impairment, or have been acted upon with a non-consenting person.

  • Examples – voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, fetishistic, transvestic, sexual masochism, sexual sadism and paedophilic disorder.
  • They are more common in men and usually begin in adolescence; acting on some of these urges is a criminal offence, and acts against children come under the POCSO Act.

3. Gender dysphoria / gender incongruence

  • DSM-5 – distress arising from a marked incongruence between a person's experienced gender and the sex assigned at birth.
  • ICD-11 has moved gender incongruence out of mental disorders into "conditions related to sexual health", recognising that being transgender is not a mental illness; care focuses on support and gender-affirming services.

Management

Assessment

  • A sexual history taken in private with a non-judgemental attitude – nature and duration of the problem, situational or generalised, relationship issues, beliefs and myths, medical illnesses, medicines and substances.
  • Physical examination and tests – blood sugar, lipids, thyroid function, testosterone and prolactin when indicated.

Treatment of sexual dysfunctions

  • Treat medical causes; review and change drugs causing dysfunction (a common cause of non-adherence to psychotropics).
  • Psychoeducation and sex education – correct myths (for example, about masturbation and night emissions); improve communication between partners; couple therapy.
  • Sex therapy – sensate focus exercises (Masters and Johnson) to reduce performance anxiety; stop–start and squeeze techniques for premature ejaculation; pelvic floor relaxation and graded vaginal dilators for vaginismus.
  • Drugs – PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) for erectile disorder (never with nitrates); SSRIs or dapoxetine for premature ejaculation; hormone therapy where deficient; vacuum devices, injections or prosthesis in selected cases.

Treatment of paraphilic disorders

  • Cognitive behaviour therapy, relapse prevention and victim-empathy work; SSRIs to reduce urges; anti-androgen drugs in severe cases with informed consent; treatment of comorbid conditions; attention to legal requirements and the safety of others.

Care related to gender dysphoria

  • Psychological support for distress, depression and minority stress; family counselling; referral for gender-affirming care according to standards of care; respect for rights under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.

Nursing management of patients with sexual disorders

  1. Self-awareness – the nurse examines her own attitudes and values so that personal beliefs do not affect care; uses professional, respectful language.
  2. Privacy and trust – discuss sexual concerns in a private setting; assure confidentiality (except where law requires reporting, such as abuse of a child).
  3. Use the PLISSIT model – give Permission to discuss concerns, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions, and refer for Intensive Therapy when needed.
  4. Health education – anatomy and physiology of sexual response, effects of illness and drugs, correction of myths (Dhat), safe sex practices and prevention of sexually transmitted infections.
  5. Medication teaching – correct use and side effects of PDE-5 inhibitors and other drugs; report psychotropic-related sexual side effects instead of stopping medicines.
  6. Involve the partner (with the patient's consent) in counselling and sex therapy exercises.
  7. Support self-esteem – address anxiety, guilt and depression; encourage expression of feelings.
  8. Safety and protection on the ward – recognise and set limits on sexually inappropriate behaviour (for example, in mania or dementia) while preserving dignity; protect vulnerable patients.
  9. Legal responsibilities – follow mandatory reporting under POCSO when children are at risk; maintain accurate records.
  10. Respectful care of transgender persons – use the preferred name and pronouns, ensure privacy during examinations, and avoid discrimination.

Common sexual myths that the nurse should correct | Myth | Fact | |---|---| | Masturbation causes weakness, blindness or loss of manhood | Masturbation is a normal sexual behaviour and does not damage health | | Night emissions ("wet dreams") are a disease | They are a normal physiological event in adolescent boys and young men | | Loss of semen makes the body weak (Dhat) | Semen is continuously produced; its loss does not cause weakness | | Penis size decides sexual satisfaction | Size has little relation to satisfaction; communication and intimacy matter more | | Sexual problems are always due to age | Many problems are due to treatable causes such as diabetes, drugs, anxiety or depression |

Geriatric considerations – sexual interest often continues into old age; changes in response are normal, but illness, drugs, loss of a partner and lack of privacy (for example, in institutions) affect sexual life. Older adults deserve the same respectful assessment and treatment.

Role in prevention – age-appropriate sexuality education in schools and adolescent clinics, early treatment of physical illnesses, careful choice of psychotropic drugs, and an open, accepting environment where patients can talk about sexual concerns without fear or shame.

Taking a sexual history – the BETTER approach

  • Bring up the topic – the nurse introduces it as part of routine care.
  • Explain that sexuality is part of quality of life and that the patient can talk about it.
  • Tell the patient that help and resources are available.
  • Timing – the patient may choose to discuss it now or later.
  • Educate about the possible effects of illness and treatment on sexual function.
  • Record the assessment and plan in the patient's notes.

Conclusion Sexual disorders include sexual dysfunctions, paraphilic disorders and gender dysphoria (now termed gender incongruence and not a mental disorder in ICD-11). They arise from physical, psychological, relationship and cultural factors. Management combines assessment, treatment of causes, psychoeducation, sex and couple therapy and medication, while the nurse provides private, non-judgemental, confidential care using the PLISSIT approach, health education and attention to legal and ethical responsibilities.

question: Explain antisocial personality disorder and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Antisocial (dissocial) personality disorder (ASPD) is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, occurring since the age of 15 years, in a person who is at least 18 years old and who showed features of conduct disorder in childhood. It is more common in men and very common in prison populations.

Causes

  • Genetic and biological – family history, low physiological arousal (low resting heart rate), reduced fear response, frontal lobe dysfunction.
  • Childhood factors – abuse and neglect, harsh and inconsistent discipline, parental antisocial behaviour or substance use, broken homes; childhood conduct disorder and ADHD.
  • Social factors – poverty, delinquent peers, exposure to violence.

Clinical features

  • Repeated violation of laws and rules – stealing, cheating, violence, property damage.
  • Deceitfulness – repeated lying, use of aliases, conning others for profit or pleasure.
  • Impulsivity, failure to plan ahead; irritability and aggressiveness (repeated fights or assaults).
  • Reckless disregard for the safety of self or others (dangerous driving, substance use).
  • Irresponsibility – failure to keep jobs or pay debts.
  • Lack of remorse or guilt; blames others; superficial charm and manipulation; low tolerance of frustration.
  • Complications – substance use, imprisonment, violence, injuries and early death.

Management

  • No medicine cures ASPD; treatment is difficult because the person rarely sees a need to change.
  • Psychological – CBT, anger management, problem-solving training, contingency management, therapeutic communities, treatment of substance use.
  • Medication for specific problems – mood stabilisers or antipsychotics for aggression and impulsivity; treatment of comorbid ADHD and depression.

Nursing management

  1. Clear, consistent limits – explain rules and consequences in advance and enforce them uniformly by all staff, without punishment, anger or arguing.
  2. Recognise and confront manipulation – avoid special favours, bargaining and secrets; communicate within the team.
  3. Safety – assess the risk of aggression; maintain a safe distance and an exit route; de-escalation; protect other patients and staff.
  4. Encourage responsibility – help the patient accept the consequences of actions; reinforce honest and responsible behaviour.
  5. Anger and impulse control – teach recognition of anger and alternative responses (walking away, talking, exercise); problem solving.
  6. Treat substance use and involve the family where possible; vocational training.
  7. Self-awareness – nurses may feel used or angry; peer support and supervision help maintain a therapeutic, non-punitive approach.

Conclusion Antisocial personality disorder is a long-standing pattern of disregard for others' rights with deceit, impulsivity, aggression and lack of remorse, beginning with conduct problems in childhood. Management is difficult and relies on behavioural approaches, treatment of substance use and firm, consistent, non-punitive nursing care with attention to safety.

question: Explain the nursing management of a patient with manipulative behaviour.
answer_html:
Definition Manipulation is a behaviour in which a person tries to control or influence others indirectly – through deception, flattery, threats or exploitation – to meet his or her own needs, without regard for the needs of others. It is commonly seen in borderline and antisocial personality disorders and in people with substance dependence, and also in anyone who feels powerless.

Common manipulative behaviours on the ward

  • Flattery ("You are the only nurse who understands me").
  • Splitting – playing staff members against each other.
  • Bargaining and demanding special privileges or exceptions to rules.
  • Testing limits repeatedly; breaking rules and then pleading.
  • Guilt induction, threats (including threats of self-harm), complaints, lying and seductive behaviour.
  • Requests to keep secrets from other staff.

Nursing management

  1. Recognise the behaviour and your own reaction – feelings of being special, guilty or angry are clues; discuss with colleagues.
  2. Set clear, reasonable and enforceable limits – state what is expected, the reasons and the consequences in advance, in a calm, matter-of-fact way.
  3. Consistency by all staff – a written care plan known to every team member; regular team meetings to share information and prevent splitting; one staff member may be the main contact for negotiations.
  4. Avoid special favours, secret agreements, arguing, defensiveness, bargaining and power struggles; do not take personal offence.
  5. Communicate directly – address the behaviour openly ("I notice you asked three nurses the same question"); keep promises.
  6. Encourage direct expression of needs – teach and reinforce assertive (not manipulative) ways of asking for help; give attention for appropriate behaviour rather than for manipulation.
  7. Offer choices within limits to give the patient a sense of control.
  8. Take all threats of self-harm seriously – assess risk and ensure safety, while maintaining limits on other behaviour.
  9. Help the patient accept responsibility for actions and their consequences.
  10. Document behaviour, limits set and responses accurately.

Conclusion Manipulative behaviour is an indirect way of meeting needs, often seen in personality disorders and substance dependence. It is managed by recognising it, setting clear and consistent limits agreed by the whole team, avoiding special favours and power struggles, encouraging direct expression of needs and rewarding appropriate behaviour, while keeping the patient safe.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: Explain the PLISSIT model and the nurse's role in sexual health counselling.
answer_html:
Introduction Sexual health is part of holistic care, yet patients rarely raise sexual concerns and nurses often avoid them. The PLISSIT model (Annon, 1976) gives nurses a simple, graded framework for addressing sexual concerns at a level matched to their knowledge and skill.

The four levels of PLISSIT

  1. P – Permission
    • The nurse gives the patient permission to talk about sexual concerns and reassures that such concerns are normal and common – for example, "Many people with diabetes notice changes in their sexual life; would you like to talk about this?"
    • Also gives permission to continue behaviours that are healthy and safe.
  2. LI – Limited Information
    • Gives specific factual information relevant to the concern – how an illness, surgery or drug affects sexual function, correction of myths (for example, about masturbation or loss of semen), normal sexual response.
  3. SS – Specific Suggestions
    • Practical advice to deal with a particular problem – timing of sexual activity and comfortable positions after a heart attack or hip surgery, use of lubricants, timing of medicines, pelvic floor exercises, sensate focus exercises, managing a stoma during intimacy.
  4. IT – Intensive Therapy
    • Referral to a psychiatrist, sex therapist, urologist or gynaecologist for complex problems – for example, severe dysfunction, paraphilic disorders, relationship crises or past sexual trauma.
    • The Ex-PLISSIT (extended) model adds that permission-giving runs through all stages and stresses reflection and review.

Nurse's role in sexual health counselling

  • Self-awareness and comfort with the topic; non-judgemental, culturally sensitive approach.
  • Privacy and confidentiality; use of simple, clear language and correct terms.
  • Routinely include sexual health in assessment, especially in chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, cancer, spinal injury), after surgery (mastectomy, hysterectomy, stoma), during pregnancy and menopause, and in psychiatric patients on drugs that impair sexual function.
  • Explain sexual side effects of medicines and encourage the patient to report them rather than stop treatment.
  • Health education on safe sex, contraception and STI prevention; correction of common myths.
  • Involve the partner with the patient's consent.
  • Know when to refer and keep records.

Conclusion The PLISSIT model – Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions and Intensive Therapy – helps nurses address sexual concerns at the appropriate level. With self-awareness, privacy, accurate information and timely referral, nurses can integrate sexual health counselling into holistic care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: What is gender incongruence? State the nurse's approach to a transgender patient.
answer_html:
Gender incongruence is a marked and persistent difference between a person's experienced gender and the sex assigned at birth. ICD-11 places it under "conditions related to sexual health" and not among mental disorders; DSM-5 uses the term gender dysphoria for the distress that may accompany this incongruence. Nurse's approach

  • Treat the person with respect and dignity; use the preferred name and pronouns.
  • Ensure privacy during examinations, appropriate ward placement and confidentiality.
  • Provide support for distress, depression or anxiety arising from stigma and discrimination (minority stress); involve the family when appropriate.
  • Refer for gender-affirming care as needed; respect the rights guaranteed by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, including non-discrimination in health care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: What is Dhat syndrome?
answer_html:
Dhat syndrome is a culture-bound syndrome of South Asia in which (usually young) men are anxious and preoccupied with the belief that they are losing "dhat" (semen) through urine, night emissions or masturbation, and that this loss causes their ill health.

  • It arises from the traditional belief that semen is a precious "vital fluid" whose loss weakens the body.
  • Symptoms – weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, poor concentration, anxiety, depression, and sexual complaints such as premature ejaculation or erectile difficulty; whitish urine (often due to phosphates) is cited as proof.
  • Management – sympathetic listening, reassurance and sex education to correct myths, CBT, treatment of associated anxiety or depression, and advice to avoid quack remedies.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: What is sensate focus therapy?
answer_html:
Sensate focus therapy is a behavioural sex therapy technique developed by Masters and Johnson for couples with sexual dysfunction (for example, erectile disorder, arousal or orgasmic problems) in which performance anxiety plays a role.

  • The couple is first asked to avoid intercourse and to take turns giving and receiving non-demand, pleasurable touching, initially of non-genital areas, focusing on sensations rather than performance.
  • In later stages genital touching is allowed, and finally intercourse is gradually reintroduced.
  • It reduces anxiety, improves communication and intimacy, and helps natural sexual responses return.
  • It is given under the guidance of a trained therapist, often combined with education and other treatments.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Personality and Sexual Disorders
question: What is splitting? How does the nurse manage it?
answer_html:
Splitting is a primitive defence mechanism in which a person is unable to see both good and bad qualities in the same person or in himself, and so views people as either all good or all bad. It is typical of borderline personality disorder.

  • On the ward, the patient may idealise some staff members ("the best nurse") and devalue others, causing conflict and disagreement within the team. Nursing management

  • Recognise splitting and discuss it in team meetings; maintain one consistent care plan followed by all staff.

  • Do not accept flattery or criticism of colleagues; avoid taking sides.
  • Point out both positive and negative aspects of situations and people in a balanced way, and help the patient tolerate mixed feelings.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: (a) Define intellectual disability and classify it according to IQ. (4 marks) (b) Explain the causes, clinical features and assessment of intellectual disability. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management, nursing care and prevention of intellectual disability. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of intellectual disability by IQ
labels: about 85%); IQ 35–49 moderate (mental age 6–9 years); IQ 20–34 severe (mental age 3–6 years); IQ below 20 profound (mental age below 3 years); normal IQ 90–109

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (4 marks)

Definition Intellectual disability (ID) – called disorders of intellectual development in ICD-11 and earlier mental retardation – is a condition beginning during the developmental period and characterised by:

  1. Deficits in intellectual functions – reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, academic learning and learning from experience, usually with an IQ about two standard deviations or more below the mean (below about 70); and
  2. Deficits in adaptive functioning – in conceptual, social and practical skills of daily living, so that the person needs support at home, school, work or in the community. - It affects about 1–2% of the population.

Classification by IQ (ICD-10)

Severity IQ Mental age (adult) Approximate share Main features
Mild 50–69 9–12 years About 85% Educable; learns reading and writing to about class 6 level; can live independently with some support
Moderate 35–49 6–9 years About 10% Trainable; self-care and simple work under supervision
Severe 20–34 3–6 years 3–4% Limited speech; needs supervision in daily activities; often with physical problems
Profound Below 20 Below 3 years 1–2% Needs total care; severe motor and sensory deficits
  • DSM-5 grades severity mainly by adaptive functioning rather than IQ alone.

(b) Causes, clinical features and assessment (5 marks)

Causes (a cause can be found in many moderate to profound cases)

  1. Prenatal
    • Genetic and chromosomal – Down syndrome (the commonest genetic cause), fragile X syndrome (the commonest inherited cause), Rett syndrome, inborn errors of metabolism (phenylketonuria, galactosaemia), congenital hypothyroidism.
    • Maternal infections – TORCH, Zika; iodine deficiency, malnutrition, alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome), drugs, radiation, maternal diabetes and pre-eclampsia.
  2. Perinatal – birth asphyxia, prematurity, very low birth weight, birth injury, kernicterus, neonatal hypoglycaemia, sepsis.
  3. Postnatal – meningitis, encephalitis, head injury, near-drowning, lead poisoning, severe malnutrition, hypothyroidism, severe psychosocial deprivation.

Clinical features

  • Delayed developmental milestones – motor, speech, social and self-help skills.
  • Slow learning, poor school performance, difficulty with abstract concepts, short attention span.
  • Immature behaviour, poor judgement, difficulty in social relationships; vulnerability to exploitation.
  • Associated problems – epilepsy, cerebral palsy, visual and hearing defects, ADHD, autism, behaviour problems (aggression, self-injury), feeding difficulties.
  • Dysmorphic features in syndromes (for example, the facial features of Down syndrome).

Assessment

  • History – family history, consanguinity, pregnancy and birth history, developmental milestones, school performance, illnesses, behaviour.
  • Physical and neurological examination – head circumference, dysmorphic features, skin markers, vision and hearing.
  • Psychological tests
    • Intelligence tests – Binet–Kamat Test (Indian adaptation of the Stanford–Binet), Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC), Seguin Form Board, Raven's Progressive Matrices; Bayley Scales and the Developmental Screening Test for young children.
    • Adaptive behaviour – Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) (social quotient).
  • Investigations – thyroid function, metabolic screening, chromosomal analysis (karyotype, fragile X DNA test), MRI brain, EEG if seizures, hearing and vision tests.
  • IQ = (mental age ÷ chronological age) × 100 in the classical formula.

(c) Management, nursing care and prevention (6 marks)

Management (no cure; aim – maximum independence and quality of life)

  • Early intervention and stimulation through District Early Intervention Centres; physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy.
  • Special or inclusive education with an individualised education plan; vocational training and sheltered workshops for adolescents and adults.
  • Behaviour modification for teaching skills and reducing problem behaviours.
  • Treatment of associated conditions – anticonvulsants, spectacles and hearing aids, treatment of hypothyroidism; risperidone for severe aggression or self-injury as prescribed.
  • Family counselling and support; legal guardianship and welfare benefits (National Trust, disability certificate and UDID card).

Nursing care

  1. Assessment of abilities and needs – what the child can do, not only what he cannot.
  2. Teaching self-care skills – feeding, dressing, toileting, bathing and grooming using task analysis (breaking a task into small steps), shaping, chaining, prompting and positive reinforcement (praise, rewards).
  3. Promoting communication – simple, short sentences, gestures and pictures; patience and repetition.
  4. Safety – supervision to prevent accidents, poisoning, wandering and exploitation; seizure precautions; protection from abuse.
  5. Physical health – nutrition, immunisation, dental care, management of constipation, regular vision and hearing checks.
  6. Managing problem behaviours – identify triggers, consistent routine, reward desired behaviour, ignore minor attention-seeking behaviour, time-out; protect from self-injury.
  7. Socialisation and play – group play, outings, inclusion in family and community activities.
  8. Family support – help parents through grief and guilt; teach them training techniques; prevent overprotection and rejection; respite care; link with parent support groups and services.
  9. Sexual health and protection in adolescence – age-appropriate education, menstrual hygiene, protection from abuse.

Prevention

  • Primary – genetic counselling for high-risk couples; good antenatal care, iodised salt, folic acid, rubella vaccination, avoiding alcohol, drugs and radiation in pregnancy; prevention of birth asphyxia through skilled birth attendance and neonatal resuscitation; newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism and metabolic disorders; immunisation against meningitis and encephalitis; prevention of head injury and lead exposure; nutrition.
  • Secondary – early detection through developmental screening (RBSK) and early treatment of correctable causes (hypothyroidism, PKU).
  • Tertiary – rehabilitation, special education and vocational training to prevent further disability.

Behaviour modification techniques used in teaching children with ID

  • Shaping – rewarding closer and closer approximations of the desired behaviour (for example, first holding a spoon, then lifting food, then eating independently).
  • Chaining – teaching the steps of a task in sequence; in backward chaining the child completes the last step first and gradually takes over earlier steps (useful for dressing).
  • Prompting and fading – physical, gestural or verbal prompts are given and then gradually withdrawn as the child learns.
  • Modelling – the nurse or parent demonstrates the behaviour for the child to imitate.
  • Token economy – tokens or stickers earned for desired behaviour are exchanged for a reward.
  • Extinction and time-out – withdrawing attention from undesirable behaviour that is not dangerous.

Legal and welfare support – intellectual disability is a recognised disability under the RPwD Act, 2016, entitling the child to a disability certificate and UDID card, free education up to 18 years, aids and appliances, scholarships and, through the National Trust, legal guardianship, the Niramaya health insurance scheme and day-care and respite services.

Down syndrome – the commonest genetic cause of ID

  • Due to trisomy 21 (an extra chromosome 21); risk increases with maternal age.
  • Features – upward-slanting eyes, epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, short stature, hypotonia, mild to moderate ID.
  • Associated problems – congenital heart disease, hypothyroidism, hearing and vision problems, leukaemia and early Alzheimer's disease.
  • Antenatal screening and counselling are offered to all pregnant women, especially those above 35 years.

Nursing importance Many children with intellectual disability, especially mild ID, can learn self-care, schooling and simple occupations. The nurse's role in early identification, teaching skills through behaviour modification, safety and empowering families decides how independent the child becomes.

Conclusion Intellectual disability is a developmental condition with deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning, classified as mild, moderate, severe and profound. It has prenatal, perinatal and postnatal causes and is assessed by history, examination, IQ and adaptive behaviour tests. Management focuses on early intervention, special education, behaviour modification and family support, and many causes are preventable through good maternal and child health care.
