question: (a) Define autism spectrum disorder and explain its causes. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and the early warning signs of autism. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a child with autism spectrum disorder. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (4 marks)

Definition Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by:

  1. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts; and
  2. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, - present from early childhood and causing significant impairment. The term "spectrum" reflects wide variation in severity – from children who need very substantial support (level 3) to those who need some support (level 1). Intellectual ability ranges from intellectual disability to above-average intelligence. - It affects about 1 in 100 children worldwide; boys are affected about four times more often than girls.

Causes

  • Genetic – strong heritability; higher risk in siblings; associated with fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis and other genetic syndromes.
  • Neurobiological – differences in brain development and connectivity.
  • Prenatal and perinatal risk factors – advanced parental age, prematurity and very low birth weight, maternal infection, valproate exposure in pregnancy.
  • Vaccines do not cause autism – this myth has been disproved by many large studies; parental behaviour ("cold parenting") is also not a cause.

(b) Clinical features and early warning signs (5 marks)

1. Deficits in social communication and interaction

  • Poor eye contact, does not respond to name, little social smile or sharing of enjoyment.
  • Lack of pointing and showing (joint attention), limited use of gestures and facial expressions.
  • Delayed or absent speech; echolalia (repeating words or phrases), pronoun reversal, unusual tone; difficulty in starting or sustaining conversation.
  • Difficulty in understanding others' feelings; prefers to play alone; little pretend (imaginative) play.

2. Restricted, repetitive behaviours and interests

  • Stereotyped movements – hand flapping, rocking, spinning, toe walking.
  • Insistence on sameness – extreme distress at small changes in routine; rigid rituals.
  • Restricted, intense interests – lining up toys, fascination with wheels, fans or numbers.
  • Sensory differences – over- or under-sensitivity to sound, touch, light, taste or pain; covering ears; smelling or licking objects.

Associated problems – intellectual disability, epilepsy, ADHD, anxiety, sleep problems, feeding selectivity, self-injury, aggression, gastrointestinal problems.

Early warning signs ("red flags")

  • No babbling or pointing by 12 months.
  • No single words by 16 months; no two-word phrases by 24 months.
  • Loss of any language or social skills at any age (regression).
  • Not responding to name, poor eye contact, no social smile, unusual repetitive play.

Screening and assessment – M-CHAT (Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers) at 18–24 months; INCLEN Diagnostic Tool for ASD; Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA) (used for disability certification); developmental assessment, hearing test, and evaluation for associated conditions.

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Management – early, intensive and individualised; there is no cure, but outcomes improve greatly with early intervention.

  • Behavioural interventions – applied behaviour analysis (ABA) and other early intensive behavioural programmes to teach communication, social and self-help skills and reduce problem behaviours.
  • Speech and language therapy; alternative communication – PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System), sign language, communication devices.
  • Occupational therapy – fine motor skills, daily living skills, sensory integration.
  • Structured teaching (TEACCH) using visual schedules and organised environments; social skills training.
  • Parent-mediated interventions – training parents to use therapy techniques throughout the day.
  • Special or inclusive education with an individualised plan.
  • Medication only for associated problems – risperidone or aripiprazole for severe irritability and aggression, melatonin for sleep, treatment of epilepsy and ADHD.
  • Avoid unproven treatments (for example, chelation, special "cures"), which waste money and may harm.

Nursing care

  1. Structured, predictable routine – the same sequence of daily activities; visual schedules and picture cards; prepare the child in advance for any change (warnings, social stories).
  2. Communication – use the child's name, simple, concrete and short sentences, one instruction at a time, gestures and pictures; allow time to respond; do not insist on eye contact.
  3. Reduce sensory overload – a calm, quiet environment, dim lights, a familiar caregiver, a "safe corner"; identify sounds or textures that upset the child.
  4. Safety – supervise to prevent wandering, falls, pica and self-injury (helmet or protective padding if head-banging); remove dangerous objects.
  5. Teaching self-care and social skills – break tasks into steps, model behaviour, reward desired behaviour immediately; encourage play with others.
  6. Managing problem behaviour – identify triggers and the function of the behaviour; stay calm; redirect; avoid reinforcing tantrums.
  7. Physical health – nutrition despite food selectivity, sleep hygiene, dental care, immunisation; prepare carefully for procedures (picture stories, minimal waiting).
  8. Family support – explain the condition and the importance of early therapy, relieve guilt, train parents, link with support groups, respite care and benefits under the RPwD Act (ASD is a recognised disability); care for siblings.

Differences between autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability | Feature | Autism spectrum disorder | Intellectual disability | |---|---|---| | Core problem | Social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviours | Global delay in intellectual and adaptive functioning | | Social interest | Reduced; poor eye contact and joint attention even when IQ is normal | Social interest usually present, appropriate to mental age | | Intelligence | Ranges from ID to above average; uneven skills | Uniformly low | | Repetitive behaviours and sensory issues | Prominent | Less prominent | | Speech | Delayed or unusual (echolalia, pronoun reversal) | Delayed but used socially | - The two conditions frequently occur together, so assessment must look for both.

Course and prognosis – autism is lifelong, but symptoms and abilities change with age and intervention. Children who develop useful speech by about 5 years and have higher intellectual ability usually do better; many adults with autism study, work and live independently with appropriate support, while others need lifelong care. Adolescence can bring anxiety, depression and seizures, which need attention.

Management of sensory problems – identify the child's sensitivities (noise, crowds, textures of food or clothes); use ear defenders, quiet spaces, gradual exposure and sensory activities planned by the occupational therapist; avoid forcing the child into overwhelming situations.

Communication tips taught to parents

  • Get down to the child's eye level and say the child's name before speaking.
  • Use short, simple sentences and the same words for the same things; avoid sarcasm and idioms, which the child may take literally.
  • Show as well as tell – pictures, objects, gestures and visual schedules.
  • Give the child time to respond; repeat calmly if needed.
  • Follow the child's interests to start interaction, and reward every attempt to communicate.
  • Warn the child before changes ("After lunch we will go to the doctor").
  • Keep a consistent daily routine across home, school and therapy.

Nursing importance Early recognition of red flags by nurses during routine child health visits and prompt referral for intervention, along with structured, sensory-aware and family-centred care, can transform the development and quality of life of children with autism.

Conclusion Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition with deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviours, mainly of genetic and neurobiological origin – not caused by vaccines or parenting. Early warning signs include absence of babbling, pointing or words and any loss of skills. Early behavioural, speech and occupational therapy, structured teaching, parent training and supportive nursing care help children reach their potential.

question: (a) Define attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and explain its causes. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis of ADHD. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a child with ADHD, including guidance to parents and teachers. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (4 marks)

Definition Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (hyperkinetic disorder in ICD-10) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity–impulsivity that is inappropriate for the child's developmental level, begins before 12 years of age, is present in two or more settings (home, school) and interferes with functioning.

  • It affects about 5–7% of school-age children, more boys than girls (girls more often have the inattentive type and are under-recognised); it often continues into adulthood.
  • Presentations – predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive–impulsive, and combined.

Causes

  • Genetic – highly heritable; runs in families.
  • Neurobiological – dysregulation of dopamine and noradrenaline in the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia, which control attention, planning and inhibition; delayed brain maturation.
  • Prenatal and perinatal – prematurity and low birth weight, maternal smoking, alcohol and drug use in pregnancy, birth complications.
  • Environmental – lead exposure, brain injury, severe early deprivation.
  • ADHD is not caused by sugar, poor parenting or television, although a chaotic environment can worsen symptoms.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (5 marks)

Inattention

  • Fails to give close attention to details; careless mistakes in schoolwork.
  • Difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play; does not seem to listen when spoken to.
  • Does not follow instructions or finish tasks; poorly organised; avoids tasks requiring mental effort.
  • Loses things, is easily distracted and forgetful in daily activities.

Hyperactivity

  • Fidgets, squirms, leaves the seat in class; runs about or climbs in inappropriate situations.
  • Cannot play quietly; is "always on the go"; talks excessively.

Impulsivity

  • Blurts out answers, cannot wait for a turn, interrupts or intrudes on others; acts without thinking (accidents, injuries).

Consequences and associated problems – poor school performance despite normal intelligence, injuries, low self-esteem, peer rejection, oppositional defiant and conduct disorder, learning disorders, anxiety, depression, and later substance use.

Diagnosis

  • Clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria – at least six symptoms of inattention and/or six of hyperactivity–impulsivity for at least 6 months, several present before 12 years, in two or more settings, with clear impairment.
  • Information from parents and teachers; rating scales (Conners, Vanderbilt).
  • Exclude other causes – hearing or vision problems, learning disorders, intellectual disability, sleep problems (sleep apnoea), thyroid disease, absence seizures, anxiety, depression, family stress.

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Management

  1. Psychoeducation of the child, parents and teachers – ADHD is a real, treatable condition, not laziness or bad behaviour.
  2. Behavioural parent training – the first-line treatment for preschool children and important at all ages: consistent rules, praise and rewards, token economy, time-out, structured routines.
  3. School interventions – seating near the teacher and away from distractions, short tasks with breaks, written and oral instructions, a daily report card, extra time in examinations, positive feedback.
  4. Medication (usually from 6 years of age, when behaviour measures are not enough)
    • Stimulants – methylphenidate (immediate or extended release) is the drug most used in India; it improves attention and reduces hyperactivity in most children.
    • Non-stimulant – atomoxetine; clonidine or guanfacine in selected cases.
    • Side effects of stimulants – reduced appetite and weight loss, insomnia, headache, abdominal pain, irritability, increased heart rate and BP, slowing of growth, and sometimes tics.
  5. Treatment of associated problems – learning disorders, anxiety, conduct problems; social skills training; CBT for older children.

Nursing care

  • Structured environment – consistent daily routine, a quiet place for study, minimal distractions, clear rules displayed.
  • Instructions – get the child's attention first (eye contact), give one simple instruction at a time, ask the child to repeat it, break tasks into small steps.
  • Positive reinforcement – immediate praise and rewards for completing tasks and calm behaviour; avoid harsh criticism.
  • Safety – supervision during play; teach road and water safety; the child is accident-prone.
  • Physical activity – regular outlets for energy (sports, outdoor play).
  • Medication administration – give methylphenidate in the morning after breakfast, with any second dose by early afternoon to avoid insomnia; do not crush extended-release tablets; monitor appetite, weight, height (growth chart), pulse, BP and sleep; store securely (controlled drug) and keep count.
  • Self-esteem – focus on strengths and talents; protect from labelling and teasing.
  • Parent and teacher guidance – training in behaviour management, regular communication between home and school, realistic expectations, and support for parental stress.

Is it ADHD or just an active child? | Normally active child | Child with ADHD | |---|---| | Can sit and attend to interesting tasks for an age-appropriate time | Difficulty sustaining attention even in activities of interest | | Activity is purposeful and can be controlled when asked | Restlessness is excessive, purposeless and hard to control | | Behaviour varies with situations; no significant impairment | Symptoms occur in two or more settings and impair school, home and social life | | Learns from mistakes and consequences | Repeats the same mistakes; acts without thinking |

Common nursing diagnoses

  • Risk for injury related to impulsivity and hyperactivity.
  • Impaired social interaction related to intrusive and impulsive behaviour.
  • Chronic low self-esteem related to repeated failure and criticism.
  • Impaired parenting / caregiver role strain related to the demands of the child's behaviour.
  • Imbalanced nutrition related to appetite suppression from stimulants.

Practical tips for teachers

  • Seat the child in front, near the teacher and away from windows and doors.
  • Give short assignments, check work frequently and allow movement breaks (for example, distributing books).
  • Use visual timetables, checklists and colour-coded folders.
  • Praise publicly, correct privately; maintain a daily home–school communication diary.

ADHD in adolescents and adults – hyperactivity often reduces with age, but inattention, disorganisation, impulsive decisions, risky driving and substance use may continue; continued treatment, coaching and support with study and work skills are needed.

Key strategies in behavioural parent training

  1. Special time – 10–15 minutes daily of positive, child-led play to strengthen the relationship.
  2. Effective commands – get the child's attention, give one clear instruction, wait, and praise compliance.
  3. Praise and rewards – catch the child being good; use a sticker or token chart for target behaviours such as finishing homework.
  4. Planned ignoring of minor attention-seeking behaviour.
  5. Consistent consequences – time-out or loss of a privilege for rule-breaking, applied calmly every time.
  6. Structure – fixed times for waking, meals, homework, play and sleep; a quiet homework area; breaking homework into short sessions.
  7. Parents' own coping – stress management and support, as parenting a child with ADHD is demanding.

Nursing importance Untreated ADHD leads to school failure, injuries and low self-esteem. Nurses identify children with ADHD in schools and clinics, teach parents and teachers practical behaviour strategies, and ensure safe medication use with monitoring of growth and side effects.

Conclusion ADHD is a common neurodevelopmental disorder of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, of mainly genetic and neurobiological origin, diagnosed clinically from reports in several settings. Management combines psychoeducation, behavioural parent training, school accommodations and, in older children, medication such as methylphenidate, with structured, positive and safety-conscious nursing care.

question: (a) Define anorexia nervosa and explain its causes. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and medical complications of anorexia nervosa. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of an adolescent with anorexia nervosa. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (4 marks)

Definition Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder characterised by:

  1. Restriction of food intake leading to a significantly low body weight for the person's age, sex, developmental stage and physical health;
  2. Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behaviour that prevents weight gain; and
  3. Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced (body image distortion), undue influence of weight on self-evaluation, or lack of recognition of the seriousness of the low weight. - Types – restricting type (weight loss by dieting, fasting and excessive exercise) and binge-eating/purging type. - It usually begins in adolescence (14–18 years), mostly in girls, and is increasingly seen in Indian urban adolescents; it has one of the highest death rates of all psychiatric disorders.

Causes – multifactorial:

  • Biological – genetic predisposition, serotonin and appetite-regulation disturbances, early puberty.
  • Psychological – perfectionism, low self-esteem, need for control, anxiety and obsessional traits, difficulty expressing emotions.
  • Family factors – high expectations, conflict, overprotection; family history of eating disorders, depression or anxiety (the family is now seen as an important part of the solution, not as the cause).
  • Sociocultural – the "thin ideal" in media and social media, dieting culture, teasing about weight, activities emphasising weight (modelling, dance, athletics).
  • Triggers – puberty, stressful life events, starting a diet.

(b) Clinical features and medical complications (5 marks)

Psychological and behavioural features

  • Marked weight loss or failure to gain expected weight in a growing adolescent.
  • Preoccupation with food, calories and body shape; food rituals (cutting food into small pieces, eating slowly, hiding food); avoiding family meals.
  • Excessive exercise; denial of hunger and of being underweight; sees self as fat despite being thin.
  • Irritability, social withdrawal, depression, anxiety, obsessive features.
  • In the binge-purge type – episodes of binge eating and self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives or diuretics.

Physical features and medical complications (mainly due to starvation)

  • Cardiovascular – bradycardia, hypotension, postural dizziness, arrhythmias (risk of sudden death), reduced heart size.
  • Temperature – hypothermia, cold intolerance, cold blue extremities.
  • Skin and hair – dry skin, lanugo (fine downy hair), hair loss, yellowish skin (carotenaemia).
  • Endocrine – amenorrhoea or delayed puberty, low sex hormones, osteoporosis and fractures, growth retardation.
  • Gastrointestinal – constipation, delayed gastric emptying, abdominal discomfort.
  • Blood and metabolic – anaemia, low white cell count, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, especially with purging).
  • Purging complications – dental enamel erosion, enlarged parotid glands, calluses on knuckles, oesophageal injury.
  • Refeeding syndrome during early nutritional rehabilitation.
  • Depression and risk of suicide.

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Management – by a multidisciplinary team (psychiatrist, paediatrician/physician, dietitian, psychologist, nurse, family).

  1. Medical assessment and stabilisation – vital signs, ECG, electrolytes, blood sugar, blood count; hospitalisation for very low weight, rapid weight loss, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbances, fainting, refusal to eat or suicidal risk.
  2. Nutritional rehabilitation – a structured meal plan prepared by a dietitian; intake is started cautiously and increased gradually, with nasogastric feeding only if needed; prevention of refeeding syndrome by daily monitoring of phosphate, potassium and magnesium in the first week, and thiamine supplementation.
  3. Psychological treatment
    • Family-based treatment (FBT) – the first-line treatment for adolescents: parents are coached to take charge of their child's eating until health is restored, then control is gradually returned.
    • Enhanced cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT-E) for older adolescents and adults; interpersonal and psychodynamic therapies.
  4. Medication – no drug treats the core illness; antidepressants or low-dose antipsychotics may be used for associated depression, anxiety or obsessive thinking.
  5. Long-term follow-up and relapse prevention.

Nursing care

  1. Therapeutic alliance – a warm, non-judgemental, consistent relationship; understand that the illness, not the adolescent, resists eating; avoid power struggles and arguments about food.
  2. Monitoring physical status – vital signs including postural pulse and BP, temperature, ECG as ordered, intake and output, weight measured at the same time and in the same way (for example, after voiding, in a hospital gown) according to unit policy; laboratory results.
  3. Supervised meals – the nurse stays with the patient during meals and snacks for an agreed time, offers support and encouragement, and observes for hiding or discarding food; supervision after meals to prevent purging, as per the care plan.
  4. Activity – limit excessive exercise while medically unstable; gradually introduce appropriate activity.
  5. Refeeding safety – watch for oedema, breathlessness, palpitations, confusion or weakness and report; ensure ordered electrolyte tests.
  6. Body image and self-esteem – encourage expression of feelings; focus on health, strengths and interests rather than appearance; avoid comments on weight or body shape.
  7. Positive reinforcement – recognise progress in eating and cooperation (for example, with privileges agreed in the plan).
  8. Safety – assess mood and suicide risk regularly.
  9. Family involvement – educate the family about the illness, refeeding and meal support; reduce blame and conflict; support siblings.
  10. Discharge planning – meal plan, follow-up with the team, early warning signs of relapse, school liaison.

Differences between anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa | Feature | Anorexia nervosa | Bulimia nervosa | |---|---|---| | Body weight | Significantly low | Usually normal or slightly above normal | | Main behaviour | Restriction of intake, excessive exercise | Recurrent binges followed by compensatory behaviour | | Awareness of illness | Often denies the problem | Usually aware and ashamed; hides it | | Amenorrhoea | Common | Less common; irregular periods | | Personality | Perfectionist, controlled | Impulsive, emotionally unstable | | Medical risk | Starvation effects, bradycardia, osteoporosis, refeeding syndrome | Electrolyte imbalance, dental erosion, oesophageal injury |

Warning signs for parents and teachers – rapid weight loss or failure to grow, skipping meals, rigid food rules, sudden vegetarian or "clean eating" claims used to restrict food, excessive exercise even when unwell, wearing loose clothes to hide the body, frequent weighing, going to the toilet immediately after meals, withdrawal from friends and irritability. Early referral greatly improves the outcome.

Prevention and the role of family and school

  • Promote a healthy, non-judgemental attitude to food and body size at home and in school; avoid teasing or comments about weight.
  • Teach media literacy – that images in media and social media are often edited and unrealistic.
  • Encourage regular family meals and open communication about feelings.
  • Sports coaches and dance teachers should focus on health and strength rather than weight.
  • School health nurses should screen for weight loss and eating concerns and refer early; early treatment gives the best chance of full recovery.

Nursing importance Anorexia nervosa can be fatal, but recovery is possible with early, sustained treatment. Nurses provide the daily structure, medical monitoring, meal support and emotional care that make nutritional and psychological recovery possible.

Conclusion Anorexia nervosa is characterised by restriction of food intake, low body weight, fear of weight gain and body image disturbance, arising from biological, psychological, family and sociocultural factors. Starvation causes serious cardiac, metabolic, endocrine and bone complications. Management includes medical stabilisation, careful nutritional rehabilitation with prevention of refeeding syndrome, family-based treatment or CBT, and skilled, compassionate nursing care with family involvement.

question: Explain bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Bulimia nervosa Definition – an eating disorder with:

  1. Recurrent episodes of binge eating – eating an unusually large amount of food in a short period with a sense of loss of control;
  2. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain – self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise;
  3. Both occurring on average at least once a week for 3 months; and
  4. Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight. - Most patients have a normal or near-normal weight, so the illness is often hidden; it usually begins in late adolescence and young adulthood, mostly in women.

Causes – low self-esteem, depression, anxiety, impulsivity, history of dieting, trauma or abuse, family and sociocultural pressures; often associated with depression, substance use and personality disorders.

Clinical features and complications

  • Secret binges, often triggered by stress or negative mood, followed by guilt and purging.
  • Hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting) – weakness, arrhythmias, kidney problems.
  • Dental enamel erosion, enlarged parotid glands, sore throat, calluses on the knuckles (Russell's sign).
  • Oesophagitis, oesophageal tears, bloating, constipation (laxative misuse), dehydration, menstrual irregularity.
  • Depression and risk of self-harm.

Binge-eating disorder

  • Recurrent binge eating with loss of control and marked distress, but without regular compensatory behaviours; often associated with obesity, diabetes and hypertension; affects both sexes.

Management

  • Cognitive behaviour therapy (enhanced CBT-E) – the most effective treatment: establishing a regular eating pattern, identifying triggers, challenging thoughts about weight and shape, alternative coping strategies, relapse prevention.
  • Medication – fluoxetine reduces binge–purge episodes in bulimia; treatment of depression and anxiety.
  • Medical care – correction of electrolytes, dental care; weight management for those with obesity in binge-eating disorder (without severe dieting, which triggers binges).

Nursing management

  • Build trust and a non-judgemental relationship; encourage honest reporting of binges and purging.
  • Help plan regular meals and snacks; teach the patient to keep a food and mood diary to identify triggers.
  • Supervision after meals in hospital to prevent vomiting, as per plan; monitor weight, vital signs and serum potassium.
  • Teach alternative coping strategies – relaxation, distraction, problem solving, assertive expression of feelings.
  • Dental hygiene advice (rinse with water after vomiting, avoid brushing immediately after).
  • Assess mood and suicide risk; involve the family; link to follow-up therapy.

Conclusion Bulimia nervosa consists of recurrent binges with compensatory purging in a person of usually normal weight, and binge-eating disorder of binges without purging, often with obesity. CBT that restores regular eating and addresses thoughts about shape and weight, fluoxetine, correction of medical complications and supportive nursing care lead to recovery in many patients.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: Explain specific learning disorder in children and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Specific learning disorder (SLD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder in which a child has persistent difficulty in learning and using academic skills – reading, writing or mathematics – that is well below the level expected for age, despite normal intelligence, adequate teaching and absence of visual, hearing or neurological causes. The difficulties persist for at least 6 months in spite of extra help. It affects about 5–15% of school children.

Types

  1. With impairment in reading (dyslexia) – slow, effortful, inaccurate reading; guessing words; reversal of letters (b/d, p/q) and words (was/saw); poor comprehension.
  2. With impairment in written expression (dysgraphia) – poor spelling, grammar and punctuation, poorly organised sentences, slow and illegible handwriting.
  3. With impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia) – difficulty with number sense, memorising number facts, calculation and mathematical reasoning.

Causes – genetic factors (runs in families), differences in brain areas involved in language and number processing, prematurity and low birth weight; not due to laziness or low intelligence.

Associated problems – ADHD (common), anxiety, low self-esteem, behaviour problems, school refusal and drop-out if not identified.

Assessment

  • History from parents and teachers, school records, examination of vision and hearing.
  • Psychoeducational assessment – IQ testing (normal) and tests of reading, writing and arithmetic (for example, the NIMHANS Index for Specific Learning Disabilities) showing a gap between ability and achievement.

Management

  • Remedial education by special educators – structured, multisensory teaching (seeing, hearing, touching, moving), phonics-based reading programmes, step-by-step mathematics.
  • Individualised education plan with regular review.
  • Accommodations in school and examinations – extra time, a reader or scribe, use of a calculator, oral tests, exemption from a second or third language as per board rules.
  • Assistive technology – audiobooks, text-to-speech and spell-check software.
  • SLD is recognised as a disability under the RPwD Act, 2016, entitling eligible students to certification and support.
  • Treatment of ADHD and emotional problems; counselling to build self-esteem.

Role of the nurse

  • Early identification in school health programmes – children with poor school performance despite normal ability; referral for assessment.
  • Educate parents and teachers that the child is not lazy or stupid; encourage praise for effort and strengths.
  • Support the child emotionally; coordinate with special educators and the school.

Conclusion Specific learning disorder is a neurodevelopmental difficulty in reading (dyslexia), writing (dysgraphia) or mathematics (dyscalculia) in children of normal intelligence. Early identification, remedial multisensory education, school and examination accommodations and emotional support enable these children to succeed academically.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: Explain conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder in children and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Conduct disorder (CD) Definition – a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate social norms or rules are violated, with at least three of the following in the past 12 months:

  1. Aggression to people and animals – bullying, fights, use of weapons, cruelty to people or animals, robbery, forcing sexual activity.
  2. Destruction of property – fire setting, vandalism.
  3. Deceitfulness or theft – lying to obtain goods, breaking into houses, shoplifting.
  4. Serious violation of rules – staying out at night, running away from home, truancy from school before 13 years. - Childhood-onset type (before 10 years) has a poorer prognosis than adolescent-onset type; some have "limited prosocial emotions" (callous, unemotional traits).

Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD)

  • A pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behaviour, and vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months, mainly towards parents and teachers – frequent temper loss, arguing with adults, refusing to follow rules, deliberately annoying others, blaming others.
  • There is no serious aggression, destruction or violation of others' rights; some children with ODD later develop conduct disorder.

Causes – genetic and temperamental factors, ADHD, learning disorders, harsh, inconsistent or neglectful parenting, child abuse, parental conflict, parental substance use or criminality, deviant peers, poverty and exposure to violence.

Complications – school failure and drop-out, substance use, injuries, delinquency and contact with the juvenile justice system; conduct disorder may progress to antisocial personality disorder in adulthood.

Management

  • Parent management training – consistent rules, positive reinforcement, effective commands, non-violent discipline (time-out, loss of privileges).
  • Problem-solving skills training, anger management and social skills training (CBT) for the child.
  • Family therapy and multisystemic therapy (working with family, school and community for adolescents).
  • School-based interventions; treatment of ADHD, learning disorders and depression.
  • Medication only for specific symptoms – for example, short-term risperidone for severe aggression.

Nursing management

  • Establish a firm, fair and consistent relationship; explain rules and consequences clearly and apply them uniformly; avoid power struggles and physical punishment.
  • Reinforce positive behaviour with praise and privileges.
  • Teach anger management – recognising early signs of anger, counting, walking away, talking about feelings.
  • Ensure safety of the child and others; remove dangerous objects; de-escalate aggression early.
  • Encourage constructive activities, sports and responsibilities.
  • Educate and support parents; coordinate with school, counsellors and, when needed, child protection and juvenile justice services.

Conclusion Conduct disorder involves serious, repetitive violation of others' rights and social rules, while ODD involves persistent anger, defiance and vindictiveness without serious aggression. Both arise from child, family and social factors, and are best managed by parent training, problem-solving and anger-management skills, family and school interventions and consistent, positive nursing care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: Explain the nursing assessment of a child with behavioural and emotional disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Assessment of children differs from that of adults because children often cannot describe their feelings in words, their behaviour must be judged against developmental norms, and information must be gathered from several sources – parents, teachers and the child.

1. History (from parents, caregivers and teachers)

  • Presenting problems – onset, duration, frequency, settings (home, school), triggers and effect on functioning.
  • Developmental history – milestones (motor, speech, social, toilet training), and any regression.
  • Prenatal, birth and neonatal history – maternal illness, drugs, birth asphyxia, prematurity, neonatal jaundice.
  • Medical history – seizures, head injury, chronic illness, medications; family history of psychiatric illness, intellectual disability, substance use.
  • Temperament and personality – easy or difficult child, activity level, adaptability.
  • School history – performance, attendance, relationships with teachers and peers, bullying, teacher's report.
  • Family and social history – family structure, relationships, parenting style, conflict, abuse, socio-economic situation.

2. Physical and neurological examination

  • Growth (height, weight, head circumference), dysmorphic features, neurocutaneous markers (for example, café-au-lait spots), signs of abuse or neglect, vision and hearing, motor coordination and soft neurological signs.

3. Mental status examination adapted for children

  • Done largely by observation during play, drawing and informal conversation in a child-friendly room.
  • Appearance, activity level, attention span, interaction with parents and examiner, eye contact, speech and language, mood and affect, fears and worries, content of play and drawings (themes of aggression or abuse), thought content and perception (hallucinations in older children), orientation, memory, intelligence (approximate) and judgement.

4. Interview with the adolescent

  • Interview the adolescent alone as well as with parents; assure confidentiality within safety limits; use the HEADSSS framework – Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety.

5. Psychological and developmental tests

  • Developmental screening – Developmental Screening Test, Trivandrum Developmental Screening Chart, Denver II.
  • Intelligence tests – Binet–Kamat Test, Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC), Seguin Form Board, Raven's Progressive Matrices.
  • Adaptive behaviour – Vineland Social Maturity Scale.
  • Rating scales and screening tools – Child Behaviour Checklist, Conners scale for ADHD, M-CHAT and ISAA for autism, NIMHANS index for learning disability, depression and anxiety scales.

6. Investigations as indicated – thyroid tests, EEG, neuroimaging, genetic tests, hearing tests.

Role of the nurse

  • Create a warm, child-friendly environment with toys and drawing materials; build rapport with the child and family.
  • Observe the child's behaviour in the waiting area, play and interaction with parents and record accurately.
  • Collect history using simple language; reassure parents; arrange tests; maintain confidentiality; contribute to the team's formulation and care plan.

Conclusion Assessment of a child with behavioural and emotional disorders requires a detailed developmental, medical, school and family history from multiple informants, physical examination, a play-based mental status examination, interviewing adolescents alone, and standardised developmental, intelligence and rating tests. The nurse's observation, rapport and recording are central to accurate assessment.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: List four behavioural disorders occurring during childhood.
answer_html:
Common behavioural and emotional disorders of childhood are:

  1. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) – inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.
  2. Conduct disorder – repeated violation of others' rights and social rules (aggression, stealing, destruction).
  3. Oppositional defiant disorder – angry, argumentative, defiant behaviour towards authority figures.
  4. Autism spectrum disorder – impaired social communication with restricted, repetitive behaviours. - Others – tic disorders (Tourette syndrome), elimination disorders (enuresis, encopresis), separation anxiety disorder, specific learning disorder and intellectual disability.
  • These disorders are identified through the history from parents and teachers and need early referral to a child guidance clinic.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: What is Tourette syndrome?
answer_html:
Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental tic disorder with multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for more than one year, beginning before 18 years (usually at 5–7 years).

  • Tics are sudden, rapid, repetitive, non-rhythmic movements (eye blinking, head jerking, shoulder shrugging) or sounds (throat clearing, sniffing, grunting, words); they wax and wane, worsen with stress and are often preceded by an urge that is relieved by the tic.
  • Coprolalia (involuntary obscene words) occurs only in a minority.
  • Commonly associated with ADHD and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
  • Management – education of family and school, habit reversal training / comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (CBIT); medicines (clonidine, aripiprazole, haloperidol) only for severe tics; many improve in late adolescence.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: What is pica? State its nursing management.
answer_html:
Pica is a feeding and eating disorder in which a person repeatedly eats non-nutritive, non-food substances – such as mud, chalk, slate pencils, paper, paint, hair or ice – for at least one month, at an age when this is developmentally inappropriate (usually after 2 years) and not part of a cultural practice.

  • Seen in young children, persons with intellectual disability or autism, in iron (and zinc) deficiency and in pregnancy.
  • Complications – lead poisoning, worm infestation, dental damage, constipation and intestinal obstruction (bezoar).
  • Nursing management – check for and correct iron deficiency, deworm as prescribed, close supervision and removal of the substances from reach, behavioural therapy (rewarding appropriate eating, redirecting to safe activities), a balanced diet with regular meals, and education of parents and caregivers.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: What is separation anxiety disorder?
answer_html:
Separation anxiety disorder is excessive and developmentally inappropriate fear or anxiety about separation from home or attachment figures (usually parents), lasting at least 4 weeks in children, and causing distress or impairment.

  • Features – excessive distress when separation occurs or is expected, persistent worry that harm will come to parents or that some event will cause separation, reluctance or refusal to go to school or sleep alone, nightmares about separation, and physical complaints (headache, stomach-ache) on separation.
  • Some separation anxiety is normal between 8 months and 3 years; the disorder is diagnosed when it persists or is excessive for the child's age.
  • Management – reassurance and psychoeducation of parents, CBT with graded exposure to separation, consistent routines, avoiding overprotection, cooperation with school; SSRIs only in severe cases.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Behavioural and Emotional Disorders of Childhood and Adolescence
question: State the nursing points in giving stimulant medication to a child with ADHD.
answer_html:
Nursing points for stimulant medication (for example, methylphenidate)

  • Give the dose in the morning, with or after breakfast, and any second dose by early afternoon to prevent insomnia; swallow extended-release tablets whole.
  • Monitor appetite, weight and height on a growth chart (appetite suppression, growth slowing); encourage a good breakfast and evening meal.
  • Check pulse and BP regularly; ask about sleep, headache, abdominal pain, mood changes and tics, and report them.
  • Store securely (controlled drug) and keep a count of tablets to prevent misuse.
  • Drug holidays (weekends, vacations) only as advised by the doctor.
  • Combine with behavioural strategies; review benefits with parents and teachers.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: Mrs. Kamala, aged 72 years, operated for fracture of the neck of the femur, becomes acutely confused on the second post-operative night. She pulls at her IV line, says she can see insects on the wall and does not recognise her daughter. She is diagnosed with delirium. (a) Define delirium and explain its causes and risk factors. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, types and assessment of delirium. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of Mrs. Kamala. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Common causes of delirium in the elderly

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and risk factors (4 marks)

Definition Delirium (acute confusional state) is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, with disturbance of cognition (memory, orientation, language, perception), that develops over hours to days and is caused by an underlying medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, or medication. It is a medical emergency – sometimes called "acute brain failure" – and is associated with longer hospital stay, falls, later dementia and increased mortality.

  • It is very common in hospital – in about 10–30% of elderly medical patients, up to half of elderly patients after hip fracture surgery (like Mrs. Kamala), and in most ventilated ICU patients.

Causes – usually more than one:

  1. Infections – urinary tract infection, pneumonia, wound infection, septicaemia, meningitis.
  2. Metabolic – dehydration, hyponatraemia, hypo- or hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, thyroid disorders, thiamine deficiency.
  3. Hypoxia – respiratory failure, heart failure, severe anaemia, blood loss after surgery.
  4. Drugs – anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids, antihistamines, anti-Parkinson drugs, digoxin, polypharmacy.
  5. Withdrawal – alcohol and sedatives.
  6. Brain disorders – stroke, head injury, seizures (post-ictal), encephalitis, tumours.
  7. Post-operative and other factors – anaesthesia, surgery, pain, urinary retention, constipation, fever, sleep deprivation, sensory deprivation (no spectacles or hearing aid), unfamiliar ICU environment, physical restraints, urinary catheters.

Risk factors

  • Age above 65 years; pre-existing dementia or cognitive impairment; previous delirium.
  • Severe illness, frailty, multiple illnesses and medicines.
  • Visual and hearing impairment, dehydration, malnutrition, alcohol use.
  • Major surgery (hip fracture, cardiac surgery), ICU admission.

(b) Clinical features, types and assessment (5 marks)

Clinical features

  • Acute onset over hours to days and a fluctuating course – often better in the morning and worse in the evening and night.
  • Disturbed attention – easily distracted, unable to focus or follow a conversation (the core feature).
  • Altered level of consciousness – clouding, drowsiness or hyper-alertness.
  • Disorientation to time and place (and person in severe cases); recent memory impairment.
  • Perceptual disturbances – visual hallucinations (insects on the wall, as in Mrs. Kamala), illusions and misinterpretation of shadows and noises.
  • Disorganised thinking and incoherent speech; transient persecutory delusions.
  • Psychomotor changes – agitation, picking at bedclothes, pulling at lines and tubes, or slowness and withdrawal.
  • Disturbed sleep–wake cycle – sleepy by day, awake and agitated at night.
  • Emotional changes – fear, anxiety, irritability, crying.
  • Signs of the underlying cause – fever, tachycardia, sweating, dehydration.

Types

  1. Hyperactive delirium – restlessness, agitation, hallucinations, aggression (for example, delirium tremens).
  2. Hypoactive delirium – quiet, drowsy, withdrawn, slow; the commonest type in the elderly and the most often missed.
  3. Mixed delirium – alternating between the two.

Assessment

  • Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) – delirium is present if there is (1) acute onset and fluctuating course and (2) inattention, plus either (3) disorganised thinking or (4) altered level of consciousness. CAM-ICU is used for ventilated patients; the 4AT is a quick bedside test.
  • History from family – baseline mental state, onset, drugs, alcohol use.
  • Physical examination – vital signs, hydration, chest, urine, wound, bladder, bowel, neurological signs.
  • Investigations – complete blood count, electrolytes, blood glucose, urea and creatinine, liver function, calcium, urine routine and culture, chest X-ray, ECG, blood culture, oxygen saturation or blood gas, drug levels; CT brain, lumbar puncture or EEG when indicated.

(c) Management and nursing care of Mrs. Kamala (6 marks)

Medical management

  1. Identify and treat the underlying cause(s) – the most important step: antibiotics for infection, correction of fluids and electrolytes, oxygen, blood transfusion for anaemia, treatment of pain, relief of urinary retention and constipation, review and stop offending drugs, thiamine in alcohol users.
  2. Non-pharmacological measures – first line for all patients (see nursing care).
  3. Medication only when necessary – for severe agitation that endangers the patient or others, or distressing hallucinations: low-dose haloperidol or an atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine) for the shortest time, as prescribed; benzodiazepines are avoided (they worsen delirium) except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
  4. Avoid physical restraints, which increase agitation and injury.

Nursing care

  1. Safety
    • Nurse close to the nursing station with frequent observation; low bed, call bell within reach, non-slip footwear, adequate lighting; remove harmful objects.
    • Protect IV lines and catheters (cover or secure them); remove unnecessary tubes as early as possible.
    • Avoid restraints – use a sitter or family member to stay with her instead.
  2. Reorientation and communication
    • Introduce yourself each time; call her by name; use short, simple sentences, one at a time, in a calm voice; face her and maintain eye contact.
    • Provide clocks, calendars and orientation boards; tell her where she is and why, gently and repeatedly.
    • Do not argue about hallucinations – reassure her that she is safe and that you do not see insects; switch on the light and remove shadows.
  3. Environment
    • Well-lit during the day, dim and quiet at night; reduce noise and alarms; avoid frequent changes of room and staff.
    • Familiar objects and family – encourage her daughter to stay, bring photographs and talk about familiar topics.
  4. Sensory aids – make sure she wears her spectacles, hearing aid and dentures.
  5. Sleep – promote a normal sleep pattern: daytime activity and natural light, avoiding daytime naps, grouping night-time care to avoid waking her, a warm drink, avoiding sedatives.
  6. Hydration and nutrition – encourage and assist with fluids and meals; maintain an intake and output chart; correct dehydration.
  7. Elimination – regular toileting, check for urinary retention (bladder scan) and constipation; avoid catheters unless needed.
  8. Pain management – regular analgesia after surgery (untreated pain causes delirium); use observational pain scales if she cannot report pain.
  9. Mobility – early mobilisation with physiotherapy as allowed after surgery; prevent falls and pressure sores.
  10. Monitoring – vital signs, SpO2, level of consciousness, daily CAM assessment, intake and output, laboratory results and response to treatment; report any deterioration.
  11. Medication safety – give antipsychotics as prescribed and watch for over-sedation, falls and extrapyramidal effects.
  12. Family support and education – explain that delirium is a temporary, treatable condition caused by her illness, not madness; teach them how to orient and comfort her; warn that recovery may take days to weeks and that she should be followed up for memory problems.

Prevention – early mobilisation, hydration, nutrition, sleep, sensory aids, orientation, avoidance of unnecessary drugs and catheters, and good pain control prevent about one-third of cases of delirium in elderly patients.

Nursing importance Nurses are with patients round the clock and are best placed to notice the early, fluctuating changes of delirium – especially the quiet, hypoactive type. Prompt recognition, search for the cause and calm, structured, non-restraining care save lives and reduce long-term cognitive decline.

Conclusion Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition caused by medical illness, drugs or withdrawal, common in elderly post-operative patients like Mrs. Kamala. It presents with inattention, disorientation, hallucinations and sleep–wake disturbance in hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed forms and is detected with the CAM. Management is treatment of the cause with non-drug measures – safety, reorientation, sensory aids, sleep, hydration and family presence – and cautious use of low-dose antipsychotics only when needed.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: Mr. Sharma, aged 74 years, a retired teacher, is brought by his son with progressive forgetfulness for three years. He repeats the same questions, has got lost in his own neighbourhood and can no longer manage money; recently he has become irritable and suspicious. He is diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia. (a) Define dementia and list its causes and types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the stages and clinical features of Alzheimer's disease. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of Mr. Sharma, including support for the caregivers. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Stages of Alzheimer's disease
labels: difficulty with money and complex tasks – middle (moderate): disorientation
needs help with daily activities – late (severe): does not recognise family

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and types (4 marks)

Definition Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder in DSM-5) is a syndrome of chronic or progressive decline in cognitive functions – memory, thinking, orientation, comprehension, calculation, learning capacity, language and judgement – greater than expected from normal ageing, occurring in clear consciousness and interfering with independence in everyday activities. It is often accompanied by changes in mood, behaviour and personality.

  • Dementia is one of the leading causes of disability and dependence in older people; an estimated 8–9 million older Indians are living with dementia, and the number is rising with population ageing.

Causes and types

  1. Degenerative (primary) dementias
    • Alzheimer's disease – the commonest cause (60–70%).
    • Lewy body dementia – fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, sensitivity to antipsychotics.
    • Frontotemporal dementia – early personality change, disinhibition and language problems, usually before 65 years.
    • Parkinson's disease dementia, Huntington's disease.
  2. Vascular dementia – the second commonest; due to strokes and small-vessel disease; stepwise deterioration, focal neurological signs, associated with hypertension and diabetes.
  3. Mixed dementia – Alzheimer's and vascular changes together (common in the elderly).
  4. Secondary and potentially reversible causes (about 5–10%)
    • Hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency.
    • Normal pressure hydrocephalus (triad of gait difficulty, urinary incontinence and dementia).
    • Chronic subdural haematoma, brain tumour, neurosyphilis, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder.
    • Alcohol-related brain damage, drugs (anticholinergics, sedatives).
    • Depression in the elderly ("pseudodementia").

(b) Stages and clinical features of Alzheimer's disease (5 marks)

Pathology and risk factors

  • Beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein), loss of neurons especially in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex, and deficiency of acetylcholine.
  • Risk factors – advancing age, family history, the APOE ε4 gene, Down syndrome, head injury; and modifiable factors – hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity, low education, hearing loss, depression and social isolation.

1. Early (mild) stage (lasting 2–4 years)

  • Forgetfulness of recent events – repeats questions, misplaces things, forgets appointments and names.
  • Difficulty in complex tasks – managing money (as in Mr. Sharma), cooking, using the phone; word-finding difficulty.
  • Gets lost in unfamiliar places; reduced initiative; anxiety, depression, irritability.
  • Social behaviour often preserved, so the illness is easily missed or dismissed as "old age".

2. Middle (moderate) stage

  • Marked memory loss – recent memory severely affected and older memories begin to fade.
  • Disorientation in time and place; gets lost even in familiar places (his own neighbourhood).
  • The "4 As" – amnesia, aphasia (language difficulty), apraxia (inability to perform tasks such as dressing despite normal strength) and agnosia (failure to recognise objects or people).
  • Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) – suspiciousness and delusions of theft, hallucinations, agitation, aggression, wandering, sundowning, sleep disturbance, disinhibition, apathy.
  • Needs help with dressing, bathing and toileting; incontinence begins.

3. Late (severe) stage

  • Severe memory loss – does not recognise family members, even himself in the mirror.
  • Loss of speech, inability to walk, rigidity and contractures, swallowing difficulty, weight loss.
  • Double incontinence and total dependence.
  • Complications – aspiration pneumonia, urinary infections, pressure sores, falls and fractures; death usually 8–10 years after diagnosis.

Assessment and diagnosis

  • Detailed history from an informant; mental status examination.
  • Cognitive screening – Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE) for those with little schooling, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), clock-drawing test.
  • Investigations to exclude reversible causes – blood count, thyroid function, vitamin B12, blood sugar, electrolytes, renal and liver function, VDRL, HIV; CT or MRI brain (cortical and hippocampal atrophy, infarcts).

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Medical management

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors – donepezil, rivastigmine (also as a skin patch) and galantamine for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; side effects – nausea, diarrhoea, loss of appetite, slow pulse.
  • Memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate to severe disease.
  • These drugs give modest symptomatic benefit and do not stop the disease; newer anti-amyloid antibodies are approved in some countries for early disease but are costly and not widely available.
  • BPSD – non-drug approaches first; antidepressants for depression; low-dose antipsychotics only for severe distressing psychosis or aggression, for a short time and with caution (risk of stroke and death); avoid benzodiazepines and anticholinergic drugs.
  • Control of BP, diabetes and other vascular risk factors; correction of hearing and vision; treatment of depression and infections.
  • Psychosocial interventions – cognitive stimulation, reminiscence, music, physical exercise, structured daily routine; day-care centres; legal and financial planning while capacity is retained (advance directive and nominated representative under MHCA 2017); palliative care in the late stage.

Nursing care of Mr. Sharma

  1. Safety
    • Supervise him; ID bracelet or card with name, address and phone number; door alarms or locks to prevent wandering; inform neighbours.
    • Remove hazards – loose rugs, clutter; good lighting; grab bars in the toilet; lock away medicines, sharp objects, matches and chemicals; safety of the gas stove; no driving.
  2. Orientation and memory support
    • A consistent daily routine; large clocks and calendars; labels and pictures on doors (toilet, bedroom); family photographs; a notebook or whiteboard for reminders.
  3. Communication
    • Approach from the front, call him by name, speak slowly in short, simple sentences; ask one question at a time with yes/no choices; use gestures and touch.
    • Do not argue about false beliefs (such as theft) – reassure, redirect, help him look for "lost" things.
  4. Activities of daily living
    • Encourage independence for as long as possible; simplify tasks – lay out clothes in order, step-by-step instructions, easy-to-wear clothing.
    • Assist with bathing, grooming and oral care; regular toileting every 2–3 hours to reduce incontinence.
  5. Nutrition and hydration – regular mealtimes, finger foods, supervision, adequate fluids; weekly weight; in the late stage, soft food and careful feeding to prevent aspiration.
  6. Sleep and sundowning – daytime activity and exposure to daylight, limited naps, avoiding tea and coffee in the evening, calm evening routine, good lighting at dusk.
  7. Managing behavioural symptoms – look for triggers (pain, hunger, constipation, infection, noise, overstimulation); distraction, music, a calm voice; ensure safety during aggression.
  8. Physical health – supervise medicines (pill organiser), watch for side effects, infections, constipation, dehydration, falls and pressure sores; assess pain by observation.
  9. Meaningful activity – simple household tasks, gardening, prayer, music and reminiscence about his teaching career to maintain dignity and mood.

Support for caregivers

  • Educate the family about the illness, its progressive course and what to expect at each stage.
  • Teach practical skills – communication, handling difficult behaviour, safe bathing and feeding.
  • Watch for caregiver stress, depression and burnout; encourage sharing of responsibilities, respite care, day-care centres and support groups (for example, the Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India).
  • Help with legal and financial planning and access to services; be alert to elder abuse and neglect.
  • Plan for palliative and end-of-life care in the late stage with dignity and comfort.

Nursing importance Most people with dementia are cared for at home by family members. The nurse's guidance on safety, communication, daily care and management of behaviour, together with support for exhausted caregivers, preserves the dignity and quality of life of both the patient and the family.

Conclusion Dementia is a progressive decline in memory and other cognitive functions that impairs daily life; Alzheimer's disease is the commonest cause, followed by vascular dementia, and some causes are reversible. Alzheimer's disease progresses from mild forgetfulness through disorientation, the "4 As" and behavioural symptoms to total dependence. Management combines cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine, control of risk factors, psychosocial approaches and comprehensive nursing care of safety, orientation, communication, daily activities and behaviour, with strong support for caregivers.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: Explain amnestic disorders, with special reference to Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.
answer_html:
Definition Amnestic (amnesic) disorders are organic brain disorders characterised by prominent impairment of memory – especially the ability to learn new information (anterograde amnesia) and to recall recent past events (retrograde amnesia) – while attention, consciousness and other intellectual functions are relatively preserved. This distinguishes them from delirium (impaired attention and consciousness) and dementia (global cognitive decline).

Causes

  • Thiamine deficiency – Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome (chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, prolonged vomiting, hyperemesis gravidarum, after bariatric surgery).
  • Head injury; hypoxic brain damage (cardiac arrest, carbon monoxide poisoning, near-hanging or drowning).
  • Herpes simplex encephalitis; strokes affecting the thalamus or hippocampus; tumours near the third ventricle; surgery on both temporal lobes.
  • Transient causes – benzodiazepines and other drugs, ECT, transient global amnesia (sudden episode lasting hours in middle-aged and elderly people).

Wernicke's encephalopathy – an acute emergency due to thiamine deficiency:

  • Triad of confusion, ataxia (unsteady gait) and ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus, eye movement paralysis); not all features are always present.
  • Treatment – high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately, given before glucose; if untreated it progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome or death.

Korsakoff's syndrome (Korsakoff's psychosis) – the chronic amnestic stage:

  • Severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia – cannot form new memories.
  • Confabulation – unknowingly fills gaps in memory with imaginary events.
  • Disorientation in time, lack of insight, apathy; other intellectual functions relatively intact.
  • Prognosis – with abstinence and thiamine, about a quarter recover, about half improve partially and a quarter show little change.

Management

  • Treat the cause – thiamine (and other vitamins), abstinence from alcohol, treatment of encephalitis or head injury.
  • Good nutrition; cognitive rehabilitation; supportive and long-term care when recovery is incomplete.

Nursing management

  • Safety – supervision to prevent getting lost, falls and accidents; assistance with gait in ataxia.
  • Memory aids – diary or notebook, calendars, alarms, labelled rooms and drawers, written daily schedule, photographs; consistent staff and routine.
  • Reorientation – gently provide correct information; do not confront or ridicule confabulation, which is not deliberate lying.
  • Nutrition – vitamin-rich diet, supervised meals; give thiamine as prescribed.
  • Alcohol abstinence support – counselling, relapse prevention, family involvement, self-help groups.
  • Family education – nature of memory loss, the need for supervision, realistic expectations and rehabilitation services.

Conclusion Amnestic disorders cause marked loss of recent memory and new learning with relatively preserved attention and intellect. The most important cause is thiamine deficiency in chronic alcohol use, leading to Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) and Korsakoff's syndrome (amnesia with confabulation). Early thiamine, abstinence and nursing care using memory aids, safety measures and gentle reorientation are essential.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: Explain reality orientation, validation therapy and other cognitive approaches used in the care of patients with dementia.
answer_html:
Introduction Along with medicines, non-pharmacological cognitive and psychosocial approaches improve orientation, mood, behaviour and quality of life of people with dementia. The choice depends on the stage of dementia and the person's needs.

1. Reality orientation (RO)

  • Aim – to reduce confusion by repeatedly presenting basic information about time, place, person and current events.
  • 24-hour (informal) RO – every staff member and family member orients the person during every contact ("Good morning, Mr. Sharma, it is Monday, and I am nurse Asha; it is time for breakfast").
  • Classroom (formal) RO – small group sessions with an orientation board (day, date, weather, next meal, place), discussion of news, festivals and seasons.
  • Environment – large clocks and calendars, signs and pictures on doors, newspapers, consistent routines.
  • Best for mild to moderate dementia and delirium; it should be applied sensitively – repeatedly confronting a person with severe dementia with painful facts (for example, that a spouse has died) can cause distress.

2. Validation therapy (Naomi Feil)

  • Accepts the reality and feelings of the disoriented elderly person rather than correcting them; the nurse "enters the person's world".
  • Techniques – empathic listening, acknowledging the emotion behind the words, rephrasing, asking about the past, gentle touch and eye contact, matching the person's tone.
  • Example – a patient anxiously waiting for her late mother is asked about her mother and comforted, instead of being told bluntly that her mother is dead.
  • Best for moderate to severe dementia; reduces agitation and preserves dignity.

3. Reminiscence therapy

  • Discussion of past experiences using photographs, old songs, objects and life story books, individually or in groups.
  • Improves mood, communication, self-esteem and a sense of identity.

4. Cognitive stimulation therapy (CST)

  • Structured group sessions (usually 14 sessions over 7 weeks) with themed activities – word games, number games, current affairs, music, categorising objects – that stimulate thinking and memory in an enjoyable way.
  • Shown to improve cognition and quality of life in mild to moderate dementia.

5. Other approaches – music therapy, art and craft, gentle exercise, gardening, pet therapy, sensory stimulation (touch, smell), and simple purposeful tasks (folding clothes, sorting objects) matched to remaining abilities.

Nursing role

  • Assess the person's cognitive level, interests and life history; choose and plan suitable approaches.
  • Conduct sessions or guide activities; train family caregivers to use orientation, validation and reminiscence at home.
  • Keep the environment calm and predictable; observe and record responses and adjust the approach.

Conclusion Reality orientation helps confused patients in the earlier stages, validation therapy respects the emotional reality of those with advanced dementia, and reminiscence and cognitive stimulation therapy improve mood, communication and cognition. Nurses use these approaches daily and teach them to families to provide person-centred dementia care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: Differentiate between delirium and dementia.
answer_html:
Feature Delirium Dementia
Onset Acute (hours to days) Insidious (months to years)
Course Fluctuating, worse at night Slowly progressive, stable over a day
Consciousness Clouded or altered Clear until late stage
Attention Markedly impaired (core feature) Relatively preserved in early stages
Hallucinations Common, especially visual Less common (except Lewy body dementia)
Cause Acute medical illness, drugs, withdrawal Degenerative or vascular brain disease
Reversibility Usually reversible when cause is treated Mostly irreversible and progressive
Urgency Medical emergency Requires long-term care
- A patient with dementia is at high risk of developing delirium, and both may coexist.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: What is sundowning?
answer_html:
Sundowning (sundown syndrome) is the increase in confusion, restlessness, agitation, wandering or anxiety in the late afternoon, evening and night seen in people with dementia (and sometimes delirium).

  • Causes – fatigue at the end of the day, reduced light and increased shadows, disturbance of the body clock (circadian rhythm), unmet needs (hunger, pain, toileting), overstimulation or boredom, and changes in staff at shift time.
  • Management – daytime activity and exposure to daylight, limited daytime naps, good lighting in the evening, a calm, predictable evening routine, quiet surroundings, avoiding tea and coffee later in the day, checking for pain and toileting needs, and the presence of a familiar person.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Nursing Management of Organic Brain Disorders
question: What is pseudodementia?
answer_html:
Pseudodementia (depressive pseudodementia) is cognitive impairment caused by depression in an older person that resembles dementia but improves when the depression is treated.

  • Features suggesting pseudodementia – rapid onset with a clear starting point, past history of depression, depressed mood, the patient complains a lot about poor memory (people with dementia usually minimise it), frequent "I don't know" answers with little effort, inconsistent test performance and preserved attention.
  • Management – treat the depression with antidepressants and psychotherapy; cognition usually improves.
  • It is important because it is treatable; however, these patients have a higher risk of developing dementia later, so follow-up is needed.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: (a) Explain the causes and risk factors of violence in psychiatric patients and the warning signs of impending aggression. (5 marks) (b) Describe the management of a violent patient, including de-escalation, rapid tranquillisation and the use of physical restraint as per the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017. (7 marks) (c) Explain the post-incident care. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Phases of the assault cycle
labels: threats) – crisis phase (physical aggression) – recovery phase (calming) – post-crisis depression phase (remorse
exhaustion); nursing interventions at each phase: identify triggers
safety and restraint as last resort

answer_html:
(a) Causes, risk factors and warning signs (5 marks)

Introduction Violence (aggression) – verbal threats or physical attacks against people or property – is one of the commonest psychiatric emergencies. Most people with mental illness are not violent, but the risk is increased during acute illness, especially with substance use. Violence must be prevented and managed in a way that keeps everyone safe and respects the patient's dignity and legal rights.

Causes and risk factors

  1. Psychiatric conditions
    • Schizophrenia with command hallucinations or persecutory delusions, acute psychosis.
    • Mania – irritability, grandiosity, intolerance of limits.
    • Substance intoxication or withdrawal – alcohol, stimulants, cannabis; delirium tremens.
    • Delirium and dementia; intellectual disability with frustration.
    • Personality disorders – antisocial and borderline.
    • Organic brain conditions – head injury, epilepsy, frontal lobe lesions.
  2. Patient factors
    • Past history of violence – the best single predictor.
    • Young age, male sex, impulsivity, poor frustration tolerance, non-adherence to medication, involuntary admission, recent loss or humiliation.
  3. Environmental and staff factors
    • Overcrowding, noise, heat, lack of privacy and activities, long waiting times.
    • Restrictive or coercive practices, unclear rules, inconsistent limits.
    • Staff behaviour – authoritarian or provocative approach, ignoring requests, poor communication, inadequate staffing and training.

Warning signs of impending aggression

  • Motor – pacing, restlessness, clenched fists or jaw, tense posture, banging or throwing objects, slamming doors.
  • Verbal – loud, rapid or threatening speech, shouting, swearing, sarcasm, verbal threats, demanding behaviour.
  • Facial and non-verbal – staring or glaring, avoiding eye contact, flushed face, dilated pupils, rapid breathing.
  • Invasion of personal space, following staff, refusal of food or medicines.
  • Increasing psychotic symptoms (frightened, suspicious), signs of intoxication.
  • Risk assessment tools such as the Brøset Violence Checklist (confusion, irritability, boisterousness, verbal threats, physical threats, attacking objects) help predict violence in the next 24 hours.

The assault cycle – triggering, escalation, crisis (violence), recovery and post-crisis depression phases; early intervention in the triggering and escalation phases prevents the crisis.

(b) Management of a violent patient (7 marks)

1. Prevention

  • A therapeutic ward environment with activities, privacy and adequate staffing; clear, consistent rules explained to patients.
  • Early identification of triggers and warning signs; regular risk assessment; PRN oral medication offered early.
  • Training of staff in communication, de-escalation and safe holding techniques.

2. Verbal de-escalation (first-line)

  • Approach calmly with enough staff to show support (a "show of concern" rather than force); one staff member talks.
  • Maintain a safe distance (more than an arm's length), stand at an angle, keep hands visible; keep exit routes open for both patient and staff; do not corner the patient.
  • Speak calmly, slowly and softly; use the patient's name; listen actively and acknowledge feelings ("I can see you are very angry").
  • Avoid arguing, criticising, threatening, laughing, sudden movements or touching.
  • Ask what the patient needs; offer choices (talk in a quieter room, have a drink, take PRN medicine); set clear, simple limits.
  • Remove other patients and potentially dangerous objects from the area.
  • Encourage time-out in a quiet area voluntarily. (Under MHCA 2017, seclusion and solitary confinement are prohibited.)

3. Rapid tranquillisation (when de-escalation fails and there is risk of harm)

  • Oral medication first if the patient accepts – lorazepam, haloperidol, olanzapine or risperidone as prescribed.
  • Intramuscular medication if oral is refused or ineffective – commonly haloperidol with promethazine IM (widely used in India), IM lorazepam, or IM olanzapine (not given together with IM benzodiazepines), as per the doctor's order and protocol.
  • Monitoring after IM medication – pulse, BP, respiration, temperature, SpO2 and level of consciousness every 15 minutes for at least an hour, then regularly until the patient is fully alert; watch for respiratory depression, hypotension, acute dystonia (keep anticholinergic drugs ready) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; resuscitation equipment at hand.

4. Physical restraint – the last resort (MHCA 2017, Section 97)

  • Legal conditions – physical restraint may be used only when it is the only means available to prevent imminent and immediate harm to the patient or others; it must be authorised by the psychiatrist in charge; it must not be used as punishment, deterrent or because of staff shortage; it is used for no longer than absolutely necessary; the reasons and duration are recorded in the medical notes; the nominated representative is informed within 24 hours; and the establishment reports all instances of restraint to the Mental Health Review Board every month. Chaining in any form is prohibited.
  • Procedure
    • A trained team of at least four or five staff, with a team leader; plan who holds which limb; remove the patient's spectacles, jewellery and sharp objects.
    • Explain briefly and calmly what is being done and why.
    • Use soft, padded restraints; restrain in the supine position with the head raised or side-lying – avoid the prone position and pressure on the chest or neck (risk of positional asphyxia).
  • Care during restraint
