    • Continuous one-to-one observation; vital signs and circulation, colour, warmth and sensation of restrained limbs every 15 minutes.
    • Release one limb at a time at least every 2 hours for movement; offer fluids, food and toilet; maintain privacy and dignity.
    • Reassess frequently and remove restraint as soon as the patient is calm.
  • Documentation – time of start and release, reasons, behaviour, observations, care given and authorisation.

5. Treat the underlying cause – psychosis, mania, intoxication or withdrawal, delirium, pain or medical illness.

(c) Post-incident care (3 marks)

  • Physical check of the patient and staff for injuries; medical treatment as needed.
  • Debriefing with the patient once calm – discuss what happened, triggers, feelings and alternative ways to cope; reassure that care continues; restore the relationship.
  • Staff debriefing and support – review the incident, allow expression of feelings, offer support to injured or distressed staff.
  • Support other patients who witnessed the incident.
  • Documentation and incident reporting; inform the family or nominated representative.
  • Review the care plan – identify triggers, adjust medication and the environment, update the risk assessment and plan preventive strategies.

Ward-level and organisational measures for staff safety

  • Adequate staffing and skill mix, especially at night and during admissions; male and female staff on every shift.
  • Regular training of all staff in risk assessment, de-escalation, breakaway techniques and safe holding, with periodic mock drills.
  • Safe ward design – wide corridors, good visibility from the nursing station, two exits from interview rooms, furniture that cannot be thrown, unbreakable glass, removal of ligature points and loose objects.
  • Alarm systems – personal alarms or call bells, and a clear plan for who responds when an alarm is raised.
  • Clear written policy on the management of violence, rapid tranquillisation and restraint, consistent with MHCA 2017 and known to every staff member.
  • Handover of risk information at every change of shift, so that patients who are at high risk are identified early and observed more closely.
  • Therapeutic activities and structured routine – occupational therapy, recreation, physical exercise and regular contact with staff reduce boredom and frustration, which are common triggers of aggression.

Ethical and legal points

  • The patient keeps the right to dignity and humane treatment even when violent; force is used only in proportion to the risk and for the shortest time.
  • Seclusion and chaining are prohibited, and restraint is never used for the convenience of staff.
  • Every use of rapid tranquillisation or restraint is documented and reviewed, and the patient and the nominated representative are informed of the reasons.

Nursing importance Nurses are most often the first to recognise rising tension and the ones most exposed to aggression. Skilled de-escalation, safe rapid tranquillisation with careful monitoring, restraint only as a lawful last resort and good post-incident care protect patients and staff and preserve the therapeutic relationship.

Conclusion Violence in psychiatric settings is linked to psychosis, mania, substance use, organic states, personality factors, past violence and the ward environment, and is usually preceded by warning signs. Management follows a graded approach – prevention, verbal de-escalation, rapid tranquillisation and, only as a last resort, lawful physical restraint under Section 97 of MHCA 2017 – followed by debriefing, documentation and review of the care plan.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Mr. Rahul, a 19-year-old college student, is brought to the emergency department after attempting suicide by poisoning following failure in his examinations. After medical stabilisation he is admitted to the psychiatric ward. (a) Explain the risk factors and warning signs of suicide. (5 marks) (b) Explain the assessment of suicide risk. (3 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of Rahul, including the legal aspects and the prevention of suicide. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Risk factors and warning signs (5 marks)

Introduction Suicide is a major public health problem. According to the National Crime Records Bureau, about 1.7 lakh people died by suicide in India in 2024 (rate about 12.2 per lakh); family problems and illness are the commonest reported causes, and young adults form a large share. For every death there are many more suicide attempts. An attempted suicide is a psychiatric emergency and the strongest predictor of a future suicide.

Risk factors

  1. Psychiatric illness – depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, alcohol and drug use, personality disorders (especially borderline), anxiety disorders, eating disorders.
  2. Previous suicide attempt – the most important risk factor; also self-harm.
  3. Psychological factors – hopelessness, impulsivity, perfectionism, low self-esteem, poor problem-solving skills, feelings of being a burden.
  4. Life events – failure in examinations (as in Rahul), academic pressure, relationship break-up, bereavement, divorce, unemployment, debt and financial loss, domestic violence, bullying, abuse, legal problems.
  5. Social factors – isolation, lack of support, family conflict, family history of suicide, recent suicide of someone known (contagion), irresponsible media reporting.
  6. Physical illness – chronic pain, disability, cancer, HIV, recent diagnosis of serious illness.
  7. Access to means – easy availability of pesticides, medicines and other means.
  8. Demographic factors – young adults and the elderly; men die by suicide more often, women attempt more often; students, farmers and daily wage workers; sexual and gender minorities; prisoners.
  9. Recent discharge from a psychiatric hospital – a high-risk period.

Protective factors – strong family and social support, connectedness, religious and cultural beliefs, responsibility for children, problem-solving skills, access to mental health care and restricted access to means.

Warning signs

  • Talking or writing about death, wanting to die, being a burden or having no reason to live.
  • Expressing hopelessness, helplessness or worthlessness; feeling trapped.
  • Withdrawing from family and friends; loss of interest; changes in sleep and appetite.
  • Making final arrangements – giving away valued possessions, saying goodbye.
  • Searching for means; increased alcohol or drug use; reckless behaviour.
  • Sudden calmness or cheerfulness after a period of depression (may indicate a decision has been made).
  • Extreme mood swings, rage, anxiety or agitation.

(b) Assessment of suicide risk (3 marks)

  • Ask directly and empathetically about suicidal thoughts – asking does not put the idea into the person's mind and often brings relief.
  • Explore
    • Suicidal ideation – frequency, intensity, duration.
    • Intent – how strongly the person wished to die; whether he regrets surviving.
    • Plan and preparation – details, timing, access to means, precautions against being discovered.
    • Lethality of the present attempt and history of previous attempts.
    • Hopelessness, current psychiatric symptoms, substance use.
    • Protective factors and support systems; reasons for living.
  • Tools – SAD PERSONS scale, Beck's Suicide Intent Scale, Beck Hopelessness Scale, Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale.
  • Collateral information from family and friends; physical condition after the attempt.
  • Risk formulation – low, moderate or high risk, reviewed regularly, which determines the level of observation and care.

(c) Nursing management, legal aspects and prevention (7 marks)

1. Immediate care (emergency department)

  • Airway, breathing and circulation; management of the poisoning or injury according to medical protocol, in the ICU if needed.
  • Medico-legal documentation as per hospital policy; preserve samples if required.
  • A non-judgemental, caring attitude – avoid blaming or lecturing ("Why did you do this?").
  • Psychiatric referral for every patient after a suicide attempt.

2. Ensuring safety in the ward (suicide precautions)

  • Level of observation according to risk – constant (one-to-one, within arm's length) observation for high risk, including during toileting and sleep; close observation (every 15 minutes) for moderate risk; never leave the patient alone in the early period.
  • Safe environment – remove sharp objects, belts, cords, dupattas, glass, razors, medicines and chemicals; check belongings and items brought by visitors; supervise bathroom use; secure windows; use a room near the nursing station.
  • Medication safety – check that tablets are swallowed (no hoarding); give liquid forms if needed.
  • Special vigilance at change of shift, at night, early in antidepressant treatment (energy improves before mood) and when the patient appears suddenly better.

3. Therapeutic relationship and psychological care

  • Spend time with Rahul; listen; encourage him to express feelings of shame, anger and hopelessness; accept him as a person.
  • Instil hope – exam failure is a setback that can be overcome; explore other options and strengths.
  • Help him identify reasons for living and supports.
  • Problem-solving and coping skills – break problems into manageable steps; relaxation; healthy ways to deal with stress.

4. Treatment of underlying conditions – antidepressants or other medicines as prescribed; lithium in bipolar disorder (reduces suicide risk); ECT for severe depression with high suicide risk; psychotherapy (CBT, problem-solving therapy, DBT for repeated self-harm); treatment of substance use.

5. Safety planning (developed with the patient before discharge, instead of relying on "no-suicide contracts")

  • Personal warning signs; internal coping strategies; people and places that distract; family and friends to contact; professionals and helplines – Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416); making the environment safe by removing or locking up means (pesticides, medicines).

6. Family involvement – educate about warning signs, supervision, means restriction at home, avoiding criticism and academic pressure, supportive communication; family therapy.

7. Discharge and follow-up – the weeks after discharge are high risk; arrange an early follow-up appointment (within a week), telephone contact and links with college counselling services.

Legal aspects

  • Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – a person who attempts suicide shall be presumed to have severe stress and shall not be tried and punished, and the government has a duty to provide care, treatment and rehabilitation to reduce the risk of recurrence.
  • The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 has not retained the general offence of attempted suicide (old IPC Section 309); only an attempt made to compel or restrain a public servant from lawful duty is punishable (BNS Section 226).
  • Medico-legal records are maintained, and confidentiality is respected.

Prevention of suicide

  • National Suicide Prevention Strategy (2022) – aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% by 2030 through mental health services in every district, school and college wellness programmes, means restriction and responsible media reporting.
  • Means restriction – regulation and safe storage of highly toxic pesticides, limiting access to medicines.
  • Gatekeeper training of teachers, wardens, ASHAs and police to identify and refer people at risk.
  • Responsible media reporting – avoiding sensational reporting and details of method.
  • Early detection and treatment of depression and substance use; reducing stigma; Tele-MANAS and District Mental Health Programme services; life-skills and stress-management programmes for students.

Nursing importance Many people who attempt suicide are seen first by nurses in emergency departments and wards. A compassionate approach, careful risk assessment, close observation in the high-risk period, safety planning, family involvement and follow-up can prevent a second, fatal attempt.

Conclusion Suicide risk is increased by mental illness, a previous attempt, hopelessness, stressful life events, substance use and access to means, and is often preceded by warning signs. Rahul needs emergency medical care, a structured suicide risk assessment, suicide precautions, a therapeutic relationship, treatment of any underlying disorder, a safety plan and close follow-up. MHCA 2017 and the BNS treat attempted suicide as a health crisis rather than a crime, and national strategies focus on means restriction, early care and community awareness.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain the types of psychiatric emergencies.
answer_html:
Definition A psychiatric emergency is an acute disturbance of thought, mood, behaviour or social relationship that requires immediate intervention to prevent harm to the patient or others, as judged by the patient, family, community or health professional.

Types of psychiatric emergencies

  1. Suicidal behaviour – suicidal ideas with intent or plan, attempted suicide, self-harm.
  2. Violence and aggression – excitement, assault, homicidal threats, destruction of property (psychosis, mania, intoxication, personality disorders).
  3. Stupor – catatonic, depressive, dissociative or organic stupor (mutism, immobility, refusal of food and fluids).
  4. Acute psychotic states – severe agitation, frightening hallucinations and delusions, acute psychosis, postpartum psychosis.
  5. Delirium – including delirium tremens in alcohol withdrawal.
  6. Substance-related emergencies – intoxication (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants), withdrawal states, overdose of opioids or sedatives.
  7. Drug-induced emergencies
    • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability).
    • Serotonin syndrome, acute dystonia, severe akathisia, lithium toxicity, anticholinergic toxicity.
    • Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis or seizures; overdose of psychotropic drugs.
  8. Acute anxiety states – panic attacks, acute stress reaction after trauma.
  9. Dissociative (conversion) states – psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, dissociative stupor or fugue.
  10. Crises – after rape, abuse, sudden bereavement, disasters, family crises.
  11. Medical emergencies in psychiatric patients – hypoglycaemia, epileptic seizures, head injury, severe food refusal (for example, in anorexia nervosa).

Principles of management

  • Safety first – for the patient, staff and others; adequate staff; remove dangerous objects.
  • Rapid assessment – vital signs, consciousness, history from informants; rule out medical and organic causes (hypoglycaemia, head injury, infection, intoxication).
  • De-escalation and supportive communication; appropriate medication (rapid tranquillisation, antidotes, benzodiazepines); treatment of the underlying cause.
  • Legal provisions – under Section 94 of MHCA 2017, emergency treatment may be given for up to 72 hours to prevent death, serious harm or violent behaviour, with the consent of the nominated representative where available.
  • Close observation, documentation and arranging further care; involve the family.

Role of the nurse

  • Recognise the emergency early, stay calm and call for help; never manage a dangerous situation alone.
  • Keep the patient under continuous observation, record vital signs and behaviour, give prescribed medicines and watch for side effects.
  • Communicate clearly with the patient and family, explain what is being done, and hand over accurate information to the team.

Conclusion Psychiatric emergencies include suicidal behaviour, violence, stupor, acute psychosis, delirium, substance-related states, drug-induced reactions, panic and dissociative states and acute crises. Their management requires immediate attention to safety, rapid assessment to exclude medical causes, calm de-escalation, appropriate treatment and attention to legal requirements.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain crisis intervention.
answer_html:
Definition of crisis A crisis is a state of psychological disequilibrium that occurs when a person faces a stressful event or obstacle to important life goals that cannot be overcome with the usual methods of problem solving (Caplan). It is time-limited (usually 4–6 weeks) and is a turning point – it may lead to growth and better coping, or to deterioration and mental illness.

Phases of crisis (Caplan)

  1. Rising tension – the stressor causes anxiety; the person tries usual coping methods.
  2. Increasing disorganisation – usual coping fails; anxiety and helplessness increase.
  3. Mobilisation of resources – the person tries new or emergency ways of coping; the problem may be redefined or resolved.
  4. Major disorganisation – if unresolved, severe anxiety, depression, psychosis, substance use or suicidal behaviour may follow.

Balancing factors (Aguilera) – whether a stressful event becomes a crisis depends on:

  • Realistic perception of the event.
  • Adequate situational support (family, friends).
  • Adequate coping mechanisms.
  • If one or more is absent, disequilibrium continues and a crisis results.

Crisis intervention Definition – a short-term, active and focused helping process that aims to resolve the immediate crisis and restore the person to at least the pre-crisis level of functioning.

Goals – ensure safety; reduce the emotional impact; help the person cope with the present situation; prevent the development of serious psychological problems; promote growth.

Principles

  • Immediate intervention – help is given as soon as possible.
  • Action-oriented, directive approach – the helper is active.
  • Focus on the present problem and limited goals (here and now), not on long-standing issues.
  • Safety first – assess and manage suicide and homicide risk.
  • Support and hope – convey that the crisis can be resolved.
  • Enhance self-esteem and self-reliance; mobilise the person's own strengths and support network.

Steps of crisis intervention (nursing process)

  1. Assessment – the precipitating event and its meaning for the person, risk to self or others, current coping and past coping, available supports, physical and mental state.
  2. Planning – define the problem, set realistic short-term goals with the person, identify alternatives and resources.
  3. Intervention
    • Environmental manipulation – changing the situation (for example, temporary removal from an abusive home, shelter, admission).
    • General support – listening, warmth, reassurance, acceptance.
    • Generic approach – standard interventions for common crises such as bereavement.
    • Individual approach – tailored to the person's unique situation.
    • Encourage ventilation of feelings, clarify the problem, explore solutions, teach coping and problem-solving skills, link with family and community resources.
  4. Evaluation and anticipatory planning – check whether the crisis has resolved and the person has returned to pre-crisis functioning; plan how to cope with similar situations in future; refer for longer-term therapy if needed.

Role of the nurse – early identification of people in crisis (in wards, emergency, community, disasters), immediate supportive presence, safety assessment, counselling, mobilising family and community support, referral and follow-up.

Conclusion A crisis is a time-limited state of disequilibrium when usual coping fails; its outcome depends on perception of the event, situational support and coping mechanisms. Crisis intervention is an immediate, focused, active process to ensure safety, relieve distress, mobilise resources and restore functioning, in which nurses play a central role.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain the techniques of counselling used by the mental health nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Counselling is a professional, helping relationship in which the counsellor assists a person to understand his or her feelings and problems, explore options and make decisions to cope more effectively. Mental health nurses counsel patients in crisis, patients with emotional problems and their families. Effective counselling depends on specific techniques used within a trusting relationship.

Techniques of counselling

A. Building the relationship

  1. Attending behaviour (SOLER) – Sit squarely facing the client, Open posture, Lean slightly forward, Eye contact (culturally appropriate), Relaxed manner.
  2. Active listening – full attention to words, tone and body language without interrupting.
  3. Empathy – understanding the client's feelings from his or her point of view and communicating it ("You feel let down by everyone").
  4. Acceptance and genuineness – non-judgemental attitude, honesty and warmth.

B. Exploring the problem

  1. Open-ended questions – encourage the client to talk ("What has been happening since…?").
  2. Paraphrasing – restating the content of what the client said in the counsellor's own words.
  3. Reflection of feelings – identifying and reflecting the emotions behind the words.
  4. Clarification – asking for more detail when statements are vague ("What do you mean by 'everything is finished'?").
  5. Use of silence – allows the client time to think and express feelings.
  6. Focusing – keeping the discussion on the most important issue.
  7. Summarising – pulling together the main points at intervals and at the end of a session.

C. Promoting understanding and change

  1. Ventilation (catharsis) – encouraging free expression of pent-up feelings such as grief and anger.
  2. Confrontation – gently pointing out discrepancies between words and actions, within a trusting relationship.
  3. Interpretation – helping the client see a possible meaning or pattern in behaviour.
  4. Information giving – providing accurate facts about the illness, treatment and services.
  5. Realistic reassurance and instilling hope – avoiding false reassurance ("Everything will be fine").
  6. Problem-solving – identify the problem, list alternatives, weigh pros and cons, choose and try a solution, evaluate.
  7. Cognitive restructuring – identifying negative or unrealistic thoughts and replacing them with balanced ones.
  8. Relaxation and stress-management training – deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation.
  9. Motivational interviewing – resolving ambivalence about change (for example, in substance use).
  10. Anticipatory guidance – preparing the client to cope with expected future difficulties.
  11. Termination – planned ending, reviewing progress and arranging follow-up or referral.

Techniques to avoid – advising and deciding for the client, moralising, false reassurance, interrogating with "why" questions, arguing, changing the subject.

Conclusion Counselling in mental health nursing uses attending, active listening and empathy to build trust; open questions, paraphrasing, reflection, clarification and summarising to explore problems; and ventilation, problem solving, cognitive restructuring, relaxation, information and anticipatory guidance to help the client cope and grow.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain delirium tremens and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Delirium tremens (DTs) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, a medical emergency characterised by delirium (clouding of consciousness and confusion), vivid hallucinations, tremors and autonomic hyperactivity, occurring in persons with long-standing heavy alcohol use after sudden stopping or reduction of drinking.

Onset – usually 48–72 hours after the last drink, and may last up to 5–7 days.

Risk factors – previous DTs or withdrawal seizures, long duration and heavy amount of drinking, older age, co-existing illness (infection, liver disease, injury, surgery), electrolyte imbalance, malnutrition.

Clinical features

  • Clouding of consciousness, disorientation to time and place, fluctuating course, poor attention.
  • Vivid hallucinations – visual (small animals or insects – zoopsia), tactile (insects crawling on the skin – formication) and auditory; illusions; intense fear and agitation.
  • Coarse tremors, restlessness, insomnia, picking movements.
  • Autonomic hyperactivity – fever, profuse sweating, tachycardia, raised BP, dilated pupils.
  • Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium and magnesium); seizures may precede or accompany it.

Complications – dehydration, hyperthermia, arrhythmias, aspiration pneumonia, injuries, Wernicke's encephalopathy, and death (mortality is low with good treatment but high without it).

Management

  • Admission to an ICU or high-dependency unit.
  • Benzodiazepines in adequate doses – IV or oral diazepam or lorazepam (lorazepam in liver disease), given until the patient is calm and lightly sedated, according to withdrawal scores.
  • Thiamine in high doses IV before glucose, plus other vitamins.
  • IV fluids and correction of potassium, magnesium and phosphate; control of fever.
  • Treatment of infection, injury or other medical problems; antipsychotics only as an adjunct for severe hallucinations (they lower the seizure threshold).

Nursing management

  • Constant observation in a quiet, well-lit room (shadows increase misinterpretation); nurse near the station.
  • Safety – low bed, padded side rails, remove harmful objects; avoid physical restraint where possible (if used, follow MHCA 2017 rules); seizure precautions.
  • Monitor temperature, pulse, BP, respiration, SpO2, level of consciousness and withdrawal severity (CIWA-Ar) frequently; report fever, rising pulse, falling BP or decreasing consciousness.
  • Give medicines as prescribed; watch for over-sedation and respiratory depression.
  • Fluid balance – IV fluids, intake and output, oral fluids when able; tepid sponging for fever.
  • Reorientation and reassurance – calm voice, simple explanations, consistent staff, family presence; do not argue with hallucinations.
  • Position on the side if drowsy (prevent aspiration); mouth and skin care; nutrition when able.
  • After recovery – counselling and referral for de-addiction treatment and relapse prevention.

Conclusion Delirium tremens is a life-threatening state of alcohol withdrawal beginning 2–3 days after stopping drinking, with confusion, vivid hallucinations, tremors, fever and autonomic hyperactivity. Early, adequate benzodiazepines, thiamine before glucose, fluid and electrolyte correction and intensive, safety-focused nursing care reduce complications and deaths.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain psychiatric stupor and the nursing management of a stuporous patient.
answer_html:
Definition Stupor is a state of marked reduction or absence of voluntary movement (akinesia) and speech (mutism), with failure to respond to the environment, although consciousness is relatively preserved – the patient may follow events with the eyes and later remember what happened. It is a psychiatric emergency because the patient cannot eat, drink or care for himself.

Types and causes

  1. Catatonic stupor – in schizophrenia and, very often, mood disorders; with posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, echo phenomena.
  2. Depressive stupor – in severe depression; sad facial expression, extreme psychomotor retardation.
  3. Manic stupor – rare.
  4. Dissociative (conversion) stupor – after severe stress; may respond to suggestion.
  5. Organic stupor – encephalitis, brain tumours, epilepsy (non-convulsive status), metabolic disorders, drug toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome – these must be excluded first.

Assessment and management

  • Rule out organic causes – neurological examination, blood tests, EEG, CT/MRI.
  • Lorazepam challenge – rapid improvement after IV or IM lorazepam supports catatonia; continued lorazepam is the first-line treatment.
  • ECT – highly effective in catatonic and depressive stupor, often life-saving.
  • Treat the underlying psychiatric or medical condition; IV fluids and nasogastric feeding as needed.

Complications – dehydration, malnutrition, electrolyte imbalance, retention of urine and constipation, aspiration pneumonia, pressure sores, contractures, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and sudden catatonic excitement.

Nursing management

  1. Nutrition and hydration – offer fluids and soft foods patiently; nasogastric feeding or IV fluids as ordered; strict intake and output; daily weight.
  2. Elimination – watch for urinary retention (catheterisation if ordered) and constipation; regular toileting.
  3. Hygiene – bed bath, mouth care, eye care (eyes may stay open), hair and nail care.
  4. Pressure area care – turn every 2 hours, pressure-relieving mattress, skin inspection.
  5. Mobility – passive range-of-motion exercises; prevent contractures; DVT prevention (mobilisation, stockings, anticoagulants as ordered).
  6. Communication – talk to the patient as if he can hear and understand (he often can); explain every procedure; avoid saying anything hurtful at the bedside; maintain dignity.
  7. Safety – be alert to sudden excitement or aggression when stupor lifts; keep the environment safe.
  8. Monitoring – vital signs, especially temperature and BP (watch for NMS in patients on antipsychotics), respiration, SpO2, and response to treatment.
  9. Care during ECT and lorazepam therapy; support the family.

Conclusion Stupor is a state of mutism and immobility with relatively preserved consciousness, caused by catatonia, depression, dissociation or organic disease. After excluding organic causes, it is treated with lorazepam and ECT, and the nurse provides total care – nutrition, hydration, elimination, hygiene, pressure area care, prevention of DVT and respectful communication – until recovery.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain Stuart's stress adaptation model and the nursing interventions for coping enhancement.
answer_html:
Introduction Stuart's stress adaptation model (Gail Stuart) explains mental health and illness as a continuum of coping responses – from adaptive to maladaptive – resulting from the interaction of predisposing factors, stressors and coping. It guides the nurse in assessment and in choosing interventions according to the stage of illness.

Components of the model

  1. Predisposing factors – conditions that increase vulnerability: biological (genetics, health, brain chemistry), psychological (personality, past experiences, self-concept) and sociocultural (age, education, income, culture, social support).
  2. Precipitating stressors – events perceived as challenging, threatening or demanding – internal or external, their timing, duration and number.
  3. Appraisal of the stressor – the meaning the person gives to the event, expressed as cognitive, affective, physiological, behavioural and social responses.
  4. Coping resources – personal abilities, social support, material assets and positive beliefs.
  5. Coping mechanisms – efforts to manage stress: problem-focused, cognitively focused and emotion-focused; constructive or destructive (defence mechanisms).
  6. Continuum of coping responses – from adaptive responses (mental health) to maladaptive responses (mental illness).

Stages of treatment and nursing goals

  • Crisis stage – goal: environmental stabilisation and safety; nursing: managing the environment, protecting the patient.
  • Acute stage – goal: remission of symptoms; nursing: treatment planning, medication, therapy, role modelling.
  • Maintenance stage – goal: complete recovery; nursing: reinforcement, advocacy, education, follow-up.
  • Health promotion stage – goal: optimal level of wellness; nursing: health education, inspiration, validation.

Selye's general adaptation syndrome (the physiological basis) – alarm reaction, stage of resistance and stage of exhaustion with prolonged stress.

Nursing interventions for coping enhancement

  • Assess the stressors, their meaning to the person, coping style and resources.
  • Encourage expression of feelings and validate them.
  • Problem-solving training – identifying the problem and choosing practical solutions.
  • Relaxation techniques – deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, meditation, yoga.
  • Cognitive restructuring – challenging negative, catastrophic thoughts.
  • Strengthening social support – involving family, friends and support groups.
  • Healthy lifestyle – regular sleep, exercise, nutrition, limiting alcohol, tobacco and caffeine.
  • Time management, assertiveness training and setting realistic goals.
  • Spiritual and cultural resources – prayer, meaningful activities.
  • Reinforcing previously successful coping strategies and teaching new ones.

Conclusion Stuart's stress adaptation model views mental health and illness along a continuum of coping responses shaped by predisposing factors, stressors, appraisal, coping resources and coping mechanisms, and links each stage of treatment to specific nursing goals. Coping enhancement through problem solving, relaxation, cognitive restructuring, social support and healthy living helps patients move towards adaptive responses.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: Explain the maladaptive behaviour of individuals and groups in stress, crisis and disaster, and its management.
answer_html:
Introduction When stress is severe or a crisis or disaster overwhelms usual coping, people may respond with maladaptive behaviour – responses that relieve tension for a short time but increase harm, distress or dysfunction. Such behaviour can occur in individuals and can spread rapidly through groups and communities.

A. Maladaptive behaviour of individuals

  1. Emotional – severe anxiety and panic, anger outbursts, emotional numbness, helplessness and hopelessness, excessive guilt.
  2. Behavioural
    • Aggression and violence, including domestic violence; impulsive or reckless acts.
    • Self-harm and suicidal behaviour.
    • Misuse of alcohol, tobacco and sleeping pills.
    • Withdrawal and isolation, neglect of self-care and of dependants, absence from work or school.
    • Regression (childish behaviour, excessive dependence), disturbed eating and sleep.
  3. Cognitive – confusion, poor judgement, rumination, catastrophic thinking, blaming oneself or others, magical thinking.
  4. Excessive or rigid use of defence mechanisms – denial, projection, displacement, regression.
  5. Somatic – psychosomatic complaints, and conversion or dissociative symptoms (fainting, "fits", inability to walk).

B. Maladaptive behaviour of groups

  1. Panic and stampede – sudden mass flight from a perceived threat, especially in crowds with blocked exits.
  2. Mass hysteria (mass psychogenic illness) – clusters of fainting, breathlessness, headache or itching that spread by suggestion, often in schools, hostels or factories, without any physical cause.
  3. Rumours and misinformation – spread rapidly through word of mouth and social media, increasing fear and mistrust.
  4. Scapegoating and stigmatisation – blaming a person, community or group (for example, patients and health workers during epidemics), leading to discrimination and communal tension.
  5. Mob violence, rioting and looting; attacks on relief workers or hospitals.
  6. Panic buying and hoarding of food, medicines and fuel.
  7. Collective apathy ("disaster syndrome") and excessive dependence on relief, or collective denial and refusal of safety measures such as evacuation or vaccination.

Contributing factors – a sudden, severe or uncertain threat; lack of accurate information; loss of leadership and order; crowding and fatigue; emotional contagion; and previous mistrust.

C. Management and nursing interventions For individuals

  • Ensure safety – assess the risk of suicide, violence and substance misuse; remove means of harm.
  • Calm, supportive presence; reduce noise and stimulation; give simple, clear, honest information.
  • Encourage expression of feelings; teach relaxation, problem solving and healthy coping; restore routine, sleep and meals.
  • Crisis intervention and psychological first aid; mobilise family and social support; refer those with severe or persistent symptoms.

For groups and communities

  • Accurate, timely and consistent information from a credible source to counter rumours (risk communication).
  • Visible leadership and organisation – involve community, religious and youth leaders; assign roles to volunteers.
  • Crowd management – clear exits, marshals, queuing and orderly distribution of relief.
  • In mass hysteria – separate affected persons from onlookers, calm reassurance, rule out physical causes, avoid dramatic attention and close the location briefly if needed.
  • Prevent stigma and scapegoating through health education; ensure fair and transparent distribution of relief.
  • Preparedness – mock drills, community disaster plans and training of volunteers.

Conclusion Under severe stress, crisis or disaster, individuals may respond with aggression, self-harm, substance misuse, withdrawal or regression, and groups with panic, mass hysteria, rumours, scapegoating, mob violence or hoarding. Ensuring safety, calm and accurate information, crisis support, good leadership, crowd management and community preparedness – areas in which nurses play an active role – reduce such behaviour and its harm.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: What is catatonic excitement? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Catatonic excitement is a state of sudden, extreme, purposeless motor activity – restlessness, shouting, impulsive and sometimes violent acts – that is not influenced by external stimuli; it may alternate with catatonic stupor and occurs in schizophrenia, mood disorders and organic conditions.

  • It is a psychiatric emergency because of the risk of injury to self and others, exhaustion, dehydration and hyperthermia, and it may progress to life-threatening malignant catatonia.
  • Management – ensure safety with adequate staff and a calm, low-stimulus environment; lorazepam (IV or IM) as prescribed; ECT if there is no response; maintain hydration and nutrition; monitor temperature, pulse and BP; exclude organic causes and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: What is the assault cycle? List its phases.
answer_html:
The assault cycle describes the sequence of stages through which aggressive behaviour develops and subsides; recognising them allows the nurse to intervene early.

  1. Triggering phase – a stressor (frustration, refusal of a request, hallucinations) causes rising anxiety.
  2. Escalation phase – pacing, loud speech, clenched fists and threats; verbal de-escalation is most effective here.
  3. Crisis phase – loss of control and physical aggression; safety measures and, if needed, medication or restraint.
  4. Recovery phase – the patient calms down; observation continues as aggression may recur.
  5. Post-crisis depression phase – exhaustion, remorse or guilt; debriefing and planning to prevent recurrence.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Psychiatric Emergencies and Crisis Intervention
question: What is acute dystonia? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Acute dystonia is a sudden, painful, involuntary sustained contraction of muscles, an extrapyramidal side effect that usually appears within hours to a few days of starting or increasing an antipsychotic (especially high-potency drugs such as haloperidol); it is commoner in young men.

  • Features – torticollis (twisting of the neck), oculogyric crisis (eyes rolled upwards), tongue protrusion, jaw spasm, arching of the back; laryngeal dystonia can obstruct the airway – an emergency.
  • Management – reassure the frightened patient; give an anticholinergic or antihistamine injection (for example, promethazine or benztropine IM/IV) as prescribed – relief occurs within minutes; continue oral anticholinergic (trihexyphenidyl) for a few days; review the antipsychotic dose; secure the airway in laryngeal dystonia.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: (a) Explain the salient features of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017. (5 marks) (b) Describe the procedures for admission and discharge of persons with mental illness under the Act. (7 marks) (c) Explain the role and responsibilities of the nurse in implementing the Act. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Admission pathways under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
labels: 24-hour hold for assessment) – admission of minor (application by nominated representative
Board informed within 72 hours) – supported admission up to 30 days (severe mental illness with risk to self or others or inability to care for self
Board informed) – supported admission beyond 30 days (two psychiatrists
90/120/180 days) – emergency treatment up to 72 hours

answer_html:
(a) Salient features of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (5 marks)

Background

  • The Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA), 2017 received the President's assent on 7 April 2017 and came into force on 29 May 2018, repealing the Mental Health Act, 1987.
  • It was enacted to bring Indian law in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD, 2006), which India ratified in 2007.
  • It has 16 chapters and 126 sections, and its stated purpose is to provide mental healthcare and services and to protect, promote and fulfil the rights of persons with mental illness during the delivery of care.

Main features

  1. Definitions
    • Mental illness – a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgement, behaviour, capacity to recognise reality or ability to meet the ordinary demands of life, including conditions associated with alcohol and drug abuse, but excluding intellectual disability (mental retardation).
    • Mental health nurse – a person with a diploma or degree in general nursing or psychiatric nursing recognised by the Indian Nursing Council and registered with the State Nursing Council; mental health nurses, clinical psychologists and psychiatric social workers are registered with the State Mental Health Authority and are included among mental health professionals.
  2. Determination of mental illness – only according to nationally or internationally accepted medical standards (such as ICD), never on the basis of political, economic or social status, religion, caste, or non-conformity with social, moral or cultural values; past treatment alone is not a ground.
  3. Presumption of capacity – every person is presumed to have capacity to make mental healthcare decisions if he can understand relevant information, appreciate the consequences of a decision and communicate it.
  4. Advance directive – an adult may state in writing how he wishes, or does not wish, to be treated for mental illness and whom he appoints as nominated representative.
  5. Nominated representative – a person chosen by the patient (or, failing that, a relative, caregiver or a person appointed by the Board) who supports decision-making when the patient lacks capacity.
  6. Rights of persons with mental illness (Chapter V) – access to mental healthcare, community living, protection from cruel and degrading treatment, equality, information, confidentiality, access to records, personal contacts, legal aid and making complaints.
  7. Duties of the Government – mental health promotion and prevention programmes, suicide prevention, awareness to reduce stigma, training of human resources including nurses, and integration of mental health into general health services.
  8. Regulatory bodies – the Central Mental Health Authority, State Mental Health Authorities, compulsory registration of all mental health establishments, and Mental Health Review Boards at district level.
  9. Regulated admission, treatment and discharge – independent admission is the norm; supported admission is permitted only under strict conditions and review.
  10. Protection from harmful practices – ECT without anaesthesia and muscle relaxants, ECT for minors (except with guardian consent and Board permission), sterilisation as a treatment for mental illness and chaining are prohibited; seclusion and solitary confinement are not allowed; restraint only as a last resort.
  11. Decriminalisation of attempted suicide (Section 115) – presumption of severe stress, with a duty of the Government to provide care and rehabilitation.
  12. Insurance parity – every insurer must provide medical insurance for mental illness on the same basis as for physical illness.
  13. Offences and penalties – fines for running an unregistered establishment and imprisonment or fine for contravening the provisions of the Act.

(b) Admission and discharge procedures (7 marks)

1. Independent admission

  • An adult who considers that he has a mental illness and wishes to be admitted may request admission to a mental health establishment.
  • He is admitted if the medical officer or psychiatrist is satisfied that the illness is severe enough to need admission, that he is likely to benefit, and that he has understood the nature and purpose of admission and requested it of his own free will (that is, he has capacity).
  • Treatment is given only with his informed consent.
  • Discharge – an independent patient can seek discharge at any time. If the mental health professional believes that he now meets the criteria for supported admission, discharge may be withheld for up to 24 hours to allow an assessment; he is then either admitted as a supported patient or discharged.
  • The medical officer may also discharge an independent patient who no longer benefits from admission or refuses treatment.

2. Admission of a minor (below 18 years)

  • On application by the nominated representative (parent or guardian).
  • Conditions: the minor is examined by two psychiatrists, or one psychiatrist and one mental health professional or medical practitioner; he has high support needs; and all community-based alternatives have been exhausted.
  • The minor is accommodated separately from adults, in an environment suited to his age and development; the nominated representative or an attendant may stay with him (a female attendant for a girl).
  • Treatment is given with the consent of the nominated representative.
  • The Mental Health Review Board is informed within 72 hours, and admissions continuing beyond 30 days are reviewed by the Board.

3. Supported admission (up to 30 days)

  • For a person with mental illness of such severity that he has recently threatened or attempted to harm himself, or behaved violently or caused others to fear harm, or shown inability to care for himself to a degree that places him at risk.
  • Two independent examinations on the day of admission or in the preceding seven days – by one psychiatrist and one mental health professional or medical practitioner.
  • They certify that admission is the least restrictive care option, after considering any advance directive, and that the person cannot make treatment decisions independently and needs very high support.
  • Application by the nominated representative; treatment with the consent of the nominated representative, while the patient's own consent is sought as soon as he regains capacity.
  • The establishment reports the admission to the Board – within 3 days for women and minors and within 7 days for others; the patient or nominated representative can apply to the Board for review.
  • Discharge occurs when the criteria are no longer met or at the end of 30 days, unless the procedure for longer admission is followed.

4. Supported admission beyond 30 days

  • When a patient continues to need high support after 30 days, two psychiatrists assess him and the establishment applies to the Board, which decides within 21 days.
  • Permitted for up to 90 days at first, extendable for up to 120 days and then up to 180 days at a time, each period reviewed by the Board.

5. Emergency treatment

  • Any registered medical practitioner may give emergency treatment, with the consent of the nominated representative where available, to prevent death or irreversible harm, serious harm to the person or others, or serious damage to property – for up to 72 hours (or until assessment at an establishment). ECT cannot be given as emergency treatment.

6. Other routes

  • Police – a police officer must take under protection a person found wandering who appears to have mental illness and is unable to care for himself or is a risk to others, inform him of the reasons and take him to a public health establishment within 24 hours for assessment; such persons must not be kept in police lock-ups or prisons.
  • Magistrate – may order assessment or admission of a person with mental illness who is produced before him or reported to be ill-treated or neglected.
  • Prisoners with mental illness – treated in the mental health establishment of the prison's medical wing or transferred with permission.

Discharge and related procedures

  • Discharge planning – the psychiatrist in charge, in consultation with the patient, nominated representative and family, prepares a plan for community-based treatment, rehabilitation and follow-up.
  • A person must not be kept in an establishment merely because he has no family, is not accepted by his family or is homeless; the Government must provide halfway homes and supported accommodation.
  • Leave of absence may be granted to a supported patient with conditions; if he leaves without leave, the police and the nominated representative are informed and he is brought back.
  • Transfer between establishments follows the prescribed procedure.
  • All admissions, discharges, restraint and emergency treatment are recorded in the prescribed registers and forms.

(c) Role and responsibilities of the nurse in implementing the Act (3 marks)

  • Know the Act and its rules and follow the correct procedure and forms for each type of admission, discharge, leave and transfer.
  • Inform patients and nominated representatives of their rights in a language they understand – the section under which the patient is admitted, the criteria used and the right to apply to the Board.
  • Respect autonomy – assess and support capacity, give information in simple terms, obtain informed consent, respect advance directives and involve the nominated representative.
  • Provide care in the least restrictive manner – de-escalation first, restraint only as permitted, no seclusion or chaining, ECT only with anaesthesia and muscle relaxants.
  • Protect confidentiality – secure records and do not release information or photographs to the media.
  • Allow personal contacts – visitors, telephone calls and letters, within lawful limits.
  • Accurate documentation and timely reporting to the psychiatrist and the Board – admissions, consent, emergency treatment and every episode of restraint.
  • Advocacy – help patients make complaints, seek legal aid and report ill-treatment or neglect.
  • Discharge planning and continuity of care – educate patients and families, link them with DMHP, rehabilitation services and Tele-MANAS, and follow up.
  • Care of persons who attempt suicide in line with Section 115, and community education to reduce stigma.

Comparison of key admission features

Type Who applies Assessment Board involvement
Independent Patient himself Medical officer or psychiatrist Not required
Minor Nominated representative Two professionals Informed within 72 hours
Supported (≤30 days) Nominated representative Psychiatrist + one other Informed within 3/7 days
Supported (>30 days) Establishment Two psychiatrists Prior approval

Nursing importance The nurse is present when patients are admitted, treated, restrained and discharged, and is often the person who explains their rights to them and their families. Correct legal procedure, respect for autonomy and dignity, careful documentation and advocacy turn the rights written in the MHCA into everyday practice on the ward.

Conclusion The MHCA 2017 is a rights-based law that defines mental illness, presumes capacity, introduces advance directives and nominated representatives, lists the rights of persons with mental illness, creates mental health authorities and review boards, protects against harmful practices and decriminalises attempted suicide. It prefers independent admission and allows minor, supported and emergency admissions only with strict safeguards and review, with planned discharge into the community. Nurses implement the Act by following its procedures, informing patients of their rights, providing least restrictive care, documenting carefully and acting as advocates.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the rights of persons with mental illness under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
tags: rights of persons with mental illness
free treatment for poor and homeless
protection from cruel inhuman degrading treatment
right to personal contacts and communication
answer_html:
Introduction Chapter V of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Sections 18–28) lists the rights of every person with mental illness. These rights are legally enforceable, and every mental health establishment and professional – including nurses – is responsible for protecting them.

Rights under the Act

  1. Right to access mental healthcare (Section 18)
    • Every person has the right to affordable, good-quality mental healthcare and treatment from services run or funded by the Government, available in every district and acceptable to the person.
    • It includes outpatient and inpatient care, halfway homes, sheltered accommodation, home-based rehabilitation and child and old-age mental health services.
    • Free treatment for persons below the poverty line and for the homeless and destitute; essential psychotropic medicines free of cost in Government facilities.
  2. Right to community living (Section 19) – to live in and be part of society, and not to remain in an establishment merely because one has no family or home.
  3. Right to protection from cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (Section 20) – a safe and hygienic environment, adequate sanitation, food and clothing, privacy, protection from physical, verbal, emotional and sexual abuse, not being forced to undertake work, no shaving of head or wearing of uniforms as a routine.
  4. Right to equality and non-discrimination (Section 21) – to be treated as equal to persons with physical illness, including equal medical insurance, and to emergency facilities and ambulance services on the same basis; no discrimination on the basis of gender, sex, sexual orientation, religion, culture, caste, social or political beliefs, class or disability.
  5. Right to information (Section 22) – the patient and nominated representative must be told the provision of law under which he is admitted, the criteria used, his right to apply to the Board for review, the nature of his illness, the proposed treatment and its side effects, in a language and manner he understands.
  6. Right to confidentiality (Section 23) – information about mental health, care and treatment is kept confidential, except when disclosed to the nominated representative, to other professionals for treatment, to prevent harm or as required by law.
  7. Restriction on release of information (Section 24) – photographs or any other information about a patient cannot be released to the media without his consent.
  8. Right to access medical records (Section 25) – to obtain copies of his clinical records, unless the professional applies to the Board to withhold specific information that could cause serious harm.
  9. Right to personal contacts and communication (Section 26) – to receive and refuse visitors, make and receive telephone or mobile calls, and send and receive letters and e-mail, subject to the rules.
  10. Right to legal aid (Section 27) – to receive free legal services under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; the magistrate, police and establishment must inform him of this right.
  11. Right to make complaints (Section 28) – about deficiencies in care, treatment and services, to the medical officer, then to the Mental Health Review Board or the State Authority.

Nursing implications

  • Explain rights to patients and families at admission and display them in the ward.
  • Ensure dignity, privacy, adequate food, clothing and a safe environment; prevent abuse.
  • Protect confidentiality and refuse media requests; facilitate visits, calls and letters.
  • Help patients obtain their records, legal aid and the complaint mechanism.

Conclusion The MHCA 2017 gives persons with mental illness the rights to access care, community living, protection from cruel treatment, equality, information, confidentiality, access to records, personal contacts, legal aid and complaint. Nurses, who spend the most time with patients, are the main guardians of these rights in daily practice.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Give an overview of the Indian Lunacy Act, 1912 and the Mental Health Act, 1987, and state why the Mental Health Act, 1987 was replaced.
tags: Central and State Mental Health Authorities
answer_html:
1. Indian Lunacy Act, 1912

  • Replaced earlier British-era laws such as the Lunatic Removal Act (1851), the Indian Lunatic Asylum Act (1858) and the Military Lunatics Act (1877).
  • Used the terms "lunatic" (an idiot or a person of unsound mind) and "asylum".
  • Admission was mainly through reception orders issued by a magistrate – on petition by a relative or friend with medical certificates, or when the police produced a "wandering" or "dangerous" lunatic, or a person not under proper care or cruelly treated; criminal lunatics were admitted by Government order; a limited provision existed for voluntary boarders.
  • Provided for licensing and inspection of asylums and for judicial proceedings regarding the property of lunatics.
  • Limitations – custodial approach focused on protecting society rather than treating the patient; stigmatising terminology; legal formalities before treatment; no provision for psychiatric units in general hospitals or for outpatient and community care; little concern for patients' rights.

2. Mental Health Act, 1987

  • Drafted on the initiative of the Indian Psychiatric Society, passed in 1987 and brought into force in all States in 1993.
  • Terminology – "mentally ill person", "psychiatric hospital" and "psychiatric nursing home".
  • Central and State Mental Health Authorities to regulate and coordinate mental health services.
  • Licensing of psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes.
  • Admission procedures
    • Voluntary admission – adults on their own request and minors on request of the guardian.
    • Admission under special circumstances – of a person unable to express willingness, on application by a relative or friend, for up to 90 days.
    • Reception orders by a magistrate – on application by a spouse or relative, or for wandering, dangerous or neglected persons brought by the police.
    • Admission of mentally ill prisoners.
  • Protection of human rights – no indignity or cruelty; no research without consent; correspondence not to be withheld.
  • Provisions for leave, discharge and appeals, judicial inquisition regarding property and appointment of guardians and managers.

3. Why the Mental Health Act, 1987 was replaced

  • Still hospital-centred and procedural, with little emphasis on community care and rehabilitation.
  • Did not ensure a right to mental healthcare or insurance parity.
  • Rights were stated only in general terms; no concept of capacity, advance directive or nominated representative.
  • No regulation of practices such as unmodified ECT or chaining.
  • No provision regarding attempted suicide, which remained a crime under IPC Section 309.
  • Not in harmony with the UNCRPD, which India ratified in 2007.
  • It was therefore repealed by the rights-based Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
Feature Lunacy Act 1912 MHA 1987 MHCA 2017
Approach Custodial Treatment-oriented Rights-based
Terms Lunatic, asylum Mentally ill person Person with mental illness
Key body Magistrate Mental Health Authorities Authorities and Review Boards
Capacity, advance directive No No Yes

Conclusion Mental health law in India has moved from the custodial Indian Lunacy Act of 1912, through the treatment-oriented Mental Health Act of 1987, to the rights-based Mental Healthcare Act of 2017, which emphasises capacity, choice, access to care and protection of rights.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 and other measures against drug abuse and illicit trafficking, with the role of the nurse.
tags: section 64A immunity for addicts volunteering for treatment
National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse
answer_html:
Introduction The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 came into force on 14 November 1985. It prohibits the cultivation, production, possession, sale, purchase, transport, import, export and consumption of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances except for medical and scientific purposes under licence, and provides for the treatment of addicts.

Substances covered

  • Narcotic drugs – opium and its derivatives (morphine, heroin or diacetylmorphine, codeine), coca leaf and cocaine, and cannabis (ganja and charas; bhang is controlled by State excise laws).
  • Psychotropic substances – listed in a schedule, such as amphetamines, LSD, MDMA, barbiturates and many benzodiazepines.

Important provisions

  1. Graded punishment for trafficking – based on whether the quantity is small, intermediate or commercial; trafficking in commercial quantity attracts long rigorous imprisonment and heavy fines, with enhanced punishment for repeat offenders; financing illicit traffic and harbouring offenders are also punishable.
  2. Consumption (Section 27) – consuming cocaine, morphine, heroin or other notified drugs is punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to one year or a fine up to ₹20,000 or both; for other drugs, up to six months or ₹10,000 or both.
  3. Treatment instead of punishment
    • Section 39 – a court may release an addict found guilty of consumption on probation for de-addiction treatment instead of sentencing him.
    • Section 64A – an addict charged with consumption or with an offence involving a small quantity who voluntarily seeks de-addiction treatment at a Government or recognised hospital is immune from prosecution, provided he completes the treatment.
    • Section 71 – the Government may establish centres for identification, treatment, care and rehabilitation of addicts.
  4. National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse – to finance measures against illicit traffic and for treatment and rehabilitation.
  5. Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) – the central agency for enforcement and coordination, set up in 1986.

Related laws and measures

  • Prevention of Illicit Traffic in NDPS Act, 1988 (PIT-NDPS) – preventive detention of traffickers.
  • Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 – controls manufacture and sale of medicines, including sedatives.
  • Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), 2003 – tobacco control; State excise and prohibition laws regulate alcohol.
  • Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan – a national campaign for awareness, community participation and de-addiction services; the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction supports prevention, treatment and rehabilitation through Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts.
  • MANAS (National Narcotics Helpline, 1933) – launched in 2024 for reporting drug trafficking and seeking advice on de-addiction and rehabilitation.

Role of the nurse

  • Safe custody of controlled drugs – double-locked cupboards, controlled drugs register, counting at handover, witnessing disposal, reporting losses.
  • Prevention – health education in schools, colleges, workplaces and communities on the dangers of drugs and the legal consequences.
  • Early identification and referral of persons with drug use to de-addiction centres; informing them about treatment as an alternative to prosecution (Sections 39 and 64A).
  • Care in de-addiction centres – withdrawal management, counselling, relapse prevention, family therapy and rehabilitation.
  • Maintaining confidentiality while following legal requirements; supporting families and self-help groups.

Conclusion The NDPS Act, 1985 prohibits non-medical use and trafficking of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, punishes trafficking severely and consumption mildly, and favours treatment for addicts through probation, immunity for those seeking treatment and Government treatment centres. Along with PIT-NDPS, COTPA, Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan and the MANAS helpline, it forms India's response to drug abuse, in which nurses contribute to safe drug custody, prevention, treatment and rehabilitation.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain forensic psychiatry, the criminal and civil responsibility of persons with mental illness, and the role of the forensic psychiatric nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Forensic psychiatry is the branch of psychiatry that deals with the legal aspects of mental illness – the assessment and treatment of persons with mental disorders who come into contact with the law, and the provision of expert opinion to courts.

A. Criminal responsibility

  1. Unsoundness of mind (insanity defence) – Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 (formerly IPC Section 84): nothing is an offence if, at the time of the act, the person, by reason of unsoundness of mind, was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. This is based on the McNaughten rules. Only legal insanity at the time of the act counts, not merely a diagnosis of mental illness.
  2. Intoxication
    • Involuntary intoxication (caused without his knowledge or against his will) that makes a person incapable of knowing the nature of the act is a defence (BNS Section 23, formerly IPC 85).
    • Voluntary intoxication is not a defence; the person is treated as having the same knowledge as a sober person.
  3. Fitness to stand trial – an accused who, because of unsoundness of mind or intellectual disability, cannot understand the proceedings or make his defence is not tried until fit. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, Chapter XXVII (formerly CrPC Sections 328–339) provides that the court refers the accused to the civil surgeon, who refers him to a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist of a Government hospital or medical college; the court may then release him on security for treatment or order care in a mental health establishment, and resume the trial when he becomes fit.
  4. Acquittal on the ground of unsoundness of mind – the court records the finding and orders safe custody or treatment of the person.
  5. Prisoners who develop mental illness – treated in the prison mental health unit or transferred under the MHCA 2017.

B. Civil responsibility

  • Contracts – a contract made by a person of unsound mind, who cannot understand it and judge its effect on his interests, is not valid (Indian Contract Act, 1872).
  • Will (testamentary capacity) – a valid will requires that the testator understands what he is doing, the extent of his property and the claims of his relatives, at the time of making it.
  • Marriage and divorce – under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a marriage is voidable if a party was incapable of valid consent because of unsoundness of mind, and severe incurable mental disorder is a ground for divorce.
  • Competence as a witness – a person of unsound mind can testify unless the illness prevents him from understanding the questions and giving rational answers (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 124, formerly Evidence Act 118).
  • Management of property and guardianship – through the nominated representative and courts; under the National Trust Act, 1999, legal guardians may be appointed for persons with intellectual disability, autism or cerebral palsy.

C. Role of the forensic psychiatric nurse

  • Care of forensic patients in forensic wards, prisons and courts – undertrials, persons acquitted on the ground of unsoundness of mind and prisoners with mental illness.
  • Assessment and observation – accurate, objective recording of behaviour, mental state and response to treatment, which may be used in court.
  • Risk assessment and management – violence, suicide and absconding; safety of patients, staff and the public.
  • Treatment and rehabilitation – medication, counselling, life-skills training and preparation for return to the community.
  • Legal duties – maintaining custody records, preparing reports, giving evidence in court when required, and respecting the rights of patients even in custody.
  • Balancing the dual role of carer and custodian ethically.

Conclusion Forensic psychiatry links mental health and law. Persons who, owing to unsoundness of mind, cannot know the nature or wrongfulness of their acts are not criminally responsible (BNS Section 22), and accused persons who are unfit to stand trial are treated before trial under the BNSS. Mental illness also affects contracts, wills, marriage and testimony. The forensic psychiatric nurse provides safe, therapeutic and lawful care to these patients and accurate records for the courts.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: What are the types of admission under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017?
answer_html:
1. Independent admission (Sections 85–86) – an adult with capacity admitted at his own request; may seek discharge at any time (subject to a 24-hour hold for assessment).
  2. Admission of a minor (Section 87) – on application by the nominated representative, after assessment by two professionals; the Board is informed within 72 hours.
  3. Supported admission up to 30 days (Section 89) – for a person with severe mental illness who is a risk to himself or others or unable to care for himself, on application by the nominated representative, after two independent examinations.
  4. Supported admission beyond 30 days (Section 90) – after assessment by two psychiatrists, with the Board's approval, for 90, 120 and then 180 days at a time. - In addition, emergency treatment may be given for up to 72 hours (Section 94), and persons may be brought for assessment by the police or on a magistrate's order, while prisoners with mental illness are treated under special provisions.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: What is an advance directive under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017? How does it differ from a living will?
answer_html:
• Advance directive (Section 5) – a written document in which an adult states, while he has capacity, how he wishes to be cared for and treated for mental illness, how he does not wish to be treated, and whom he appoints as his nominated representative.
  • It comes into effect only when he loses capacity to make mental healthcare decisions; it is registered with the Mental Health Review Board, can be revoked or changed at any time, does not apply to emergency treatment, and may be modified by the Board on application by a professional or relative.
  • Difference – a living will (recognised by the Supreme Court in the Common Cause case, 2018) concerns refusal of life-prolonging treatment at the end of life, whereas a mental health advance directive concerns the treatment of mental illness during a future episode.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Who is a nominated representative? State the duties.
answer_html:
A nominated representative is a person appointed by a person with mental illness (an adult) to support him in making mental healthcare decisions and to act for him when he lacks capacity (Section 14).

  • If none has been appointed, the following act in order of precedence – the person named in the advance directive, a relative, a caregiver, a suitable person appointed by the Board or, if none, the Director of Social Welfare; for a minor, the legal guardian.
  • Duties – consider the patient's current and past wishes, values, culture and best interests; support him in decision-making; seek information on diagnosis and treatment; give consent where the Act allows; be involved in discharge planning; and apply to the Board on his behalf against any violation of his rights.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Write the composition and functions of the Mental Health Review Board.
tags: persons with mental illness or caregivers
answer_html:
Mental Health Review Boards are quasi-judicial bodies constituted by the State Mental Health Authority for districts or groups of districts (Section 73).

  • Composition (Section 74) – a District Judge (serving or retired) as chairperson; a representative of the District Collector or District Magistrate; one psychiatrist and one medical practitioner; and two persons with mental illness, caregivers or representatives of organisations working in mental health.
  • Functions – register, review or cancel advance directives; appoint nominated representatives; review supported admissions and decide applications against them; decide on withholding of medical records; hear complaints about deficiencies in care; permit ECT for minors and psychosurgery; and inspect prisons. Its decisions can be appealed in the High Court within 30 days.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: Define mental illness as per the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
tags: substantial disorder of thinking mood perception orientation memory
answer_html:
• According to the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, mental illness means "a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgment, behaviour, capacity to recognise reality or ability to meet the ordinary demands of life", and includes mental conditions associated with the abuse of alcohol and drugs, but does not include mental retardation (intellectual disability).
  • Mental illness is determined only according to nationally or internationally accepted medical standards (such as WHO's ICD), and not on the basis of social, economic, political, religious or cultural grounds or past treatment alone.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Legal Issues in Mental Health Nursing
question: What are the McNaughten rules?
tags: nature and quality of the act
answer_html:
• The McNaughten (M'Naghten) rules were laid down by the House of Lords in England in 1843, after Daniel M'Naghten, who suffered from persecutory delusions, was acquitted of killing the Prime Minister's secretary.
  • They state that every person is presumed to be sane, and that to establish a defence of insanity it must be proved that, at the time of the act, the accused was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing, or, if he did know it, that he did not know that what he was doing was wrong.
  • Section 22 of the BNS (formerly IPC Section 84) is based on these rules; other tests include the irresistible impulse test and the Durham rule.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: (a) Explain the objectives, strategies and components of the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP). (5 marks) (b) Describe the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) and the National Tele Mental Health Programme (Tele-MANAS). (6 marks) (c) Explain the role of the nurse in the implementation of the NMHP. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Mental health service network under the NMHP
labels: community volunteers) – Ayushman Arogya Mandir (sub-centre and PHC; community health officer
medical officer) – CHC and DMHP outreach clinics – district hospital (DMHP team: psychiatrist
day care) – medical college psychiatry departments
State mental hospitals and national institutes (NIMHANS
LGBRIMH) – Tele-MANAS cells (14416) linking all levels

answer_html:
(a) Objectives, strategies and components of the NMHP (5 marks)

Background Mental disorders are a leading cause of disability in India, and the National Mental Health Survey (2015–16) found a treatment gap of about 70–92% for different disorders, with very few psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and psychiatric nurses. To bring basic mental healthcare to all, the Government of India adopted the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) in August 1982, following the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) and WHO's recommendations; India was among the first developing countries to have such a programme.

Objectives (1982)

  1. To ensure the availability and accessibility of minimum mental healthcare for all in the foreseeable future, particularly to the most vulnerable and underprivileged sections of the population.
  2. To encourage the application of mental health knowledge in general health care and in social development.
  3. To promote community participation in the development of mental health services and to stimulate efforts towards self-help in the community.

Strategies (approaches)

  • Integration of mental health with general health services – mental healthcare through existing primary health care rather than only through mental hospitals.
  • Use of the existing infrastructure of health services.
  • Task-oriented, short-term training of existing health staff – medical officers, health workers and supervisors – to recognise and manage common mental disorders.
  • Linkage with community development programmes and involvement of the community.

Components (original programme)

  1. Treatment – at every level of the health system:
    • Village and sub-centre – health workers and supervisors, under the medical officer, identify and manage psychiatric emergencies, supervise chronic patients on maintenance treatment and refer cases.
    • Primary health centre – the medical officer, assisted by health workers, diagnoses and treats common mental illnesses and epilepsy, manages emergencies and refers difficult cases.
    • District hospital – a psychiatrist and a psychiatric unit to treat referred patients and support the PHCs.
    • Mental hospitals and teaching psychiatric units – care of difficult cases, teaching, training and research.
  2. Rehabilitation – maintenance treatment of persons with psychoses and epilepsy in the community, and rehabilitation units at district hospitals and mental hospitals.
