  3. Prevention – community-based prevention, beginning with alcohol-related problems and later extending to suicide prevention and promotion of mental health.

Evolution of the programme

  • 1996 – District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) added.
  • 2003 (Tenth Plan) – restructured to include modernisation of State mental hospitals, upgradation of psychiatric wings of medical colleges and general hospitals, information, education and communication (IEC) activities, and research and training.
  • Eleventh Plan – manpower development schemes: Centres of Excellence in mental health and support for post-graduate departments in psychiatry, clinical psychology, psychiatric social work and psychiatric nursing.
  • Twelfth Plan – DMHP brought under the National Health Mission with targeted interventions for schools, colleges, workplaces and suicide prevention.
  • 2014 – first National Mental Health Policy; 2017 – Mental Healthcare Act; 2022 – Tele-MANAS; mental health services added to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs – now integrated into over 1.83 lakh of them.

(b) DMHP and Tele-MANAS (6 marks)

District Mental Health Programme (DMHP)

  • Launched in 1996 in four districts, based on the "Bellary model" of Karnataka, developed with NIMHANS, in which general medical officers given short (about nine days) training successfully diagnosed and treated common mental disorders and epilepsy at PHCs. It was expanded to 27 districts in the Ninth Plan and has now been sanctioned for 767 districts, supported through the National Health Mission.
  • Aim – to provide community-based, decentralised mental healthcare integrated with general health services, with the district as the unit.
  • Components (Bellary model)
    1. Early detection and treatment – outpatient and inpatient services at the district hospital and outreach clinics at CHCs and PHCs, with free psychotropic medicines.
    2. Training – short-term training of medical officers, nurses, health workers and ASHAs in identification, management and referral.
    3. IEC – public awareness to reduce stigma and encourage early help-seeking.
    4. Monitoring – simple record keeping and reporting for planning and evaluation.
  • Additional services added later – life-skills education and counselling in schools, college counselling services, workplace stress management, suicide prevention services, day care and a small inpatient facility at the district hospital, and follow-up and rehabilitation in the community.
  • DMHP team – psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, psychiatric social worker and psychiatric (community) nurse, supported by a monitoring and evaluation officer, case registry assistant and record keeper.

National Tele Mental Health Programme – Tele-MANAS

  • Tele-MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) was announced in the Union Budget 2022–23 and launched on 10 October 2022 (World Mental Health Day).
  • Toll-free numbers – 14416 or 1-800-891-4416; free, 24 × 7, confidential, in 20 languages chosen by the States; a Tele-MANAS mobile application has also been launched.
  • Two-tier system
    • Tier 1 – State Tele-MANAS cells with trained counsellors and mental health professionals who provide counselling and support.
    • Tier 2 – specialists at DMHP and medical college resources for physical consultation or audio-video consultation (e-Sanjeevani), with referral to DMHP, hospitals and other services.
  • NIMHANS is the nodal centre, with regional coordinating centres; 53 Tele-MANAS cells work in all 36 States and Union Territories, and more than 47 lakh calls had been handled by October 2026.
  • Common concerns of callers – stress, anxiety, low mood, sleep problems, relationship and family issues, examination stress, substance use and suicidal thoughts.

(c) Role of the nurse in implementing the NMHP (4 marks)

  1. Member of the DMHP team
    • Nursing assessment, screening and mental status examination in outpatient and outreach clinics.
    • Nursing care in the district psychiatric unit and day-care centre; administration of medicines and depot injections; monitoring of side effects.
    • Follow-up home visits, tracing defaulters and maintaining the case register.
  2. Primary-level care
    • Community health officers at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, most of whom are nurses, screen for depression, psychosis, epilepsy, dementia and substance use, give first-level care, follow up stabilised patients and refer to the DMHP.
    • ANMs and staff nurses identify mental health problems during home visits, antenatal care and NCD screening.
  3. Training and supervision of ASHAs, ANMs, multipurpose workers and teachers in early identification, psychological first aid and referral.
  4. Health education and stigma reduction – awareness camps, World Mental Health Day and World Suicide Prevention Day activities, mass media and community meetings.
  5. Targeted interventions – life-skills sessions in schools, counselling in colleges, stress management in workplaces, gatekeeper training for suicide prevention, and support for the elderly.
  6. Tele-MANAS – popularise the helpline; nurses working as counsellors provide tele-counselling, and nurses at district level follow up referred callers.
  7. Rehabilitation and family support – psychoeducation, relapse prevention, linking families with self-help groups, NGOs, disability benefits and vocational services.
  8. Records, reporting and research – accurate documentation and data for monitoring the programme; participation in operational research.
  9. Advocacy – protecting patients' rights under the MHCA 2017 and helping them obtain free treatment and medicines.

Nursing importance With very few psychiatrists in the country, nurses – from the community health officer at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir to the psychiatric nurse of the DMHP team – are the backbone of community mental healthcare. Their work in screening, follow-up, training, awareness and rehabilitation determines whether the NMHP reaches people in villages and towns.

Conclusion The NMHP, launched in 1982, aims to provide minimum mental healthcare for all by integrating mental health with general health services, training existing staff and involving the community. Its operational arm, the DMHP (1996), now sanctioned for 767 districts, provides early detection, treatment, training, awareness and targeted interventions, while Tele-MANAS (2022) offers free, round-the-clock tele-mental health support in many languages. Nurses implement the programme at every level through care, follow-up, training, education, rehabilitation and advocacy.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Describe the mental health agencies – governmental and non-governmental, national and international – and their role in mental health care.
tags: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

diagram.caption: Mental health agencies
labels: Mental Health Authorities and Review Boards

answer_html:
Introduction A mental health agency is an organisation – governmental or non-governmental, national or international – that works for the promotion of mental health, prevention of mental illness, treatment, rehabilitation, training, research or protection of the rights of persons with mental illness. Since mental health needs are vast and professionals are few, many agencies work together, and the mental health nurse must know them in order to refer, network and collaborate.

A. International agencies

  1. World Health Organization (WHO)
    • Provides technical guidance, standards and support to member countries through its department of mental health and substance use.
    • Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP, 2008) and the mhGAP Intervention Guide – to scale up care for mental, neurological and substance use disorders through non-specialist health workers.
    • Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2030 – leadership and governance, community-based services, promotion and prevention, information systems and research.
    • QualityRights initiative to improve the quality of care and human rights in mental health services; the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11); the Mental Health Atlas; the World Mental Health Report (2022); and suicide prevention guidance (LIVE LIFE).
  2. UNICEF – mental health and psychosocial support for children and adolescents, especially in emergencies; parenting and school programmes.
  3. United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) – prevention of drug use, treatment standards and control of drug trafficking.
  4. UNHCR and the International Organization for Migration – psychosocial support for refugees and displaced persons.
  5. International Labour Organization (ILO) – mental health and stress at the workplace.
  6. World Bank – funding and highlighting the economic burden of mental disorders (disability-adjusted life years).
  7. World Federation for Mental Health (WFMH, founded 1948) – advocacy and public education; it began World Mental Health Day on 10 October (since 1992).
  8. Professional and humanitarian bodies – the World Psychiatric Association, the International Council of Nurses, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent (psychosocial support in disasters) and Médecins Sans Frontières.

B. National governmental agencies (India)

  1. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Directorate General of Health Services)
    • National Mental Health Programme, District Mental Health Programme, Tele-MANAS (14416) and mental health services in Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
    • Related programmes – Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (adolescent mental health), Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (early identification of developmental delays and disabilities) and the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly.
  2. Statutory bodies
    • Central Mental Health Authority and State Mental Health Authorities (registration of establishments and professionals, standards); Mental Health Review Boards (protection of rights) under the MHCA 2017.
    • The National Human Rights Commission, which monitors mental hospitals; the National Commission for Women; and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights.
  3. National institutes and mental hospitals
    • National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru – an Institute of National Importance for clinical care, training and research; it conducted the National Mental Health Survey and is the nodal centre for Tele-MANAS.
    • Central Institute of Psychiatry (CIP), Ranchi; Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health (LGBRIMH), Tezpur; Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS), Delhi.
    • State mental hospitals – in Maharashtra, the Regional Mental Hospitals at Nagpur, Pune (Yerawada), Thane and Ratnagiri; psychiatry departments of medical colleges and AIIMS; Centres of Excellence.
  4. Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
    • National Institute of Social Defence; Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan and Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts; Elderline (14567) for senior citizens.
    • Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities – the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (mental illness is a specified disability), the National Trust (for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual and multiple disabilities), the Rehabilitation Council of India and the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities.
  5. Ministry of Women and Child Development – One Stop Centres, Women Helpline 181 and the Child Helpline 1098 under Mission Vatsalya.
  6. Ministry of Education – MANODARPAN, psychosocial support for students, and school counselling through NCERT.
  7. Ministry of Home Affairs – the Narcotics Control Bureau and MANAS helpline (1933); prison mental health.
  8. Research bodies – the Indian Council of Medical Research; medical services of the armed forces and railways.

C. Non-governmental and voluntary agencies

  1. Service and rehabilitation organisations
    • Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), Chennai – treatment, rehabilitation and research in schizophrenia.
    • The Banyan, Chennai, Ashadeep, Guwahati and Iswar Sankalpa, Kolkata – care of homeless persons with mental illness.
    • Richmond Fellowship Society (India) – halfway homes and psychosocial rehabilitation.
    • Sangath, Goa – community mental health care and research using lay counsellors.
    • Muktangan Rehabilitation Centre, Pune – de-addiction and rehabilitation.
    • Schizophrenia Awareness Association, Pune; Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India (ARDSI); organisations for autism and intellectual disability.
  2. Self-help and peer-support groups – Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, Al-Anon and caregiver support groups.
  3. Helplines and crisis support – voluntary suicide prevention and emotional support helplines such as Sneha (Chennai), AASRA (Mumbai), iCALL (TISS) and the Vandrevala Foundation.
  4. Professional associations – the Indian Psychiatric Society, the Indian Society of Psychiatric Nurses, associations of clinical psychologists and psychiatric social workers, and the Trained Nurses' Association of India.
  5. Others – the Indian Red Cross Society, service clubs (Rotary, Lions), religious and charitable trusts, and foundations supported by corporate social responsibility that run awareness campaigns (for example, the Live Love Laugh Foundation).

D. Functions of mental health agencies

  • Service delivery – outpatient, inpatient, community and crisis services.
  • Rehabilitation – day care, halfway homes, vocational training and supported employment.
  • Training of professionals and community workers.
  • Research and surveillance.
  • Advocacy and protection of rights, legal aid and policy development.
  • Awareness and stigma reduction; support for families.
  • Funding and technical support.

E. Role of the nurse

  • Keep an up-to-date directory of agencies and helplines in the district.
  • Refer and link patients and families to appropriate agencies – de-addiction, rehabilitation, legal aid, disability benefits, homeless shelters and support groups.
  • Collaborate with NGOs in camps, awareness programmes and rehabilitation; volunteer and participate in professional associations.
  • Use international guidelines such as mhGAP in nursing care and training.
  • Advocate for resources and services for persons with mental illness.

Nursing importance No single agency can meet the mental health needs of a community. A nurse who knows the agencies working at international, national, state and district levels can connect patients and families with treatment, rehabilitation, legal protection and social support, and can draw on them for training and awareness work.

Conclusion Mental health care in India is supported by international agencies such as WHO, UNICEF, UNODC and WFMH; by governmental agencies – ministries, mental health authorities, national institutes, State mental hospitals and national programmes; and by non-governmental organisations, self-help groups, helplines and professional bodies. Together they provide services, rehabilitation, training, research, advocacy and awareness, and the nurse uses this network for referral, collaboration and advocacy.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Differentiate between institutionalisation and deinstitutionalisation. Explain the role of the nurse in deinstitutionalisation.
answer_html:
Institutionalisation

  • Meaning – the care of persons with mental illness in large, often isolated, long-stay institutions (mental hospitals or asylums), where they may stay for years, separated from family and society.
  • Institutional neurosis (institutionalism) – described by Russell Barton (1959): long stay in an institution produces apathy, lack of initiative, loss of interest, submissiveness, deterioration of personal habits, inability to plan for the future and loss of individuality. Erving Goffman called such hospitals "total institutions".
  • Causes – loss of contact with the outside world, enforced idleness, an authoritarian ward routine, loss of personal possessions and friends, over-sedation and lack of prospects outside.
  • Problems – stigma, overcrowding, poor living conditions and human rights violations (in India, the death of chained patients in a fire at Erwadi in 2001 led to Supreme Court directions against chaining), high cost and loss of social and work skills.
  • Advantages – safety and specialised care for a few patients with severe, treatment-resistant illness or high risk, and relief for exhausted families.

Deinstitutionalisation

  • Meaning – the process of shifting care from long-stay mental hospitals to community-based services, so that people with mental illness live in the community with support.
  • History – began in the 1950s–60s, helped by antipsychotic drugs (chlorpromazine, 1952), the human rights movement, evidence of institutional neurosis and the high cost of hospitals; for example, the USA's Community Mental Health Centers Act (1963) and Italy's Law 180 (1978), which closed asylums.
  • Three components
    1. Prevention of unnecessary admission by providing community alternatives.
    2. Discharge of long-stay patients who have been adequately prepared for community living.
    3. Establishment of community support systems – outpatient and community clinics, day care, halfway homes, supported housing, assertive community treatment, crisis services and vocational rehabilitation.
  • Problems when community services are inadequate – the "revolving door" pattern of repeated admissions, homelessness, transinstitutionalisation (to prisons, beggars' homes or nursing homes), neglect and heavy burden on families.
  • In India – the MHCA 2017 gives a right to community living and forbids keeping a person in an establishment merely because he has no family or home; the DMHP, psychiatric units in general hospitals, halfway homes and NGOs support community care.
Aspect Institutionalisation Deinstitutionalisation
Place of care Large mental hospital Community, family, general hospital
Duration Long stay Short stay, follow-up
Focus Custody and control Recovery, rights and inclusion
Effect on patient Dependence, institutional neurosis Independence, social skills

Role of the nurse in deinstitutionalisation

  • Prepare long-stay patients for discharge – training in self-care, money handling, cooking, use of transport and medication self-management; graded outings.
  • Family work – psychoeducation, counselling to accept the patient back, reducing high expressed emotion and caregiver burden.
  • Liaison with community services – DMHP, halfway homes, day-care centres, NGOs and vocational programmes; arrange follow-up before discharge.
  • Follow-up and home visits – adherence, early signs of relapse, crisis help.
  • Advocacy – for community resources, disability benefits and the patient's right to live in the community.

Conclusion Institutionalisation means long-term care in large mental hospitals, which often produces institutional neurosis and violates rights, whereas deinstitutionalisation shifts care to the community with prevention of unnecessary admission, prepared discharge and community support systems. It succeeds only when community services are adequate, and the nurse plays a key role in preparation, family work, liaison, follow-up and advocacy.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the mental health issues of people living with HIV/AIDS and the role of the mental health nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction People living with HIV/AIDS (PLHIV) have a much higher rate of mental health problems than the general population, and mental illness in turn increases the risk of acquiring HIV and reduces adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Mental health care is therefore an essential part of HIV care.

Mental health issues

  1. Psychological reactions to the diagnosis – shock, disbelief, denial, fear of death, anger, guilt and grief; worry about disclosure to spouse and family; uncertainty about the future.
  2. Stigma and discrimination – rejection by family and community, loss of job, social isolation and self-stigma, which lead to hopelessness and avoidance of treatment.
  3. Depression – the commonest psychiatric disorder in PLHIV; it may be missed because tiredness, poor appetite and weight loss are attributed to HIV.
  4. Anxiety disorders, adjustment disorders and post-traumatic stress – especially after sexual violence or other trauma.
  5. Suicidal ideas and attempts – higher risk, particularly soon after diagnosis or with advanced disease.
  6. Substance use disorders – alcohol and drug use increase risky behaviour; people who inject drugs may acquire HIV through shared needles.
  7. HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) – from mild problems of attention, memory and slowed thinking to HIV-associated dementia in advanced disease.
  8. Delirium and organic psychiatric syndromes – due to opportunistic infections of the brain (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculosis), lymphoma, metabolic problems; secondary mania and psychosis may occur.
  9. Medication-related effects – some antiretroviral drugs (for example, efavirenz) can cause vivid dreams, insomnia, anxiety, depression or psychosis; interactions between antiretroviral and psychotropic drugs; isoniazid-related psychosis.
  10. Family and social issues – care of children and orphans, discordant couples, caregiver burden, poverty and loss of income.
  11. Key populations – men who have sex with men, transgender persons, sex workers and people who inject drugs face double stigma and higher rates of distress.

Management

  • Screening for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety, alcohol and drug use, cognitive impairment and suicide risk as a routine part of HIV care.
  • Counselling and psychotherapy – supportive counselling, cognitive behaviour therapy, problem-solving and adherence counselling.
  • Medication – antidepressants with fewer drug interactions (for example, sertraline or escitalopram), antipsychotics in low doses, careful review of interactions with ART.
  • Treatment of substance use – de-addiction services and opioid substitution therapy centres for people who inject drugs.
  • Psychosocial support – peer support groups and networks of PLHIV, family counselling, social welfare schemes, legal protection against discrimination and palliative care in advanced disease.

Role of the mental health nurse

  • Non-judgemental, empathetic attitude; strict confidentiality of HIV status; respect for dignity.
  • Identify depression, suicidal ideas, substance use and cognitive decline early; refer and follow up.
  • Psychoeducation about HIV, ART, mental health and coping; encourage ART adherence and healthy living.
  • Support disclosure decisions and partner and family counselling; reduce stigma in the family and community.
  • Link with ART centres, ICTCs, OST centres, NGOs and support groups.
  • Care of cognitively impaired patients – safety, reorientation and supervision of medicines.
  • Practise standard precautions in psychiatric settings, especially with agitated patients, and care for her own stress and burnout.

Conclusion PLHIV often experience emotional distress, stigma, depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, substance use, neurocognitive disorders and drug-related psychiatric effects, while mental illness increases HIV risk and harms adherence. Integrated care with screening, counselling, appropriate medication and psychosocial support, delivered by non-judgemental nurses, improves both mental health and HIV outcomes.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain Caplan's model of preventive psychiatry, with emphasis on secondary and tertiary prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Gerald Caplan (1964), in Principles of Preventive Psychiatry, applied the public health model of prevention to mental illness and described three levels – primary, secondary and tertiary prevention.

1. Primary prevention – reducing the incidence (new cases) of mental disorders in the community.

  • Promotion of mental health – life-skills education, parenting skills, stress management, healthy lifestyle.
  • Specific protection – good antenatal and perinatal care, prevention of head injury and infections, iodine supplementation, reducing alcohol and drug use, support during crises.

2. Secondary prevention – reducing the prevalence of mental illness by shortening its duration through early case finding and prompt treatment.

  • Early case finding and screening
    • In primary care, schools, colleges, workplaces, antenatal clinics and old-age homes, using simple tools – PHQ-9 for depression, AUDIT for alcohol use, EPDS for postnatal depression, developmental screening for children and cognitive tests for the elderly.
    • Recognition of early warning signs by ASHAs, teachers and families.
  • Early intervention in psychosis – reducing the duration of untreated psychosis, which improves outcome.
  • Prompt and effective treatment – outpatient and community treatment, short admissions in general hospital psychiatric units, home treatment, Tele-MANAS and DMHP services.
  • Crisis intervention and emergency psychiatric services – suicide risk assessment, management of acute psychosis and intoxication.
  • Nursing role – screening, health education to encourage early help-seeking, crisis intervention, referral, ensuring treatment begins promptly and adherence in the early phase.

3. Tertiary prevention – reducing the disability and residual impairment caused by mental illness, preventing relapse and helping the person return to the highest possible level of functioning.

  • Relapse prevention – regular follow-up, medication adherence and depot injections, identification of early warning signs, avoidance of alcohol and drugs.
  • Psychosocial rehabilitation – social skills training, activities of daily living, cognitive remediation, vocational training, sheltered workshops and supported employment.
  • Family interventions – psychoeducation and reduction of high expressed emotion and caregiver burden.
  • Residential support – day-care centres, halfway homes, long-stay homes and supported housing.
  • Disability benefits – mental illness is a specified disability under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; certification and the Unique Disability ID (UDID) card give access to pensions, concessions and reservations.
  • Self-help groups and peer support; community integration and reduction of stigma.
  • Nursing role – follow-up home visits, relapse prevention, rehabilitation activities, family counselling and linkage with welfare schemes and NGOs.

Conclusion Caplan's model describes primary prevention to reduce new cases, secondary prevention to reduce prevalence through early detection and prompt treatment, and tertiary prevention to reduce disability through relapse prevention and rehabilitation. Nurses work at all three levels, and especially in screening, early referral, crisis intervention, follow-up and rehabilitation in the community.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the mental health services available at the primary, secondary and tertiary levels, and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
WHO pyramid of the optimal mix of mental health services WHO recommends that most mental health needs should be met at the lowest, least costly and most accessible levels, with specialist services used only when needed:

  • Self-care (base of the pyramid) – individuals and families managing their own mental health.
  • Informal community care – support from community workers, traditional healers, teachers, self-help groups and NGOs.
  • Mental health care through primary health care.
  • Psychiatric services in general hospitals and formal community mental health services.
  • Long-stay facilities and specialist psychiatric services (top of the pyramid) – needed by few and the most costly.

1. Primary level

  • Community and village – ASHAs, ANMs and multipurpose workers identify people with mental health problems, give basic support, encourage treatment and follow up patients on medication; community volunteers, self-help groups.
  • Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (sub-health centres and PHCs) – the community health officer and medical officer screen for and manage common mental disorders, epilepsy and substance use, give first aid in emergencies, continue maintenance treatment for stabilised patients and refer.
  • Outreach clinics of the DMHP and Tele-MANAS (14416) for tele-counselling.
  • Promotion and prevention – life-skills education, awareness, school and workplace programmes.

2. Secondary level

  • Community health centres and sub-district hospitals – specialist outreach clinics.
  • District hospital – the DMHP team (psychiatrist, clinical psychologist, psychiatric social worker and psychiatric nurse) provides psychiatric OPD, inpatient beds, emergency services, ECT where available, day care, counselling, targeted interventions in schools, colleges and workplaces, suicide prevention and training of primary-level staff.
  • General hospital psychiatric units – short-term inpatient care close to the family.

3. Tertiary level

  • Psychiatry departments of medical colleges, State mental hospitals (such as the Regional Mental Hospital, Nagpur) and national institutes (NIMHANS, CIP Ranchi, IHBAS Delhi, LGBRIMH Tezpur) and Centres of Excellence.
  • Specialised services – child and adolescent psychiatry, geriatric psychiatry, de-addiction, forensic psychiatry, neuropsychiatry, perinatal psychiatry and mother–baby units, treatment-resistant cases, ECT and rTMS.
  • Teaching, training and research; long-stay care for the few who need it.

Rehabilitation services (across levels) – day-care centres, halfway homes, long-stay homes, sheltered workshops, vocational training and supported employment, often run with NGOs and the Department of Social Justice.

Nurse's responsibilities

  • Primary level – case finding, home visits, follow-up, medication supervision, health education, training of ASHAs and referral.
  • Secondary level – nursing care in OPD and wards, depot clinics, counselling, family psychoeducation, crisis care, coordination of the DMHP team and record keeping.
  • Tertiary level – specialised nursing care (child, geriatric, addiction, forensic, ECT), therapeutic milieu, teaching and research.
  • At all levels – protection of rights under the MHCA, two-way referral, continuity of care, rehabilitation and stigma reduction.

Conclusion Following the WHO pyramid, mental health services in India range from self-care and community support, through primary care at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, secondary care through the DMHP at district hospitals, to tertiary care in medical colleges, mental hospitals and national institutes, supported by rehabilitation services. Nurses provide care, follow-up, education, referral and rehabilitation at every level.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the mental health issues of women and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Women experience depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress about twice as often as men, and in India housewives form the largest group among women who die by suicide (NCRB). Biological factors, social disadvantages and violence together make women's mental health a priority in community mental health nursing.

Risk factors

  • Biological – hormonal changes across the reproductive life cycle (menstruation, pregnancy, postpartum period, menopause).
  • Social – gender discrimination, low education and income, early marriage, dowry harassment, pressure for a male child, infertility, lack of decision-making power, multiple roles (household, work and childcare) and the burden of caring for sick family members.
  • Violence – domestic violence, sexual violence, harassment and trafficking.
  • Life events – widowhood, divorce, migration of the husband, loss of children, poverty in old age.

Common mental health problems across the life cycle

  1. Adolescence – depression, anxiety, eating disorders, self-harm, effects of bullying and abuse.
  2. Reproductive years
    • Premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
    • Perinatal mental disorders – postpartum blues, postnatal depression and postpartum psychosis, and anxiety in pregnancy.
    • Psychological effects of pregnancy loss, stillbirth, infertility and unwanted pregnancy.
    • Common mental disorders (depression, anxiety, somatic complaints) related to marital conflict and stress.
  3. Midlife – depression and anxiety during perimenopause, the "empty nest" and caregiving stress.
  4. Old age – loneliness, widowhood, dementia (more women than men live with dementia because women live longer).

Mental health effects of violence – depression, PTSD, anxiety, sleep disorders, substance use, self-harm and suicide; children who witness violence are also affected.

Special issues of women with severe mental illness – vulnerability to sexual exploitation and homelessness; contraception and pregnancy planning; safe choice of psychotropic drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding (for example, avoiding valproate in women who may become pregnant); mother–baby units; under the MHCA 2017, a child below three years should ordinarily not be separated from a mother receiving inpatient care.

Services – Tele-MANAS (14416), DMHP, perinatal mental health screening in antenatal and postnatal clinics, One Stop Centres (Sakhi), Women Helpline 181, the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, NGOs and self-help groups.

Role of the nurse

  • Screening – depression and anxiety (PHQ-9), postnatal depression (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) and suicide risk during antenatal, postnatal and family planning contacts.
  • Asking about violence privately and sensitively, believing the woman, documenting, safety planning and referral to One Stop Centres, police or legal aid with her consent.
  • Counselling and supportive psychotherapy; stress management; empowerment and assertiveness.
  • Gender-sensitive care – privacy, female staff for examinations, protection from abuse in wards.
  • Psychoeducation of the woman and family; reducing stigma; involving the husband and family in care.
  • Linkage with self-help groups, livelihood schemes, women's organisations and welfare schemes.

Conclusion Women's mental health is shaped by biological changes across the reproductive life cycle, social disadvantage and violence, leading to higher rates of depression, anxiety and PTSD. Nurses, who meet women at every stage of life, can screen, counsel, ensure safety, provide gender-sensitive care and link women with services and support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the common psychiatric problems of old age and the role of the nurse in geriatric mental health care.
answer_html:
Introduction India's elderly population (60 years and above) is growing rapidly. Old age brings physical illness, loss of roles and relationships, and dependence, and many older persons develop mental health problems that are often missed or dismissed as "normal ageing".

Common mental health problems

  1. Depression – the commonest; it often presents with physical complaints, poor sleep, loss of appetite, memory complaints or irritability rather than sadness ("masked depression"); it may resemble dementia (pseudodementia).
  2. Suicide – older men who are depressed, physically ill, living alone or recently bereaved are at high risk, and attempts are more often fatal.
  3. Anxiety disorders – generalised anxiety, fear of falling, health anxiety.
  4. Dementia and delirium – common and frequently co-existing (see the unit on organic brain disorders).
  5. Late-onset psychosis – paranoid ideas, often associated with hearing or visual loss and social isolation.
  6. Substance misuse – alcohol, tobacco and dependence on sleeping pills (benzodiazepines), which cause falls and confusion.
  7. Sleep disorders, bereavement and complicated grief, and adjustment problems after retirement or migration of children.
  8. Elder abuse and neglect – causing depression, anxiety and fear.

Risk factors – chronic physical illness and pain, disability, sensory loss, polypharmacy, loss of spouse and friends, loneliness, financial dependence, family conflict and caregiving responsibilities.

Assessment

  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment – physical, mental, functional (activities of daily living) and social.
  • Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), cognitive screening (MMSE or Hindi Mental State Examination), Confusion Assessment Method for delirium, suicide risk assessment.
  • Medication review and investigations to exclude physical causes (thyroid, vitamin B12, electrolytes).

Principles of treatment

  • "Start low, go slow" with medicines – older people are more sensitive to side effects; SSRIs (such as sertraline or escitalopram) are preferred for depression; anticholinergic drugs and benzodiazepines are avoided.
  • ECT is safe and effective for severe depression in the elderly.
  • Psychotherapy – supportive, problem-solving, reminiscence and cognitive behaviour therapy.
  • Social interventions – day-care centres, senior citizens' clubs, recreational activities, family support.

Services – geriatric psychiatry units and memory clinics, geriatric clinics under the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly, DMHP and Tele-MANAS, Elderline (14567), old-age homes, NGOs such as HelpAge India and ARDSI.

Role of the nurse

  • Early identification of depression, cognitive decline, substance misuse and suicide risk during home visits, NCD clinics and hospital care.
  • Supervise medicines, watch for side effects, falls and drug interactions; simplify regimens.
  • Promote activity and social contact – encourage hobbies, prayer, exercise, senior citizens' groups and contact with grandchildren and friends.
  • Counselling for bereavement, retirement and loneliness; reminiscence sessions.
  • Support caregivers – education, respite and support groups; watch for elder abuse.
  • Safety – fall prevention, home safety, supervision of patients with cognitive impairment.
  • Linkage with geriatric services, pensions and welfare schemes.

Conclusion The elderly commonly suffer from depression, suicide risk, anxiety, dementia, delirium, late-onset psychosis and substance misuse, often presenting atypically. Careful assessment, cautious treatment, social support and community services improve their mental health, and the nurse's role in early detection, medication supervision, counselling, caregiver support and linkage is central.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: What is a halfway home?
answer_html:
A halfway home is a transitional residential facility for persons who are recovering from mental illness and are ready to leave hospital but not yet able to live independently – it is "halfway" between hospital and community.

  • Residents live under supervision for a limited period, take part in daily living and social skills training, medication self-management, vocational training and work, and gradually return to family or independent living.
  • It prevents institutionalisation, reduces relapse and supports deinstitutionalisation; the MHCA 2017 requires the Government to provide halfway homes and supported accommodation.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: What is a day hospital (partial hospitalisation)?
answer_html:
• A day hospital provides structured psychiatric treatment during the day – medication, occupational therapy, group therapy, psychoeducation and skills training – while the patient returns home in the evening.
  • It is used as an alternative to full admission for patients who need intensive care but have family support, or as step-down care after discharge.
  • Advantages – lower cost, less stigma, preservation of family and social ties, and early return to normal life. A night hospital works the other way – patients work by day and stay in hospital at night.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: What is assertive community treatment (ACT)?
answer_html:
• Assertive community treatment (ACT) is an intensive, community-based model of care developed by Stein and Test in Madison, USA (1970s) for persons with severe mental illness who relapse frequently ("revolving door" patients).
  • A multidisciplinary team (psychiatrist, nurses, social workers, vocational specialists) with a small caseload (about 10 clients per staff member) provides treatment, rehabilitation and support in the patient's home and community, is available round the clock and actively reaches out to patients rather than waiting for them to attend.
  • It reduces hospital admissions and improves housing stability and functioning.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: Write the salient features of the National Mental Health Policy, 2014.
answer_html:
• India's first National Mental Health Policy, titled "New Pathways, New Hope", was released on 10 October 2014.
  • Vision – to promote mental health, prevent mental illness, enable recovery, promote destigmatisation and desegregation, and ensure socio-economic inclusion of persons affected by mental illness by providing accessible, affordable and quality health and social care throughout the life-span, within a rights-based framework.
  • Key areas – effective governance and accountability, promotion of mental health, prevention of mental disorders and suicide, universal access to mental health services, increased human resources, community participation, research, and monitoring and evaluation.

subject: Mental Health Nursing II
unit_title: Community Mental Health Nursing
question: What is mhGAP?
answer_html:
• The Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) was launched by WHO in 2008 to scale up services for mental, neurological and substance use disorders, especially in low- and middle-income countries where the treatment gap is large.
  • Its mhGAP Intervention Guide helps non-specialist health workers (doctors, nurses and community health workers in primary care) to assess and manage priority conditions – depression, psychoses, epilepsy, child and adolescent mental and behavioural disorders, dementia, disorders due to substance use, self-harm and suicide, and other significant mental health complaints – through task sharing.
